title: Regulation and Firms: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University - Department of Agricultural and Applied Economics and

detail.title: Regulation and Firms: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: This paper examines how local regulatory reform shapes firm dynamics in a large developing economy. We study Brazil's Lei da Liberdade Econômica (LLE, Economic Freedom Law), a 2019 federal reform that authorized municipalities to exempt "low-risk" businesses from licensing requirements. We leverage the staggered adoption by municipalities as a unique setting to evaluate how changes in the regulatory environment influence local economic activity. Using an entropy-balanced stacked difference-indifferences framework, we find that LLE adoption increased firm openings and economic activity. The evidence is consistent with the creation of new economic activity rather than pure reallocation or formalization, though both are contributing factors. We further exploit administrative records covering the universe of applications to open a firm (approximately 4.8 million records), finding that reduced time costs is a key mechanism behind the main results.

title: Implementation Challenges and Opportunities of AI Technologies in the Gas Industry
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Implementation Challenges and Opportunities of AI Technologies in the Gas Industry

keywords: of Petroleum and Gas Engineering Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract:
The gas industry is undergoing a significant digital transformation driven by the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies. AI has emerged as a powerful tool for improving operational efficiency, enhancing safety, optimizing asset performance, and supporting data-driven decision-making across various stages of gas exploration, production, transportation, storage, and distribution. Technologies such as Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Natural Language Processing (NLP), predictive analytics, and intelligent automation are increasingly being integrated into gas industry operations to address complex challenges associated with infrastructure management, demand forecasting, predictive maintenance, leak detection, and supply chain optimization. The adoption of AI enables organizations to analyze large volumes of operational data, identify hidden patterns, predict equipment failures, and improve overall operational reliability. 

Despite its considerable benefits, the implementation of AI technologies in the gas industry presents several challenges. Key obstacles include poor data quality, limited data availability, integration difficulties with legacy systems, high implementation and maintenance costs, cybersecurity concerns, regulatory compliance requirements, and a shortage of skilled professionals capable of developing and managing AI solutions. Additionally, issues related to model transparency, explainability, and ethical considerations continue to affect stakeholder trust and large-scale adoption. Organizations must also overcome resistance to organizational change and ensure that AI systems align with industry safety standards and operational requirements. 

At the same time, numerous opportunities exist for expanding AI applications within the gas sector. Advances in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), cloud computing, edge computing, digital twins, and autonomous operational systems are creating new possibilities for intelligent asset management, real-time monitoring, predictive decision-making, and sustainable energy operations. AI-driven innovations can help reduce operational costs, improve environmental performance, enhance infrastructure reliability, and support the development of smart gas networks. As digital transformation accelerates, AI is expected to play an increasingly important role in enabling safer, more efficient, and more resilient gas industry operations. This study examines the major implementation challenges and opportunities associated with AI technologies in the gas industry and provides insights into future research directions and strategic adoption frameworks for achieving sustainable technological advancement.

title: AI Regulation: A Comparison of Centralized and Decentralized Approaches in Federal Systems
affiliations: and University of Ljubljana School of Economics and Business

detail.title: AI Regulation: A Comparison of Centralized and Decentralized Approaches in Federal Systems
detail.abstract:
The regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) is at the forefront of legal scholarship, as its use has the potential to change nearly every aspect of human society. The potential for AI to impact society makes its regulation particularly relevant to legal scholars, practitioners, and lawmakers.

This research considers the benefits of centralization and decentralization in regulating AI and the implications of convergence or divergence in AI regulation within a federal system. We examine the United States (US) and European Union (EU) approaches to regulation of AI and show that there is a distinct difference in risk preferences related to the regulation of AI between the EU and US as well as a higher likelihood of negative externalities related to the regulation of AI emerging in the US than in the EU while also recognizing that the US approach of decentralized regulation of AI is more likely to lead to the identification of novel approaches to the regulation of AI which may eventually lead to positive externalities. Thus, we generally consider that each approach is not risk-neutral, though for very different reasons.

This examination focuses on the costs and benefits of centralization and decentralization within federal systems, i.e., systems in which regulatory competencies are divided between the federal and state levels. The US and EU provide useful examples of how federal approaches to regulating AI diverge. A quick look at the regulation of AI in the EU and the US shows a divergence in approaches to the regulation of AI within borders, between states inside federal systems (within the US), and across borders between different federal systems (EU and US).

title: Big Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence for Enhanced Gas Supply Chain Management
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Big Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence for Enhanced Gas Supply Chain Management

keywords: of Energy Engineering and Digital Technologies Big Data Analytics

detail.abstract:
The gas supply chain plays a critical role in ensuring the efficient production, transportation, storage, and distribution of natural gas to industrial, commercial, and residential consumers. However, increasing market volatility, fluctuating demand patterns, operational complexities, infrastructure constraints, and environmental concerns present significant challenges to effective supply chain management. In recent years, the integration of Big Data Analytics (BDA) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative approach for enhancing decision-making, operational efficiency, and strategic planning across the gas supply chain. These technologies enable organizations to collect, process, and analyze vast volumes of structured and unstructured data generated from sensors, Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices, Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, enterprise platforms, and market sources. 

This study examines the application of Big Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence in improving gas supply chain management. The research explores how advanced analytical techniques and AI-driven models support demand forecasting, inventory optimization, production planning, transportation management, predictive maintenance, risk assessment, and real-time operational monitoring. Machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, predictive analytics, and intelligent decision-support systems are increasingly utilized to identify patterns, forecast market trends, optimize resource allocation, and improve supply chain resilience. Furthermore, Big Data Analytics enhances data-driven decision-making by enabling organizations to extract valuable insights from large and complex datasets, thereby improving operational visibility and strategic responsiveness. 

The study highlights the key benefits of integrating Big Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence within gas supply chains, including improved operational efficiency, reduced costs, enhanced asset utilization, better demand forecasting accuracy, increased supply chain flexibility, and strengthened risk management capabilities. Additionally, these technologies contribute to sustainability objectives through optimized resource consumption, reduced emissions, and improved environmental compliance. Despite these advantages, challenges such as data quality issues, cybersecurity risks, integration complexities, high implementation costs, and workforce skill gaps continue to affect adoption and implementation efforts.

 The findings indicate that the convergence of Big Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence has significant potential to transform traditional gas supply chain operations into intelligent, data-driven ecosystems capable of achieving higher levels of efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. Future developments in explainable AI, digital twin technologies, edge computing, and autonomous supply chain systems are expected to further enhance the capabilities of intelligent gas supply chain management and support the ongoing digital transformation of the energy sector.

title:
Auditing AI Together: 
A Distributed Human-Auditor Study of Brand Convergence and Citation Structure in Google AI Mode
affiliations: Universitas Prasetiya Mulya

detail.title:
Auditing AI Together: 
A Distributed Human-Auditor Study of Brand Convergence and Citation Structure in Google AI Mode

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. The author has no personal, financial, or organizational relationships that could have influenced the design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, or reporting of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted as independent doctoral research. It audited a publicly accessible generative search system and did not involve experimental manipulation of human subjects, sensitive personal data, or the collection of personally identifiable information. The auditors participated voluntarily as collaborating data collectors following a shared protocol; no personal data about auditors beyond their general region were recorded or analyzed. The study complies with general ethical principles for non-invasive algorithm audit research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
Generative search engines are reshaping how consumers encounter brands, yet most algorithm audits of
these systems rely on a single operator or automated API queries — designs that cannot observe how real,
geographically dispersed users experience AI-mediated answers. This study introduces a distributed
human-auditor design: 32 vocational-school teachers across six Indonesian islands independently queried
Google AI Mode using a shared protocol of 16 category prompts spanning 13 property categories and 109
brands, under incognito, single-run conditions. The audit produced 512 prompt-level observations and
2,104 classified citations, allowing the study to examine both which brands the system surfaces and which
sources it cites.
Two patterns emerge. First, cross-auditor agreement on the set of brands surfaced was geographically flat:
a mean pairwise Jaccard convergence index of 0.48, with between-region agreement (Java–Sumatra, 0.48)
statistically indistinguishable from within-region agreement (0.47); a permutation test on the difference was
non-significant (p = 0.76). Unlike the geographic personalization documented for conventional web search
(Hannak et al., 2013), the generative layer appears to suppress geographic personalization for national-
category queries. Agreement was concentrated in a stable core of large national brands, which appeared for
97% of auditors, while disagreement was confined to a tail of less prominent names. Convergence tracked
market maturity, rising in consolidated categories (exterior paint and ceramics, 0.61) and falling in
fragmented ones (mortgage simulation, 0.32). Second, the citation base was earned-led but balanced (48.9%
earned, 22.9% owned, 7.7% social, 20.5% marketplace/platform) and inclusive rather than oligopolistic,
with a 52.2% long tail and a single top domain accounting for only 5.9% of all citations. Notably, listing
and transactional platforms — property portals and e-commerce — supplied roughly one in five citations,
a channel largely invisible in Western source taxonomies.
The paper contributes a replicable crowdsourced algorithm-audit method built on human auditors rather
than automated queries, a PESO-adapted source taxonomy with a Marketplace category suited to Southeast
Asian digital ecosystems (the MOSE framework), and a deliberately bounded reading of the evidence. The
findings are framed as a May 2026 single-engine snapshot rather than a causal test or a stability
measurement, and the convergence index is presented as a consensus measure parallel to — not a numerical
replication of — prior personalization research. The study positions these results within the emerging
practitioner agenda of AI Visibility Optimization (AIVO).

title: Prescribing Sustainability: How ESG Shapes Physicians' Drug Choices and Pharmaceutical Pricing?
affiliations: and Syracuse University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Prescribing Sustainability: How ESG Shapes Physicians' Drug Choices and Pharmaceutical Pricing?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable (this study uses de-identified secondary data).
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Whitman Roadmap Grant.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: This study examines how ESG incidents propagate through pharmaceutical supply chains by shaping downstream physicians' prescribing decisions and firms' pricing strategies. Methodology/results: Using granular claim-level prescription data, we show that physicians prescribe fewer brand-name drugs from firms implicated in negative ESG incidents, accompanied by a notable decline in unit prices. Controlling for physician-and product-level heterogeneity, we estimate a 9% reduction in daily dispensed quantities and a 21% decrease in unit prices at the time of ESG incidents. These effects are absent for generic drugs, for which physicians rarely specify the manufacturer. The decline in brand-name prescriptions appears to be driven by heightened product-quality concerns and is more pronounced in counties with higher ESG awareness-proxied by higher levels of education, income, and Democratic voting shares. Share-of-Wallet analyses among close substitutes provide direct evidence that physicians shift away from affected firms, reducing brand stickiness. Managerial implications: This study identifies physicians as an important but overlooked ESG-responsive stakeholder group and extends the literature on sustainability, corporate social irresponsibility, and healthcare supply chains. By linking upstream ESG incidents to downstream prescribing decisions and firms' pricing responses, our findings show that broader ESG externalities, beyond functional product failures, can fundamentally reshape professional decision-making and market outcomes, even in healthcare settings where clinical utility is the overriding mandate. Managers and decision makers should recognize that ESG failures can affect clinical-market demand, brand loyalty, and pricing power, and supply chain resilience; pharmaceutical firms therefore need to treat ESG performance as a strategic capability, not merely a compliance or reputational concern.

title: Beyond Linear Models: Decoding Industrial Market Volatility Using Fourier Frequency Analysis and Stochastic Jump-Diffusion (Volume I)

detail.abstract: Traditional forecasting models in asset-heavy industries-such as aerospace components, heavy forging, and specialized manufacturing-rely fundamentally on linear regressions and basic moving averages. While mathematically sound under stable economic steady-states, these methodologies systematically break down when subjected to macroeconomic volatility and asymmetric supply chain disruptions. They operate under the flawed assumption of absolute market rationality, treating nonlinear anomalies and human panic as stochastic "noise," thereby smoothing out the vital underlying harmonic signals that precede structural market shifts. This paper presents the first phase of a comprehensive industrial intelligence architecture. By abandoning pure time-domain analysis, we establish a hybrid mathematical framework. We first deploy Fourier Frequency Analysis to map the deterministic, rational cyclicality of the market. Subsequently, we model the non-cyclical, behavioral irrationality of the supply chain utilizing Stochastic Differential Equations (Jump-Diffusion Models) inspired by Robert Shiller's theories of excess market volatility. By integrating these vectors into a modified Generalized Additive Model (GAM), empirical back-testing demonstrates a reduction in forecasting error (MAPE) from 18.4% to 6.1%, achieving a 94.1% directional accuracy during severe structural shocks. Disclaimer: The empirical validations, financial figures, and market datasets utilized in this paper are derived from publicly available, indexed, and non-indexed macroeconomic industry data, augmented with mathematical simulations for academic purposes. They strictly do not reflect, utilize, or represent the confidential financial metrics, historical records, client data, or proprietary operational information of any specific corporation or the author's employer.

title: Accountable Pseudonymity: Identity Regimes as Organisational Design
affiliations: Alfaisal University and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University)

detail.title: Accountable Pseudonymity: Identity Regimes as Organisational Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual article and does not report a study involving human participants, patient data, or case-study consent.
declarations.funderStatement: No specific funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: In organisational design, identity has usually been treated as a settled administrative fact. However, classic work on anonymity and privacy has argued it is better understood as a set of relations spanning what may be known about someone, who may know it, whether their actions can be linked over time, and what happens if something goes wrong. We call a particular arrangement of these relations an identity regime. Most organisations inherit an identity regime by default, but digital organisations can design one to suit their purposes and stakeholders. We characterise identity regimes through five functions: human verification, shielding, continuity, provenance, and a reviewable sanction path. Extending prior work on accountable pseudonyms, we develop accountable pseudonymity as one configuration of these functions: persistent, verified, provenance-bearing identities that remain shielded from universal exposure but reviewable under defined conditions. We illustrate the utility of accountable pseudonymity through a discussion of two current organisational settings with imperfect identity regimes - scholarly peer review, where the regime is inherited but misallocated, and decentralised autonomous organisations (DAOs) where it is more intentionally designed but incomplete. We also discuss the framework's relevance to settings beyond these two cases. We argue identity regimes have been an understudied organisational design variable, but one of growing importance for digital organisations as AI capabilities lower the cost of civil identity exposure and enable synthetic agents to execute organisational and economic tasks.

title: A Simulation Study of Frontal Symmetrical Multiple-Blade Deflector for Aerodynamic Drag Reduction in Heavy-Duty Vehicles

detail.title: A Simulation Study of Frontal Symmetrical Multiple-Blade Deflector for Aerodynamic Drag Reduction in Heavy-Duty Vehicles

The author confirms that the research was conducted objectively and that the commercial interests did not influence the integrity of the data or the results presented.

detail.abstract: Aerodynamic drag is the primary resistance factor affecting the fuel consumption of high-profile heavy-duty vehicles. This study introduces a novel frontal symmetrical multiple-blade deflector (subject of U.S. Provisional Patent App. No. 64/065,199, titled 'Fuel Saving Front Wind Deflector') [1] designed to mitigate longitudinal drag force (, measured in Newtons [N] along the primary flow axis). Using CFD with the k-ω SST-SAS turbulence model, the system was evaluated at 50 mph (80.5 km/h) and 75 mph (120.7 km/h). A key factor is that the deflector’s efficacy is inherently linked to the specific geometry of the vehicle's front face, for this research; accordingly, the numerical model utilized, directly reflects a European flat-face (Cab-Over-Engine) architecture, which traditionally experiences severe frontal pressure stagnation. The results demonstrate significant net force reduction of 13.00% and 11.76% respectively. These calculations account for the total system impact, including forces on both the vehicle front and the deflector blades. Translating this aerodynamic efficiency to a standard European logistics profile reveals an estimated annual fuel savings of 5.85% to 6.50%, leading to significant cost overhead reductions and lower carbon emissions. As a pre-optimized design with a 40° angle of attack covering 48.9% of the frontal surface, this technology establishes a verifiable foundation for improving logistics fuel economy across diverse global vehicle architectures, furthermore, the implementation of this system allows for the simplification of vehicle manufacturing by providing a modular aerodynamic solution.

detail.abstract: In Volume I of this series, we established that traditional linear forecasting fails in volatile, asset-heavy industrial markets, and demonstrated how a hybrid framework of Fourier Frequency Analysis and Stochastic Jump-Diffusion can isolate structural demand harmonics to achieve 94.1% directional accuracy. However, predicting a market shift is only half the operational equation. The ultimate goal of an industrial enterprise is not merely to know what will happen, but to compute exactly what to do about it. This paper presents the second half of the advanced intelligence architecture: The Prescriptive Optimization Engine. By transitioning from predictive market forecasts to mathematical metaheuristic optimization, we provide a formal framework to dynamically align production schedules, human capital, and inventory buffers against highly volatile demand curves. To tackle the NP-Hard combinatorial explosion inherent in multi-facility planning, we deploy and evaluate a suite of bio-inspired metaheuristics: Genetic Algorithms (GA), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and Simulated Annealing (SA). This methodology bypasses the computational bottlenecks of classical linear programming, dynamically reducing Total Cost of Operations (TCO) by up to 15% while maintaining a 98.5% service level during severe macroeconomic fluctuations. Disclaimer: The empirical validations, financial figures, and market datasets utilized in this paper are derived from publicly available, indexed, and non-indexed macroeconomic industry data, augmented with mathematical simulations for academic purposes.

title: A Comparative Study of Numerical Methods for European Option Pricing
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Comparative Study of Numerical Methods for European Option Pricing
detail.abstract: Option pricing accuracy is paramount for effective risk management and derivative trading. This paper investigates the efficacy of seven distinct option pricing methods benchmarked against a live dataset of 200 SPY options collected in June 2026. The evaluated methods span classical frameworks (Black-Scholes, CRR binomial trees, Monte Carlo with variance reduction), stochastic volatility (the Heston model with per-option Nelder-Mead calibration), and modern deep learning architectures (MLP trained on log-moneyness, LSTM-BS hybrid, and a Variational Autoencoder for implied volatility surfaces). Results indicate that the dynamically calibrated Heston model achieves the highest precision with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.141 (95% CI: [0.11, 0.17]), accurately pricing 65% of options within 5% of market midprices. The LSTM-BS hybrid achieves a competitive MAE of 0.448, outperforming constantvolatility baselines by incorporating dynamic volatility forecasts. These findings demonstrate that while deep learning provides computational and forecasting advantages, stochastic volatility models remain the optimal framework for pricing smile-consistent options, and Monte Carlo frameworks retain definitive superiority for path-dependent derivatives.

title: The Architecture of Surrender: Re-framing Voluntary Agency Delegation as a Trust Engine in Modern Firms

detail.title: The Architecture of Surrender: Re-framing Voluntary Agency Delegation as a Trust Engine in Modern Firms
detail.abstract: Modern corporate structures with flat hierarchies, matrix management, and consensus-driven decision-making introduce systemic ambiguity, elevate internal transaction costs, and impose severe cognitive loads on personnel. We propose an alternative organizational framework: Structured Agency Exchange (SAE). By translating the operational protocols of High-Reliability Organizations (HROs), including aviation Crew Resource Management (CRM), emergency medicine timeouts, and military command structures, into organizational science, SAE frames authority as a mutually negotiated contract of voluntary agency delegation. Under SAE, subordinates yield strategic decision-making autonomy in exchange for absolute role clarity, protection from cognitive load, and psychological safety. Conversely, leadership becomes a service role defined by an absolute duty of care and fiduciary accountability. We integrate Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller 1988), Servant Leadership (Greenleaf 1977), Relational Governance (Williamson 1985), and Psychological Safety (Edmondson 1999) to establish a theoretical mapping, model transaction cost shifts, and present a practical implementation protocol (including corporate stop-action commands and explicit boundary contracts) for high-reliability organizations and modern firms.

title: Systemic Liquidity Bottlenecks and Monetary Policy Transmission to Real-Sector Credit

detail.title: Systemic Liquidity Bottlenecks and Monetary Policy Transmission to Real-Sector Credit
detail.abstract:
This article develops a liquidity-centered version of the Institutional Conversion Gap for the analysis of monetary policy transmission in emerging markets. The paper argues that monetary policy reaches the real economy only when liquidity is converted across a chain of interdependent segments: foreign-exchange liquidity, money-market circulation, sovereign and collateral-market conditions, and bank balance-sheet conversion into credit. The framework is named the Liquidity-to-Credit Transmission Index, or ILTC, and is presented as a focused ICG-LTC application. It does not treat liquidity as a single stock, a generic banking ratio or a central-bank balance-sheet item. It treats liquidity as a conversion process. A policy decision can lower or raise a policy rate, but the real economy feels the decision only when external liquidity is available, domestic liquidity circulates among intermediaries, sovereign securities do not absorb excessive balance-sheet space, and banks are willing and able to transform funding into productive credit.

The paper combines a conceptual model, a mathematical scoring architecture and a compact real-data calibration for six emerging economies: Brazil, India, Indonesia, Mexico, South Africa and Turkiye. The empirical demonstration uses public indicators from the World Bank World Development Indicators and IMF DataMapper: total reserves in months of imports, broad money relative to GDP, broad money growth, bank credit to the private sector relative to GDP, non-performing loan ratios and general government gross debt relative to GDP. These variables are not treated as a definitive country ranking. They are used to show how the model behaves when real cross-country data are inserted into the liquidity-to-credit conversion chain. Indicator values are oriented as benefit, cost or bounded-optimum variables, normalized on a 0-100 scale and aggregated using a bottleneck-sensitive Constant Elasticity of Substitution function.

The results show that the same monetary transmission problem can arise from very different bottlenecks. Brazil displays strong FX reserves and domestic liquidity depth but a low sovereign-room score under the selected debt-based proxy. Indonesia and Mexico show weaker credit-depth scores, with Mexico also constrained by lower import-cover reserves. South Africa is characterized by a more balanced but still below-frontier profile, while Turkiye shows a strong sovereign-room proxy but a very weak money-market score under the broad-money-growth bounded optimum because monetary expansion is extreme relative to a stability corridor. The central methodological finding is that arithmetic averages can conceal these weaknesses, whereas negative-CES aggregation preserves bottleneck information. The contribution is therefore both analytical and operational: ILTC offers a disciplined way to ask which liquidity segment contributes to, or blocks, the transmission of monetary policy to real-sector credit.

title: When One Fiscal Failure Becomes a Thousand Local Crises: Portable Fiscal Infrastructure for Municipal Resilience in Fragile and At-Risk States

detail.title: When One Fiscal Failure Becomes a Thousand Local Crises: Portable Fiscal Infrastructure for Municipal Resilience in Fragile and At-Risk States
detail.abstract:
In fiscally centralized fragile states, central government failure does not stay central. When transfers halt, fuel procurement stalls, and payroll collapses, every downstream municipality loses its operating budget simultaneously. The result is not a fiscal problem alone but an operating failure: drains go uncleared, pumps stop, lights fail, and residents absorb the cost through expensive private substitutes. This paper argues that the cascade from central shock to local service collapse is a structural prediction in contexts where subnational governments collect less than 5 percent of total public revenue and hold no independent fiscal machinery to absorb shocks.

Portable Fiscal Infrastructure (PFI) proposes a shared, open-source digital public infrastructure for municipal finance that reduces the per-municipality startup cost of building a lawful revenue-service cycle. Drawing on evidence from Somaliland, Tanzania, Liberia, and Kananga, and using Socotra and Aden as framing cases, the paper develops a four-layer architecture, a deployment screen with explicit non-deployment rules, a taxpayer participation mechanism tied to tax registration credentials, and a performance-based financing model. The paper argues that preventive deployment, before central failure becomes acute, offers the strongest case for building local fiscal resilience.

The concept-stage financing envelope is USD 3–10 million over 36 months for a pilot cohort of 6–10 screened municipalities across 3–5 countries. The paper treats refusal to deploy as a valid and necessary output.

title: From Incidents to Patterns: A Precautionary Framework for Identifying Asymmetric Coparenting Conflict
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Incidents to Patterns: A Precautionary Framework for Identifying Asymmetric Coparenting Conflict
detail.abstract:
Practitioners working in family law and coparenting contexts routinely face the challenge of distinguishing asymmetric coparenting conflict from the reciprocal conflict common to high-conflict separation. In many cases, significant harm accumulates long before the underlying behavioral pattern becomes clearly observable. Existing approaches to assessment, which tend to evaluate incidents in isolation and respond reactively to conflict as it arises, are poorly suited to early recognition of this distinct and directional pattern.


This paper proposes a precautionary, pattern-based framework for identifying asymmetric coparenting conflict before its consequences become unmistakable. Building on Stark's reconceptualization of domestic abuse as a pattern of coercive control, Hardesty et al.'s extension of that framework into the post-separation coparenting context, and Crossman et al.'s demonstration that coercive control frequently persists after separation, the framework addresses a gap the existing literature leaves open: how practitioners can begin to recognize asymmetric behavioral patterns early enough to make a meaningful difference.


The paper advances three related propositions. First, identification of asymmetric coparenting conflict should be precautionary rather than reactive. Second, reliable identification depends on recurring behavioral patterns observed across time, domains, and contexts rather than isolated incidents. Third, increasing structure in the coparenting relationship serves both intervention and assessment purposes by making persistent behavioral patterns more legible.


The framework is conceptual rather than empirical. Its purpose is to improve the quality of professional observation, and through that, the reliability of professional judgment, under conditions of uncertainty.

title: Benchmark Indices of Market-Implied Event Probabilities: Construction, Valuation, and Governance of the Belief Index Family

detail.title: Benchmark Indices of Market-Implied Event Probabilities: Construction, Valuation, and Governance of the Belief Index Family

detail.abstract: The event exposures that increasingly drive portfolio outcomes-elections, geopolitical escalation, regulatory and policy decisions-largely lack quotable instruments. Prediction markets price these events as binary contracts, but the signal is fragmented across hundreds of expiring order books: informative contract by contract, unusable as a benchmark. This paper documents the methodology of the Belief Index family: rules-based, thematically defined indices of market-implied event probabilities, published as informational, theoretical benchmark series. Constituents pass published eligibility and judgment screens and are weighted by the geometric mean of order book depth and trading volume, subject to a 50% concentration cap and a 1% admission floor. Each series is valued at half-hourly windows as the weighted average of constituent bid-ask midpoints. The published level-rebased to 100 at inception and chain-linked across composition changes-measures relative change in aggregate implied probability; it is not itself a probability, and it is not an executable price. Methodology revisions are versioned and prospective-only, published values are never silently restated, and data-quality flags travel with every observation. We describe the 13 live series (53,629 half-hourly observations since January 2026), verify at a July 2026 snapshot that each series' published level reproduces exactly from its published constituent record, and trace a production reconstitution event end to end. Because venue order books are not systematically archived, this point-in-time record cannot be rebuilt later; it is available free of charge for non-commercial academic research.

title: Digital Footprints Before Financial Statements: A Macroprudential Nowcasting Framework for Early Credit Risk Detection
affiliations: Central Bank of Armenia

detail.title: Digital Footprints Before Financial Statements: A Macroprudential Nowcasting Framework for Early Credit Risk Detection
detail.abstract: Official bank statistics arrive too slowly to warn policymakers before credit stress builds up, especially in small economies like Malta. This paper shows that everyday Google searches around banking, payments, and job security reveal rising loan distress in near real time, ahead of official data. A synthetic comparison economy built from similar Eurozone peers also uncovers a puzzling gap in Malta's loan quality after 2022, tied to rising interest rates and lingering pandemic effects, offering regulators a practical early-warning tool.

detail.abstract: On March 25, 2026, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google liable on the theory that platform design — not content — contributed to a user's psychological harm, sidestepping Section 230 by targeting architecture rather than speech. This paper traces that reasoning across five domains — consumer goods, firearms, language models, public administration, and the workplace ,showing that "negligent design causing foreseeable harm" recognizes no natural stopping point at social media, and extends, if applied consistently, to any industry built on behavioral design.Drawing on comparative U.S. and EU case law (Anderson v. TikTok, Smith & Wesson v. Mexico, Twitter v. Taamneh, Raine v. OpenAI) and regulatory instruments (the EU AI Act, Digital Services Act, and the withdrawn AI Liability Directive), the paper argues that the boundary between industries subject to liability and those statutorily exempted reflects historical lobbying outcomes rather than coherent legal principle.The paper closes with a philosophical clarification: expanding regulation does not require denying human freedom. A radical determinism would be self-refuting and would undermine the very critique advanced here. The defensible position instead treats freedom as a capacity — one that design can weaken and that structure, education, and regulation can strengthen.

title: Closing the Regenerative Deployment Gap: Demand-Anchored Bankability for Emerging Regenerative Capital Markets

detail.title: Closing the Regenerative Deployment Gap: Demand-Anchored Bankability for Emerging Regenerative Capital Markets
detail.abstract: Southeast Asia does not lack capital for its green and regenerative transition; it lacks the instruments that convert capital into deployed, bankable projects on the ground. This paper distinguishes the widely cited sustainable-development financing gap from a more precise and more tractable problem I term the deployment gap: the structural distance between announced capital and contracted, investible demand. I argue that beneath the deployment gap lies a capital-structure mismatch that no amount of mobilisation resolves-commercial banks underwrite short horizons against conventional collateral, the patient and venture capital suited to long-horizon regenerative builds is scarce and expensive, and between them sits a missing middle in which even contracted regenerative demand has no bankable home. Drawing on development-finance scholarship, ecosystem-services and blue-carbon literature, common-pool-resource governance theory, and the recent regional evidence base, I propose that the instrument capable of closing this gap is a demand-anchored regenerative offtake-a multi-capital, community-counterparty contract governed by a mutual rulebook and verified through digital impact measurement-and that, once verified and standardised, such contracts can be structured as convertible, bankable notes: the seed of a distinct asset class in which contracted, verified regenerative demand furnishes the credit basis on which the instrument is written.

title: Mitigating Hallucination and Confabulation in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multi-Agent Systems (MASs): Is Simplicity the Ultimate Sophistication?

detail.title: Mitigating Hallucination and Confabulation in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multi-Agent Systems (MASs): Is Simplicity the Ultimate Sophistication?
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce fluent text that is sometimes ungrounded-unsupported by any source, derived by the model's own knowledge, hence often perceived as a central reliability barrier in high-stakes scientific domains. Whilst the field calls the failure hallucination, a growing line of work argues that the more exact term is confabulation, i.e., the fluent and confident gap-filling described in clinical neuropsychology [28]. The phenomenon can be even more pronounced in Multi-Agent Systems (MASs) wherein a network of multiple specialized AI entities (agents) collaborate, coordinate, or compete within a shared environment of parallel processing and scalability, to solve complex problems. Although the two words are used interchangeably, yet they encode different mechanistic hypotheses with different empirical consequences. One of the aims of my paper is to show that a controlled investigation can reliably adjudicate between them. The work is primarily a position and architecture proposal, complemented by a component-level and scaling empirical study, and it makes a deliberately bounded claim: I do not argue that hallucination can be eliminated, which is in fact highly unlikely under the current backpropagation gradient descent training paradigm. Instead, I argue that hallucination-or better confabulation-is heterogeneous, that distinct hallucination modes have distinct mechanistic origins, and that a specific class of recurrent neural topologies and neuro-symbolic mechanisms can plausibly mitigate an identifiable subset of those modes. I outline a candidate "monitor-and-gate" architecture composed of three separate or interacting components wrapped around a base large language model: (i) a recurrent commitment-tracking feedback state that detects intra-generation self-contradiction and topical drift; (ii) a fuzzy-symbolic confidence and constraint layer that maps candidate assertions to graded membership in support categories and encodes soft domain constraints as interpretable rules; and (iii) an actor-critic reinforcement-learning controller whose reward explicitly penalizes con…dent unsupported assertion while rewarding grounded deduction and calibrated abstention. Crucially, these three components are not assembled ad hoc: each instantiates a structure within an established track record in my prior published models of noisy nonlinear dynamical systems. Specifically, I introduce a recurrent-neuron architecture for state tracking under time-varying uncertainty, and a hybrid neuro-fuzzy reinforcement-learning controller in which symbolic fuzzy inference rules with adaptively trained parameters are coupled to an Actor-Critic policy. I make the correspondence between those prior constructs and the proposed components explicit, give a formal specification of each component, walk through an extensive empirical application, and analyze computational cost and governance implications for regulated domains.

title: The Co-Benefit Dividend: When Falling Costs Retire the Need to Price Externalities

detail.title: The Co-Benefit Dividend: When Falling Costs Retire the Need to Price Externalities

detail.abstract:
Fossil-fuel use imposes on the Asia-Pacific region approximately USD 3 trillion per year of un-priced damage, through ill-health, lost labour productivity, premature mortality, and environmental degradation. On IMF estimates of the regional social cost, that is on the order of USD 700 per person per year across the region's 4.3 billion people. The reversal of this damage as the energy system decarbonises is what this paper terms the co-benefit dividend. Its defining feature is that it does not require a carbon price. Where a learning curve closes the cost gap, as in the Asia-Pacific energy transition examined here, clean-energy cost decline makes the privately rational decision coincide with the socially beneficial one, so the dividend is released as a by-product of ordinary commercial decisions. The position that falling clean-technology costs can retire the need to price an externality does not assume that innovation is exogenous. 

Acemoglu, Aghion, Bursztyn and Hemous (2012) show that the direction of technical change responds to relative prices and policy, so that once clean and dirty technologies compete, cost-reducing innovation concentrates in the leading sector and compounds its advantage. The dividend described here is the market-facing consequence of that dynamic: where directed innovation has already moved costs below the incumbent, the externality is retired by the cost curve rather than by a tax. Policy that accelerates the crossover and policy that prices the externality are complements. 

The standard economics of externalities, from Pigou to Nordhaus, holds that the private-social gap is closed only by a price. That mechanism is not wrong, but for this class of decision in Asia-Pacific the condition a price was meant to create has already been met: learning curves have aligned privately rational and socially beneficial choices without one. Pricing is therefore no longer a precondition for this dividend, though it remains a general instrument elsewhere. The paper defines the dividend, gives a transparent, reproducible basis for attributing it to a jurisdiction, portfolio, or enterprise, and grounds it in the human geography of heat, labour, inequality, and land. The implication is not that pricing is wrong, but that the dividend can be released now, by running the numbers honestly and valuing people at the same time.

title: The Blackberry Foraging Escape Hatch: A Thermodynamic, Gastrointestinal, and Economic Post-Mortem of Quitting Your Job to Eat Alleyway Brambles for Vancouver Rent

detail.title: The Blackberry Foraging Escape Hatch: A Thermodynamic, Gastrointestinal, and Economic Post-Mortem of Quitting Your Job to Eat Alleyway Brambles for Vancouver Rent
detail.abstract: The escalating macroeconomic pressures of the Vancouver rental market have necessitated the investigation of radical financial independence strategies as alternatives to a traditional job. This paper evaluates the theoretical viability of resigning from formal employment to survive exclusively on foraged invasive Rubus armeniacus (Himalayan blackberry) during its peak August fruiting season, attempting to redirect eliminated grocery expenditures toward an average $2,050 monthly basement suite rent. Utilizing an interdisciplinary approach, this study cross-references regional rental data with thermodynamic equilibrium modeling, clinical gastroenterological thresholds, and urban ecotoxicological studies. Results indicate that maintaining basal metabolic equilibrium requires foraging 5.6 to 9.3 kilograms of fruit daily, demanding up to 9 hours of continuous physical labor. This extraction rate incurs significant micro-economic overhead for dermatological first aid and triggers catastrophic mechanical and biochemical gastrointestinal failure due to overwhelming fiber (up to 500g) and fructose (up to 220g) loads. Furthermore, sustained consumption at this scale introduces severe risks of acute heavy metal bioaccumulation and punitive municipal fines. Ultimately, this extreme subsistence strategy is entirely unsustainable; rather than providing a viable economic escape hatch, it functions as a highly efficient mechanism for profound physiological collapse and financial ruin.

title: Economic Horizontal Inequality is Linked to Conflict Persistence, not onset: High-Resolution Evidence from Satellite-Derived Wealth Measures in Africa
affiliations: Linkoping University, Linkoping University and The University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Economic Horizontal Inequality is Linked to Conflict Persistence, not onset: High-Resolution Evidence from Satellite-Derived Wealth Measures in Africa
detail.abstract: Conflict research links horizontal inequality—systematic inequalities between identity groups—to armed violence, but it remains unclear whether economic inequality predicts conflict outbreak or instead shapes conflict dynamics after violence becomes plausible. We revisit this question in Africa using high-resolution satellite-derived International Wealth Index estimates to measure economic horizontal inequality among politically relevant ethnic groups and local wealth shocks. In group-year models, economic horizontal inequality is not statistically associated with conflict onset, while political marginalization is a stronger predictor. By contrast, economic horizontal inequality is associated with active-rebel group-years and higher casualty intensity among active-conflict group-years. A spatiotemporal counterfactual analysis finds that dense local wealth-shock scenarios are not associated with more conflict events on average, but estimated conditional contrasts become positive in areas with large absolute economic horizontal inequality. Economic horizontal inequality may therefore matter less as a general trigger than as a condition shaping conflict persistence, severity, and shock vulnerability.

title: Knowledge Heterogeneity and Labor Market Participation at Older Ages: Evidence from SHARE

detail.title: Knowledge Heterogeneity and Labor Market Participation at Older Ages: Evidence from SHARE
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between knowledge heterogeneity and labor market participation among older individuals in Europe. Using data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), the analysis focuses on individuals aged 50-70 and primarily uses Wave 9, with Wave 7 employed for robustness checks. Knowledge heterogeneity is measured through educational attainment and cognitive abilities, including memory performance, numeracy, and verbal fluency. Logistic regression models estimate the probability of remaining employed rather than retired while controlling for demographic characteristics, physical and mental health, household income, wealth, and country fixed effects. The analysis further investigates whether health and social networks mediate the relationship between knowledge heterogeneity and labour-market participation. By integrating educational and cognitive dimensions of human capital, this paper contributes to the literature on retirement, labor market participation, and active ageing, providing new evidence on how differences in accumulated knowledge are associated with extended working lives across European countries.

title: Norms and Coordination on Democratic Principles
affiliations: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca, University of Pennsylvania, University of Rochester - Department of Political Science and

detail.title: Norms and Coordination on Democratic Principles
detail.abstract: Democratic stability depends, in part, on the expectations that citizens have of one another. In addition to actually coordinating on democratic principles, stability requires perceptions of such coordination. For instance, do partisans believe fellow partisans or citizens generally share the same beliefs about whether ignoring an election outcome violates a principle? The perception of shared beliefs sets normative expectations that generate consistent, coordinated behaviors (i.e., it is normatively inappropriate to ignore an election outcome). Otherwise, coordination fails as norms do not generate stable behaviors. We use a large-scale, pre-registered survey of a representative sample of U.S. citizens to study whether individuals perceive their fellow partisans or the wider public as having coordinated beliefs on a set of democratic principles. On the one hand, we nd that citizens across political leanings exhibit a strong consensus that most democratic violations are inappropriate. On the other hand, they do not perceive a normative consensus on specic violations. Most notably, they perceive Americans as having variable beliefs i.e., uncoordinated on what constitutes a democratic violation. Such perceptions can undermine normative enforcement of democratic principles. Consequently, just as personal endorsements of anti-democratic actions constitute a threat to democratic functioning, so does discoordination around how to view a host of principles.

title: Fiscal Inflation in a Currency Union
affiliations: ,  and Institut Polytechnique de Paris, CREST

detail.title: Fiscal Inflation in a Currency Union
detail.abstract: We study the propagation of unfunded fiscal shocks in a currency union. For a determinate equilibrium, at most one fiscal authority can issue unfunded debt; we then accommodate multiple partially unfunded countries by introducing monetary-led and fiscal-led parallel economies. Funded government spending shocks cause inflation to diverge across countries, while unfunded shocks raise inflation union-wide, as the common central bank accommodates fiscal inflation. Euro area local projections show that positive government spending shocks in France and Italy raise inflation at home and abroad, while in Germany they lower inflation abroad, consistent with French and Italian shocks being primarily unfunded and German shocks being primarily funded. A Bayesian-estimated quantitative model confirms that unfunded fiscal shocks are a quantitatively significant driver of euro area inflation dynamics. We recover the implied inflation target of the ECB, which averages near two percent over the sample but rose above 2.5 percent during the post-pandemic episode due to fiscal pressures.

detail.abstract: I document a strong cross-sectional variance risk premium in the returns to writing singlestock put options, sorted on the ratio of near-the-money implied volatility to trailing thirty-day realized volatility. The ratio form is a scale-invariant restatement of the Goyal and Saretto (2009) cross-sectional signal (which uses the difference HV-IV) and produces a distinct withinmonth cross-sectional ordering: the two formulations agree on only 59% of decile assignments and disagree on 33% of the top-decile ("most expensive") membership on this paper's panel. On an OptionMetrics and Center for Research in Security Prices panel of 590,345 firm-months from January 2014 to August 2025, a long-short portfolio that writes five-percent out-of-the-money thirty-day puts on the highest-decile firms and buys the corresponding puts on the lowestdecile firms, within the middle market-capitalization tercile, delivers an annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.24, a Bailey and López de Prado (2014) deflated Sharpe ratio of one, and a Fama and French (2015) five-factor plus Carhart (1997) momentum alpha of +11.89% per year with a t-statistic of 7.69. The factor R 2 is 4.3%: the return is almost entirely idiosyncratic to the standard six-factor cross-section. Net of a firm-month-specific transaction cost, calibrated to the OptionMetrics best-bid and best-offer at each firm-month, the Sharpe ratio remains 1.25 across the full sample and 1.39 over the 2020-2025 out-of-sample window. The results extend the Goyal and Saretto (2009) cross-sectional straddle result to (a) a longer sample that is entirely out-of-sample relative to the original 1996-2006 window and includes the COVID-19 volatility shock and the 2022 bear market, (b) a put-only long-short wrapper with realistic transaction costs, and (c) a scale-invariant ratio restatement of the underlying signal.

title: Women's Rights in Afghanistan Under Taliban Rule: A Case Study Through the Lenses of Human Rights Law, Feminist Theory, Historical Context and Policy Analysis

detail.title: Women's Rights in Afghanistan Under Taliban Rule: A Case Study Through the Lenses of Human Rights Law, Feminist Theory, Historical Context and Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the condition of women's rights in Afghanistan under Taliban rule through the integrated lenses of human rights law, feminist theory, historical context, and policy analysis. Drawing on qualitative analysis of secondary sources, the research identifies how the Taliban's governance has systematically restricted women's access to education, employment, and public life, institutionalizing gender-based discrimination and violating international legal standards such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and CEDAW. The findings highlight how these restrictions are reinforced by historical, cultural, and religious factors, and reveal the limitations of international legal and policy frameworks in ensuring accountability and protection for Afghan women. By synthesizing multiple analytical perspectives, the study contributes to a deeper understanding of the multifaceted and persistent nature of gender oppression in Afghanistan, and underscores the need for more effective international responses to address the ongoing crisis.

title: EcoEcon: Ecological Resilience Indicators for Systemic Risk-A Retrospective Analysis of the 2008 Financial Crisis with a 2020 Negative Control

detail.title: EcoEcon: Ecological Resilience Indicators for Systemic Risk-A Retrospective Analysis of the 2008 Financial Crisis with a 2020 Negative Control
detail.abstract: Can ecological collapse theory provide early warning indicators for financial crises? We model the US economy as a biological ecosystem-sectors as species, supply chains as mutualistic dependencies, and bankruptcy cascades as extinction events-and apply three bodies of ecological theory to BEA Input-Output and FRED data: May's (1972) stability theorem, Scheffer et al.'s (2009) critical slowing down, and network robustness metrics. We construct an Economic Biodiversity Index (EBI), track network spectral gap, and compute critical slowing down signals across two episodes: the 2008 Global Financial Crisis (endogenous fold bifurcation, signal expected) and the 2020 COVID shock (exogenous perturbation, no signal expected by theory). In a retrospective analysis, two of five ecological signals behaved as theorized before 2008: spectral gap declined monotonically 2002-2007 (Kendall τ =-0.87) and housing starts variance peaked approximately 18 months before crisis onset. Logistic regression trained on these features achieves leaveone-out AUC = 1.000 (p = 0.034, permutation test) with zero false positives in cross-validation. The 2020 negative control holds: models trained on 2008 assign near-zero crisis probability to 2015-2019, and four of five ecological signals show no pre-crisis buildup before the exogenous COVID shock, consistent with the theoretical prediction. Spectral gap produces zero false alarms across ten calm-period years (2010-2019). This analysis is explicitly retrospective and limited to one positive crisis episode; generalizability requires multi-crisis validation. We propose ecological resilience indicators as a theoretically grounded and empirically promising direction for systemic risk research.
