detail.abstract: Digital ecosystems are understood as networks of complementary components coordinated across firm boundaries, yet the tools to measure and compare their structure remain underdeveloped. This paper introduces a network-based method that maps ecosystems as components connected through interfaces and tracks how that structure evolves over time. We apply it to an original, hand-collected dataset of the early Personal Computer (PC) industry over 1981 to 1987, covering almost 5,000 products by over 1,000 firms. We partition the network into ecosystems by operating system-proximity and focus on four representative cases: the IBM PC, the Apple II, the Atari 8-bit and the Commodore 64. Using degree centralisation, preferential attachment estimates and layer-by-firm decompositions, we find that the most centralised ecosystems take a near-star rather than a scale-free shape, and that this centralisation arises not from closure as such but from the uneven openness of adjacent layers. Finally, interface-governance case studies trace these patterns to the disclosure of technical documentation, the specificity of essential complements, and the licensing of intellectual property.

title: Capturing Heterogeneity: Machine Learning Approaches to Implied Volatility Forecasting
affiliations: and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Capturing Heterogeneity: Machine Learning Approaches to Implied Volatility Forecasting

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Despite documented heterogeneity in volatility dynamics across the option surface, standard implied volatility forecasting models apply homogeneous parameters throughout. We introduce a machine-learning framework that uses regression trees to partition the surface along both moneyness and maturity dimensions, identifying data-driven regions where distinct forecasting models perform best. Extending the Surface Heterogeneous Autoregressive (SHAR) framework of Dufays, Jacobs, and Rombouts (2025), we develop tree-based SHAR specifications that preserve interpretable structure while allowing model parameters to vary across the surface. Empirical analysis using S&P 500 options demonstrates that the boosted tree-based specification achieves the lowest out-of-sample forecast errors across all horizons, reducing one-month-ahead RMSE by 13 percent versus the benchmark SHAR model. The improvements are statistically significant and particularly pronounced during stress periods. The estimated tree presents economically interpretable segmentation: short-dated options exhibit higher daily persistence but lower monthly persistence than long-dated options, while deep out-of-the-money calls or puts display distinct dynamics from near-the-money contracts.

title: Planning Against Disasters in Dynamic Production Networks
affiliations: Universitat Pompeu Fabra/CREI, Banco de España and Banco de España

detail.title: Planning Against Disasters in Dynamic Production Networks
detail.abstract: In dynamic multisector economies, the planner’s optimal capital allocation can serve to minimize the aggregate impact of shocks cascading through nonlinear production networks. We show analytically in a simplified model that, under complementarity and if risk aversion is not too low, (i) optimal capital allocation under uncertainty involves deliberately over-investing, relative to the deterministic optimum, in upstream sectors in order to mitigate severe economic downturns; (ii) this strategy can reduce the average level of consumption and give rise to a high welfare cost of business cycles. Deploying novel deep-learning techniques in a general environment, we show quantitatively that: (iii) the ergodic distribution of the simulated nonlinear economy features higher mean capital levels in key upstream sectors, lower mean levels of macroeconomic aggregates, realistic aggregate volatility, and a welfare cost of business cycles two orders of magnitude larger than in standard one-sector models.

title: The Impact of Patient Capital
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU), MIT Sloan School of Management and University of Toronto

detail.title: The Impact of Patient Capital
detail.abstract: We show that investor patience shapes venture-capital (VC) investment strategies and outcomes. Exploiting a 2014 Chinese reform that opened RMB-denominated VC funds to insurers, we compare treated RMB funds to unaffected USD-denominated funds run by the same general partners (GP), both investing in Chinese startups. Insurer entry reshaped the limited partner (LP) base by displacing shorter-horizon investors such as individuals. Consequently, treated funds shifted strategy toward longer holding periods and earlier-stage investments, leading to improved portfolio company exits and innovation. GPs' bargaining power vis-à-vis LPs mediates this response. A randomized experiment with Chinese GPs corroborates the mechanism: managers explicitly tailor fund duration and project holding periods to the perceived horizons of their LP base. Our results highlight the importance of patient ultimate investors in building a successful VC ecosystem, and offer a cautionary note on the ongoing retailization of private markets.

title: AI, Task-based Production in General Equilibrium and Distribution of Labour Incomes
affiliations: Department of Economics, Jadavpur University and

detail.title: AI, Task-based Production in General Equilibrium and Distribution of Labour Incomes
detail.abstract: In a multi-sector general equilibrium model of task-based production, we examine the impact of two types of AI-driven finite changes, one in production-tasks in an AI-prone or AI-applicable sector and the other in the sector-composition of the economy, on the real wage and distribution of wage-income among workers of different skills. We establish that, contrary to the conventional wisdom of a sector-specific small Hicks-neutral type technological change unambiguously lowering real wage of the middle skilled workers despite their productivities improving, finite changes can eventually raise their real wage. But, the distribution of wage-incomes changing in favour of the high-skilled workers (relative to the middle-skilled workers) due to AI-driven finite changes will be similar to that due to small technological change, except that the relative gain of the high-skilled workers will smaller in magnitude.

title: The Standards Are in the Mail: Comparing Credit Card Supply Indicators
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: The Standards Are in the Mail: Comparing Credit Card Supply Indicators

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We provide the first lender-level analysis linking two independently constructed credit supply measures: the Federal Reserve's Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) and credit card mail offers from Mintel Comperemedia. Using a matched panel of 73 banks from 2000 to 2019, we find that quarterly mail volume growth was 18 percent lower when banks reported tightening credit card lending standards, a relationship robust to including credit demand indicators. In addition, SLOOS responses on credit limits and interest rate spreads are also correlated with these terms observed in mail offers. Our findings validate both measures as informative credit supply indicators.

title: Trade, Risk, and Resilience in General Equilibrium
affiliations: Ifo Institute, University of Applied Sciences Konstanz

detail.title: Trade, Risk, and Resilience in General Equilibrium
detail.abstract: Sanctions, export controls, and friend-shoring shift the margin of trade policy from cost alone to exposure. When supplier risks are correlated, the value of a trade relationship cannot be evaluated in isolation; it depends on the sourcing network in which it is embedded. This paper develops a general-equilibrium theory of relationship-based trade under correlated risk. Countries allocate sourcing across partners whose risks load on common factors, while terms of trade clear markets and scale the uninsured covariance carried by each relationship. The mechanism separates individually optimal de-risking from collective resilience. Reallocation away from a risky supplier raises demand for substitutes; if capacity is scarce, or if substitutes load on the same systemic factor, equilibrium prices can erode, and even reverse, the risk reduction the reallocation was meant to achieve. The model yields a risk-augmented Viner decomposition into trade creation, terms-of-trade redistribution, and induced risk. Quantitatively, this induced-risk channel is small with broad re-sourcing and abundant substitutes, but first-order for critical inputs and high-loading supplier clusters.

title: How Resilient Were Emerging Market Economies Through the 2022-23 U.S. Monetary Tightening Cycle?
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: How Resilient Were Emerging Market Economies Through the 2022-23 U.S. Monetary Tightening Cycle?

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: The cross-border spillover effects of shifts in U.S. monetary policy have long been a focus of academics and policymakers alike. A common finding in the literature is that changes in the stance of U.S. monetary policy have sizable effects on economic activity and financial markets in emerging market economies (EMEs).

title: The Regional Specialization Trade-off
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: The Regional Specialization Trade-off
detail.abstract: In 1950, highly specialized U.S. regions had higher per capita incomes than those with greater industrial diversity. Since then, however, the more specialized regions have grown persistently slower. I rationalize this novel finding in a dynamic multi-industry model featuring two opposing forces. On the one hand, specialization raises productivity via agglomeration economies. On the other hand, it increases exposure to sectoral shocks. Real factor adjustment costs and financial frictions make reallocation in response to shocks costly and long-lasting. Disciplined by U.S. Census data, the model explains half of the observed relationship between initial specialization and subsequent growth, with financial frictions accounting for more than half of this adverse effect. A constrained-efficient planner allocation reveals that less specialization can raise welfare by reducing a region’s exposure to industry-specific downturns.

title: Systemic Vacancy and Proactive Urban Regeneration in U.S. Municipalities

detail.title: Systemic Vacancy and Proactive Urban Regeneration in U.S. Municipalities
detail.abstract: American cities continue to spend millions responding to vacant buildings, yet many legal frameworks still treat vacancy as an isolated code-enforcement issue rather than a systemic governance challenge. This paper argues that local governments should address systemic vacancy as a broader governance, public safety, and public health problem. Using a Kansas municipal framework as a case study, the article examines how land-use authority, vacant property registration ordinances, tax foreclosure reform, land banking, ownership transparency, financing tools, and constitutional safeguards can be integrated into a more effective and equitable revitalization strategy. The paper proposes a governance-based approach that moves beyond punitive enforcement and emphasizes data-informed decision-making, accountability, and community-centered solutions for addressing long-term vacancy.

title: How Do Money and Tax Illusion Impact Long-Term Investments? An Experiment
affiliations: , Leibniz University Hannover, Leibniz University Hannover and Leibniz University Hannover

detail.title: How Do Money and Tax Illusion Impact Long-Term Investments? An Experiment
detail.abstract: The wealth effects of inflation and taxes on long-term savings, such as retirement investments, can be substantial. Nonetheless, individuals misperceive the impact of both taxes and inflation. Based on a unified theoretical framework, we distinguish between potential cognitive mechanisms underlying tax and inflation misperceptions and derive their implications for investment behavior. Using an incentivized, pre-registered online experiment, we test how these misperceptions influence individual investment decisions. In our baseline setting, inflation and taxation affect investment outcomes equivalently in real or after-tax terms. The results show that — even though all participants were informed about the effects of inflation and taxes on investment returns — investment distortions remain significant in both settings. Distortions driven by money illusion clearly exceed those caused by tax illusion. We find that both rational inattention and anchoring contribute to these distortions, with anchoring appearing more persistent in the inflation setting. Money illusion is therefore not only larger than tax illusion but also harder to undo. Money and tax illusion become more pronounced when future tax and inflation rates are uncertain. We then test the effectiveness of different communication strategies in this setting. Additional tabular information, visualizations, and attention nudges do not systematically reduce money or tax illusion. We show that requiring participants to view real or after-tax consequences before decision making is the most effective intervention; voluntary access has weaker effects, and later display does not systematically reduce the distortions.

reference: Italian Review of Legal History, issue 11, 2025[10.54103/2464-8914/30275]
title: Desertion in the Context of General Mobilization: Historical Experience and Modern Challenges
affiliations: National Academy of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine named after Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, National Academy of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine Named after Bohdan Khmelnitsky and

detail.title: Desertion in the Context of General Mobilization: Historical Experience and Modern Challenges

publicationDetails.detailsText: Italian Review of Legal History, issue 11, 2025[10.54103/2464-8914/30275]

detail.abstract: The general mobilization in response to armed aggression against Ukraine has significantly increased the number of service members in the Armed Forces of Ukraine and other military formations. However, this increase in military personnel accompanies a rise in military criminal offenses, particularly desertion. Desertion remains a pressing issue for the armed forces of any country engaged in active combat operations. Desertion, as a phenomenon, has a long history, with significant cases documented during the First and Second World Wars. At that time, this issue affected the armies of various countries, significantly undermining combat capability and the morale of service members. Desertion from the battlefield during active hostilities negatively influences a unit’s moral and psychological condition and cohesion, substantially reducing combat readiness and the ability to fulfill combat missions. A historical analysis of desertion indicates that it results from psychological exhaustion, the continuous nature of combat operations, and harsh service conditions (trench warfare, lack of rotations, etc.). In some cases, desertion serves as a form of protest against political or military decisions made by the command. Desertion is also significant in modern armed conflicts, particularly full-scale war. The level of desertion at different stages of warfare has had a substantial impact on their outcomes and, at times, has reached critical levels. During World War I, desertion was cited as one of the main reasons for the defeat of the empires. Reaching critical levels of desertion can lead to military defeat and even the loss of statehood in Ukraine. The level and dynamics of desertion in the Ukrainian army have prompted the government and military command to develop effective measures to reduce its occurrence. Historical experience demonstrates that combating desertion is crucial to strengthening military discipline, ensuring resilience, and maintaining the armed forces’ combat effectiveness throughout societal development.

title: External Accountability and Fiscal Transparency in Hierarchical Governance: Evidence from Chinese Cities
affiliations: Peking University, Peking University and Development Research Center of the State Council

detail.title: External Accountability and Fiscal Transparency in Hierarchical Governance: Evidence from Chinese Cities
detail.abstract: Fiscal transparency is a cornerstone of public governance, yet its determinants remain contested. This article argues that fiscal transparency is primarily driven by external accountability-market discipline and administrative hierarchy-rather than societal demand or local leaders' initiative, especially in systems lacking electoral accountability. Using an original dataset of fiscal disclosures from 294 Chinese cities (2013-2021), we construct a comprehensive fiscal transparency index covering institutional, on-budget, and off-budget dimensions. The analysis shows that market exposure and hierarchical oversight significantly increase fiscal transparency, while local societal and leadership factors have limited effects. These findings highlight the central role of institutional accountability in shaping fiscal transparency in hierarchical governance contexts.

title: Experiential Learning in Economics Courses

detail.title: Experiential Learning in Economics Courses
detail.abstract: Virginia Wesleyan University's curriculum uses a 4-credit hour model that includes an experiential learning component for each course. This paper describes various options for learningby-doing used in economics courses, many of which involve students analyzing economics concepts in popular culture and news media.

title: Learning Screening Rules under Gaming: Online Strategic Classification with Noisy Selective Feedback
affiliations: , Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management and Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management

detail.title: Learning Screening Rules under Gaming: Online Strategic Classification with Noisy Selective Feedback
detail.abstract: Automated screening systems often operate in environments where agents arrive sequentially and may strategically respond to the deployed screening rules. We study an online strategic classification problem in which a principal is initially unaware of the true feature-label relationship and sequentially deploys linear classifier-based screening rules. Agents may manipulate their reported features at some cost, and labels are observed only for agents classified as positive. The feature-label relationship is governed by an unknown linear model under bounded feature-dependent label noise. The problem confronts the intertwined challenges of strategic feature manipulation, selective feedback, and label noise. These challenges create a fundamental tension: the borderline agents most informative for learning are also the most prone to manipulation. We address these challenges with an algorithm that combines three techniques: localization, contrastive inference, and proxy-feature construction. We prove that the proposed algorithm yields classifiers that converge to the clairvoyant optimal screening rule and achieve $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ Stackelberg regret, a regret notion that accounts for agents' strategic manipulation. We further establish a matching $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ lower bound, demonstrating that this rate is optimal. Finally, we extend our framework to broader agent manipulation costs and noise models.

title: Vocabulary Resonance in US Trademark Filings: A Measurement Construct for Commercial Novelty, With Validation and Applications

detail.title: Vocabulary Resonance in US Trademark Filings: A Measurement Construct for Commercial Novelty, With Validation and Applications
detail.abstract:
The DeDeo prospective/retrospective Kullback–Leibler resonance framework (Barron et al., 2018; Murdock et al., 2017) was developed on cognitive corpora in which the author of each document is the agent whose novelty is being measured: Darwin’s reading notebooks, parlia mentary speeches of the French Revolution. This paper applies the framework to a qualitatively different corpus type, the goods/services descriptions of US trademark filings, and introduces the resulting construct, denoted ∆KL, as a filing-level measure of commercial novelty that is cheap to compute, available for millions of firms that never patent, and empirically distinct from patent-track invention.
The construct is scored on each filing’s topic distribution rather than its raw token counts, following the source papers’ own operationalization; this gives every filing a dense representation regardless of length, which matters because goods/services descriptions typically run 10–30 words. The maintenance and firm-level analyses condition on completed registration: completing registration mostly reflects whether the filer followed through to actual commercial use (nine in ten failed applications die by abandonment, not by refusal), so the conditioning separates businesses that launched from filings that remained intentions.
Three results anchor the paper. First, ∆KL marks commercial risk at the mark level, robustly across scoring choices and cohorts. Marks written in language their industry was moving toward die more often at the Section 8 use-proof gates: event-dating every cancellation in the 13.99 million-case-file prosecution record, first-gate failure rises +3.9pp across ∆KL quintiles on 4.12 million registrations 2002–2018. The penalty emerged with the 2008–2010 registration cohorts and has persisted in every cohort since; it is larger for self-filed registrations (+6.9pp) than for counsel-represented ones (+2.5pp), larger where claimed use is older (use-based +5.4pp versus intent-to-use +2.2pp), and it attenuates but persists at the year-ten renewal. Applications register as an inverse-U, with the flux-neutral middle following through to use most reliably. Re-scoring with mixed reference windows shows the gate penalty comes from breaking with the established past, not from resembling the future (−7.3pp against −3.2pp). In either scoring, merely being surprising in the moment is not the signal; the information lives in comparing how surprising a filing is against its past with whether its surprising elements are then taken up by the filings that follow. Second, a methodological caution the construct itself surfaces: under term level scoring, forward-leaning filings appear to mark better firms (higher margins, more public listings), but these firm-level associations dissolve or reverse under distribution scoring at every resolution tried, and the listing gradient dissolves under document-length controls. Term-level text measures can manufacture firm-performance correlations out of drafting style; distribution scoring is the guard. The firm-level claims are therefore not anchored here, and the within-firpatent contrast (−0.048σ, t = −7.9) is read only as evidence that the construct is distinct from patent-track invention. Third, the construct supports direct measurement of cross-industry idea diffusion: software- and tech-services-origin themes arrive in transport and advertising/retail with 1–13 year lags, theme adoption follows Bass curves with median q/p ≈ 6.5, and the cross class flow is strongly asymmetric (software originates 33 of the 72 origin-to-arrival edges and receives only 10).
The paper closes with a research agenda the construct opens: whether ideas that transfer between industries hold their value, whether suppliers to a new theme outperform its deployers, and how demographic concentration within industries relates to where new themes originate. Code and firm-year panels are public at https://github.com/ericsilver/novelty.

title: Rotation into the Trap: The Dynamics of Strategic Inattention in Auditing

detail.title: Rotation into the Trap: The Dynamics of Strategic Inattention in Auditing
detail.abstract: A companion working paper-the Equilibrium Without Collusion model (hereafter ewc; SSRN working paper, 2026)-showed that recurring IT-related control deficiencies can be an equilibrium without collusion: when the core auditor's observability λ of the specialist's work is low, strategic inattention is individually rational, the deficiency persists, and no party deviates. That argument was static. This paper makes observability a capital stock-built period by period by costly auditor attention, eroded by turnover and neglect-and shows that doing so turns the companion paper's recurrence into a trap, and turns the two policies meant to cure it into instruments that deepen it. Three results follow. First, the strategicinattention region becomes a low-observability trap: an absorbing, locally stable steady state at which attention never repays its cost, and, under a single-crossing condition, one well of a bistable system in which history selects between the trap and an engaged state. Second, the companion paper's penalty paradox acquires a second face: a heavier auditor penalty not only weakly lowers the engaged steady state (level) but widens the basin of attraction of the trap (basin). Third, mandatory partner rotation-the remedy most specific to auditingreduces to a fall in the auditor's effective discount and a rise in the effective depreciation of observability capital, and so deepens the trap rather than relieving it; modelled at the engagement level, where rotation is a recurring discrete event rather than a smooth average, it leaves the engaged state only metastable, with absorption into the trap almost sure once rotations cluster. The unifying point is a single mechanism: both penalties and rotation lower the private capitalised value of observability. The instrument that matters is therefore neither penalty severity nor rotation cadence but the transferability of the observability stock and the incumbent's stake in future quality. Throughout, the paper claims only monotone directions; bifurcations, fixed-point counts, and magnitudes are flagged as functional-formdependent and verified only numerically.

title: Experimentalist Intensification Governance: Managing Worker Negative Consequences Associated with Generative AI Experimentalist Work
affiliations: Stanford University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and New York University (NYU) - Department of Management and Organizational Behavior

detail.title: Experimentalist Intensification Governance: Managing Worker Negative Consequences Associated with Generative AI Experimentalist Work
detail.abstract: How does work intensification occur in organizations around the use of emerging technologies such as Generative AI (GenAI)? And how might such work intensification be mitigated? Existing studies examine the work intensification that occurs when workers use GenAI for individual productivity, but overlook the work intensification that may occur when workers use these technologies to create organizational solutions (solutions that have the potential to create value for a broad set of organizational stakeholders). In our comparative, qualitative field study of medical and legal workers using GenAI to create organizational solutions in an academic medical center and law firm, we find that the use of GenAI resulted in new kinds of work intensification related to workers’ engagement in experimentalist practices such as distributed trialing, collective review and revision of results, and aligning and hustling. More importantly, we find that the negative consequences for workers associated with experimentalist practices varied according to different forms of what we call experimentalist intensification governance structures in the two organizations. This study advances the sociological literature on organizational control, invisible work, and voluntary work intensification by demonstrating how experimentalist intensification governance can mitigate negative worker consequences of experimentalist work around emerging technologies such as GenAI.

reference: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 07/2026
title: Economy-wide capacity utilisation rate: Methodological framework and application to Swiss data
affiliations: Swiss National Bank and Swiss National Bank

detail.title: Economy-wide capacity utilisation rate: Methodological framework and application to Swiss data

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 07/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss National Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The utilisation rate of technical capacity is a key indicator of an economy's cyclical position and plays a crucial role in the estimation of production functions. Despite its importance, economy-wide measures of capacity utilisation are often not available. Instead, single sector series, typically that for manufacturing, are used as a proxy. However, this approach overlooks the heterogeneity of sectoral developments. Using Swiss data, we develop a methodology to estimate a series of aggregate capacity utilisation. Our measure covers eleven sectors, accounting for two thirds of the economy, and is mostly based on survey data retropolated back to Q1 1995. The sectoral shares of the capital stock are used to aggregate the sectoral capacity utilisation series. Several evaluations show that our aggregate series provides valuable information for the analysis of overall economic activity and is superior to the use of manufacturing capacity utilisation. Our methodology can serve as a basis for the construction of an aggregate capacity utilisation rate series for other countries.

title: Master's Thesis Predictive Modelling for Financial Market Analysis: A Machine Learning Approach

detail.title: Master's Thesis Predictive Modelling for Financial Market Analysis: A Machine Learning Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as part of a master's thesis at the Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, Faculty of Economics and Management.

detail.abstract: This study evaluates the predictive accuracy of standard machine learning algorithms applied to historical price and volume data for NYSE stock market prediction. A dataset of 1,026 NYSE-listed stocks comprising 6,250,312 daily observations from 1980 to 2022 is used. JPMorgan Chase serves as the primary analysis stock, with cross-sectional validation across 97 stocks. Fourteen technical indicators are engineered and five algorithm families evaluated under strict temporal 80/20 train-test split. Linear Regression achieves RMSE = $2.006 and R² = 0.9966, while tree-based models fail structurally. All classifiers achieve AUC-ROC between 0.4925 and 0.5119, statistically indistinguishable from random prediction. A Random Forest trading simulation yields −8.6% cumulative return versus 190.1% buy-and-hold. Results are consistent with the weak-form Efficient Market Hypothesis.

title: Innovation and Adam Smith's Mutual Sympathy of Sentiments

detail.title: Innovation and Adam Smith's Mutual Sympathy of Sentiments

contentType.other: Forthcoming in The Adam Smith Review

detail.abstract: This paper uses Adam Smith's concepts of mutual sympathy of sentiments and sympathetic persuasion as the foundation of a model of innovation and institutional change based on the Governing Knowledge Commons framework and Searle's ontology of institutions. A case study of disruptive innovation in the Scotch whisky industry is presented to illustrate this new paradigm. This approach enhances our understanding of innovation and institutional change as well as the broader relationship between culture and markets.

title:
The Manufacturing of Bad Faith
Mechanism Design and the Doctrine of the Affected Party
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
The Manufacturing of Bad Faith
Mechanism Design and the Doctrine of the Affected Party

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is self-represented in ongoing civil and administrative proceedings in Portugal concerning matters structurally similar to those discussed in this paper's companion application piece. The theoretical framework presented here was developed in part through that practical engagement and is offered in general form independent of any specific proceeding; no specific party, case, or jurisdiction is addressed in this paper. The author is also the founder of a commercial venture (KYC.co) whose broader product and policy work intersects with some of the institutional design concepts discussed here.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and doctrinal legal analysis; it does not involve human subjects, personal data collection, or empirical research requiring ethics review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
Legal systems routinely manufacture bad faith. They do so not through any failure of individual morality, but as the predictable output of rules that price silence at zero and candour at a cost. The mechanism is general. Wherever a body of law (i) binds two parties together in a relationship of real interdependence, (ii) offers no cheap channel through which one party may disclose a known, relevant condition before harm occurs, and (iii) defaults the allocation of liability or entitlement to the moment of crisis rather than the moment of knowledge, the system settles into a stable and undesirable equilibrium: the party holding private information about a pre-existing condition is rewarded for concealing it, the party who must act is penalised for acting, and the dispute that results is resolved years later by whichever side can sustain litigation longest. The contradiction is not incidental. It is the means by which ordinarily compliant actors are converted into strategic non-disclosers -- bad-faith actors made, not born. 

This paper names that failure, models it, and proposes a portable correction. Part I describes the manufacturing process: the "missing half" common to administrative, civil, commercial, environmental, and digital law alike. Part II models it formally, showing that the resulting gridlock is a genuine equilibrium -- which is precisely why moral exhortation cannot dislodge it, and why only a change in the payoff structure can. Part III specifies that change: the Affected Party Engine, a modular mechanism built from two interchangeable variables and one immutable procedural loop -- notice, a window, and a narrow evidentiary forfeiture -- that requires no new court, no new agency, and no admission of fault from anyone it touches. Part IV demonstrates the Engine across a range of further domains -- corporate, environmental, security, medical, consumer, and resource law -- including the hard case of resources shared through a common medium, where the mechanism must visibly bend to fit. Part V addresses why a failure this structural has gone unnamed for so long, and why the answer is neither conspiracy nor negligence but something more ordinary and more durable. The claim is not that bad actors should be punished harder. It is that the rules currently reward the wrong move, and that correcting the payoff matrix -- not the character of the players -- is both the more tractable problem and the more lasting fix. A companion paper demonstrates the Engine at full length against a single national legal system.

reference: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 08/2026
title: Forecasts, Nowcasts and Monetary Policy Lags
affiliations: University of Zurich and Swiss National Bank

detail.title: Forecasts, Nowcasts and Monetary Policy Lags

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 08/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss National Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We present a microfounded information mechanism that causes monetary policy transmission lags to be endogenously variable, even when firms are rational and face no exogenous costs of changing prices. Firms must form two distinct expectations, namely, a forecast of future demand and a nowcast of the current unobserved state, because information arrives at different frequencies. We model this setting as a partial-equilibrium, continuous-time optimal stopping problem in which firms receive a continuous noisy signal and a discrete precise signal. Because exercising the timing option to reprice has a sunk opportunity cost, an endogenous inaction region emerges; firms rationally delay adjustment until the discrete signal provides sufficient actionable information. The resulting dynamics reproduce observed Swiss price-adjustment patterns and the highly variable transmission lags of monetary policy. Thus, the framework provides a rational-agent microfoundation for lag heterogeneity.

title: Are Information Bias and Free Riding in Contingent Valuation Survey Inevitable? Evidence From the Dibru Saikhowa National Park, Assam
affiliations: Dibrugarh University - Department of Economics and Gauhati University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Are Information Bias and Free Riding in Contingent Valuation Survey Inevitable? Evidence From the Dibru Saikhowa National Park, Assam
detail.abstract: Contingent valuation method (CVM) is used to measure the value of nonmarket goods. As a stated preference technique, CVM functions under a constructed hypothetical market which enables people to express their preferences directly for a good. However, because of this hypothetical market, CVM estimates are often criticised on the ground of being affected by a set of biases. Yet, studies in favour of CVM are also plenty in number. The credit can mostly be attributed to the method's unique ability to measure both use and non-use values. The current study seeks to test for the presence of information bias and free riding behaviour in CVM responses in the context of a valuation programme for the Dibru Saikhowa National park in Assam. It also aims to investigate whether or not such anomalies can be corrected, if found any. The study adopts a complete non-parametric approach to fulfill the objectives and concludes that with appropriate precautions and corrective measures the aforesaid flaws can be avoided.

title: Making Sense of Career after Resettlement: Tensions between Meaning Systems and Career Support for People with Refugee Backgrounds in Australia
affiliations: and Griffith University

detail.title: Making Sense of Career after Resettlement: Tensions between Meaning Systems and Career Support for People with Refugee Backgrounds in Australia
detail.abstract: Refugees' longer-term settlement is closely tied to education, employment, and access to decent and meaningful work, yet little is known about how they conceptualise 'jobs', 'career' and 'career development' after resettlement. This qualitative study explored these conceptions among seven people with refugee backgrounds in Australia and consulted them about career supports gaps and recommendations. Distinguishing jobs from careers, participants framed jobs as survival-oriented and contingent, and careers as longer-term, self-aligned pathways offering direction and stability. Their conceptions of career development expanded when prompted to consider contextual pressures, relational obligations, and life responsibilities as part of, rather than separate from, the process. Career support was often experienced as job-facing, invisible, and culturally unfamiliar. The need for culturally responsive, developmentally timed career support involving families, communities, dialogue, and exposure to host-country labour-market expectations is highlighted as part of a sustainable career development agenda. Implications for career theory, practice and research are outlined.

title: The FRTB Coordination Crisis: Why Game Theory Explains Regulatory Fragmentation and How to Fix It
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The FRTB Coordination Crisis: Why Game Theory Explains Regulatory Fragmentation and How to Fix It

keywords: Undamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB)

detail.abstract: The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) stands at a crossroads. FRTB began as a standardised post-crisis reform of market risk regulation, but its execution has produced repeated delays and regulatory deviations. Implementation fragmentation has now reached a critical point. Canada, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, Switzerland and South Africa have gone live; the EU applies its market-risk requirements from January 2027—its second postponement—accompanied by a three-year package of targeted relief measures; the UK implements the Standardised Approach (SA) in 2027 and delays the Internal Models Approach (IMA) to 2028; and the United States, having re-proposed its Basel III rules in March 2026 with a lighter, internal-models-friendly market-risk design, has yet to finalise a timeline. This paper argues that the fragmentation is best understood as a coordination problem—more accurately modelled as an Assurance game than a Prisoner's Dilemma—in which jurisdictions prefer coordinated implementation but fear being first movers. The resulting incentives favour delay and produce collectively suboptimal outcomes. Drawing on game theory and the historical record of Basel II, the paper shows that jurisdictions coordinate when they establish verification systems, binding commitments and graduated response protocols. It then develops a structured implementation framework built on synchronised start dates, transparent monitoring, consultative bodies and enforcement mechanisms designed to create focal points for cooperation. Finally, it offers a practical decision framework that allows financial institutions to plan capital, systems and jurisdictional positioning under continued regulatory ambiguity.

reference: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 855
title: Enhancing Digital Services Trade: The Case of the People's Republic of China
affiliations: Asian Development Bank and Örebro University

detail.title: Enhancing Digital Services Trade: The Case of the People's Republic of China

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 855

detail.abstract: This paper studies the drivers of trade in services with a focus on the People’s Republic of China (PRC). It explores how the digital transformation of services has made services more easily tradable across borders and the policies that facilitate or hinder services trade. The paper starts with a descriptive analysis of new data on bilateral trade and sales from foreign affiliate trade statistics (FATS). Using structural gravity, it then studies the impact of regulatory reform on services trade flows as well as foreign affiliates at a granular level. Finally it applies general equilibrium structural gravity to simulate the impact of (i) regulatory reform in the information and communication technology (ICT) sector in the PRC and ii) implementation of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership on trade, sales and output in services across all economies for which data are available. The largest effect stems from regulatory reforms of the ICT sector in the PRC, which benefit all economies.

title: Conditional Asset Prices in the Campbell-Cochrane Habit Model: A Comment

detail.title: Conditional Asset Prices in the Campbell-Cochrane Habit Model: A Comment
detail.abstract:
Campbell and Cochrane (1999) helped establish habit formation
as a cornerstone of asset pricing theory. Their model’s core economic mechanism is
that, as consumption approaches habit, rising risk aversion drives up risk premia.
CC99 argue that this mechanism produces countercyclical stock-market volatility,
a leverage effect, and strong return predictability at long horizons. This comment
challenges these economic implications of the CC99 habit model.

title:
Research Question: To What Extent does Limited Access to Educational Resources Contribute to Opportunity Inequality
among Underprivileged Children?

detail.title:
Research Question: To What Extent does Limited Access to Educational Resources Contribute to Opportunity Inequality
among Underprivileged Children?
detail.abstract: Educational disparities continue to be a major obstacle to social advancement and economic growth, especially for disadvantaged children. Despite progress in global school enrolment, disparities in access to quality education, skilled teachers, digital resources, and learning opportunities continue to restrict educational attainment and future economic prospects. This research examines how varying access to educational resources impacts opportunity disparities among underprivileged children. Utilizing worldwide statistics and socioeconomic data from entities like UNESCO, UNICEF, the OECD, and the World Bank, the research investigates the effects of educational inequalities on human capital development, workforce productivity, job prospects, income disparity, and sustained economic growth. The findings suggest that limited access to educational resources reduces skill development, increases the risk of unemployment and low-income employment, and perpetuates intergenerational poverty, thereby restricting social mobility. Educational inequality also creates wider macroeconomic costs due to decreased productivity, lower economic efficiency, and slower GDP expansion. Additionally, the research assesses policy measures and community-driven efforts designed to tackle these inequalities, such as heightened public funding for education, strategies to minimize the opportunity costs of schooling, programs for digital inclusion, and assistance for girls' education. Although educational inequality intersects with various socioeconomic factors, the results suggest that limited access to educational resources is a significant factor contributing to opportunity inequality for underprivileged children. Expanding access to quality education therefore represents a crucial mechanism for strengthening human capital, promoting inclusive growth, and supporting sustainable economic development.

title: Climate Change Risks, Capital Structure Dynamics, and ESG-Driven Financial Flexibility: International Evidence from Top Emerging Economies

detail.title: Climate Change Risks, Capital Structure Dynamics, and ESG-Driven Financial Flexibility: International Evidence from Top Emerging Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to be declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The corresponding sole lead author has all the rights reserved for the contents of the manuscript and its associated replication packages used for the study.

detail.abstract: The current study examines the impacts of climate change risks on capital structure dynamics with international evidence from the top polluting emerging market economies, including Brazil, China, and India. The study shows that corporate climate risk exposure induces firms to rely more on debt financing for financial flexibility balances. The climate treatment effects on capital structure decisions remain robust when the study accounts for corporate sensitivity to global warming phenomena. Broad-based financial development, environmental policy stringency, and corporate sales growth are the ESG-driven financial flexibility mechanisms. While debt financing choices play crucial roles in financial flexibility, ESG-driven channels jointly affect corporate financing policies, leading to corporate deleveraging incentives to mitigate potential financial distress risk. Corporate dividend payout policy mediates the relationship with predicted mitigated climate exposure risk effects on corporate leverage. Furthermore, corporate sales growth and national aggregate financial developments mitigate financial constraints, with corporate proactive leverage increasing when firms are exposed to climate risks. Our international empirical evidence from the world’s top polluting emerging markets offers insightful predictions on the dynamic capital structure decisions for firms’ financial flexibility choices under the growing climate risk exposure effects with the thorough assessments of the tested ESG-driven mechanisms.

title: A Cognitive and Competitive Approach to Supply Curves: Transition from Short Run Irrationality to Long Run Rational Expectations
affiliations: Madras School of Economics

detail.title: A Cognitive and Competitive Approach to Supply Curves: Transition from Short Run Irrationality to Long Run Rational Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper studies the belief structures that generate a positively sloped short-run supply curve alongside a monetary-neutral long-run supply curve. I derive the supply curve from a relative-profit-maximizing payoff structure, modeled as a zero-sum game, to obtain the optimal Nash output response. The slope of the resulting supply curve is not fixed: it depends on an informational derivative that captures how beliefs respond to shocks. Rational Expectations (RE) is the belief structure that eliminates systematic forecast errors in the long run, but I show that a broad class of non-rational beliefs converging to RE is admissible in the short run, rather than imposing RE directly as in earlier models. To formalize this, I derive a model-specific learning equation that trades off the size of the current shock against the cognitive cost of revising beliefs. This learning equation generates short-run monetary non-neutrality, and the belief process converges to the long-run rational expectations benchmark over time.

title: Cross-Disciplinary Evidential Substitution in AI Consciousness Research An Epistemic Boundary Integrity Framework

detail.title: Cross-Disciplinary Evidential Substitution in AI Consciousness Research An Epistemic Boundary Integrity Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial interests, personal relationships, institutional affiliations, or other competing interests that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This methodological research note is based on conceptual analysis and published literature. It did not involve human participants, animals, patient data, personal data collection, interviews, experiments, or case-study subjects requiring ethics approval or informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

keywords: Reproducibility Figure 1. The EBIF Five-gate Audit Sequence
From Disciplinary Classification to Independent Scrutiny

detail.abstract: Claims about artificial consciousness increasingly combine behavioural performance, computational description, neuroscientific theory, philosophical possibility, physical analogy, and religious or spiritual interpretation. Interdisciplinarity is valuable, but it becomes scientifically unstable when evidence from one domain is used to validate a conclusion in another without an explicit, testable bridge. This focused methodological synthesis names that error cross-disciplinary evidential substitution (CDES) and develops an Epistemic Boundary Integrity Framework (EBIF). Unlike theory-derived indicator approaches, which ask whether candidate properties are instantiated, or governance principles, which regulate how research should be conducted, EBIF audits the warrant connecting evidence to attribution. It separates three evidential levels-observable behaviour, implemented mechanism, and theory-linked indicators-from a fourth target claim, phenomenal attribution, and subjects every upward inference to five checks: domain declaration, operational definition, causal bridge, rival discrimination, and independent audit. The framework does not deny the relevance of philosophy, theology, phenomenology, or physics; it assigns each a legitimate role while rejecting their use as substitutes for computational specification, empirical measurement, and falsifiable prediction. The central rule is proportionality: a conclusion should not exceed the evidence and warrant that support it. Two worked audits, operational review decisions, and a preregisterable validation strategy make the framework testable in review practice.

title: Adjudicating and Subjectivizing: The Role of Supranational Body in Governments' Fiscal Transparency
affiliations: and Australian National University (ANU)

detail.title: Adjudicating and Subjectivizing: The Role of Supranational Body in Governments' Fiscal Transparency
detail.abstract: Faced with fiscal constraints, many governments provide guarantees in public-private partnerships to incentivise private capital to complement public investment. While such guarantees enhance the creditworthiness of PPP projects, they also expose governments to significant fiscal risks if not properly accounted for and managed, raising concerns about fiscal transparency and accountability. This paper examines how accounting effects fiscal reform through its adjudicating and subjectivizing roles. Focusing on the International Monetary Fund’s efforts to promote fiscal transparency in Brazil, we analyse changes in government reporting of PPP guarantees and contingent liabilities following IMF monitoring. This study contributes to a better understanding of accounting’s roles in governance by demonstrating how supranational adjudication can drive national accounting change without coercive power, and how institutional logics shape a government’s subjectivizing behaviours. The findings have implications for international organisations seeking to foster fiscal transparency and for governments navigating external demands alongside domestic institutional logics.

title: Technological Sovereignty, Big Tech and the Military-digital complex
affiliations: Roma Tre University - Department of Economics, Sapienza University of Rome and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Technological Sovereignty, Big Tech and the Military-digital complex
detail.abstract: This article reassesses the concept of technological sovereignty and its policy implications in light of the close relationships between US-and China-based digital monopolies (i.e., Big Tech) and their respective military apparatuses. First, we empirically examine the growing influence of the private sector in R&D activities, the increasing centrality of digital technologies within sectoral and technological hierarchies, the emergence of Big Tech firms and their dominance over knowledge, infrastructures, and key technologies such as cloud computing and AI. Second, building on Coveri et al. (2025a), we analyse the mutual dependence between Big Tech and the military apparatus, showing how it reinforces the economic power of the private actors involved, weakens the state's capacity to act autonomously, and intensifies the subordination of foreign governments dependent on US and Chinese digital platforms. Third, we propose a typology of technological sovereignty that takes into account the degree of technological dependence on Big Tech, the nature of the relationship between states and digital companies, and, consequently, the state's capacity to align the activities of these companies with its own strategic objectives

detail.abstract: Conflicts of interest and corruption in Indonesia's political economy pose significant risks to its energy transition, including the Just Energy Transition Partnership. Existing legal and institutional frameworks are fragmented, inconsistently applied, and often fail to address the risk of state capture by powerful political and economic actors, especially in the extractive and energy sectors. The reliance on fossil fuel industries for political financing and the monopolistic nature of state-owned entities further complicate the shift to a low- or no-carbon system, despite the country's ambitious renewable energy targets. Potential pathways to greater anti-corruption resilience lie in improvements to beneficial ownership transparency and strengthening regulation, monitoring, and sanctioning of conflict of interest violations.

title: Social Media Exposure and the Size of the Welfare State
affiliations: University of Granada and Universidad de Granada

detail.title: Social Media Exposure and the Size of the Welfare State
detail.abstract: We study how strategically produced misinformation about the effectiveness of public spending shapes voters' support for redistribution. A profit-maximizing media platform amplifies misleading content, and voters differ both in income and in their ability to detect this content. Two political parties then compete on a tax rate and on a sanction against the platform. We show that the resulting welfare state can be much smaller than what a fully informed electorate would choose. The gap is largest in more unequal societies, where regulation must work harder before it bites. We also find that allowing parties to choose the regulatory sanction freely can partially correct the distortion, since voters tend to demand strong regulation once they value the public good. The correction is partial: the equilibrium tax rate moves closer to the unbiased benchmark than under exogenous regulation, but remains strictly below it. Moreover, even this partial correction is fragile. Whenever regulating the platform is politically costly for the proposing party, through hostile media coverage, lost campaign donations, or enforcement frictions, parties hold back on regulation, and the welfare state shrinks again. The contraction then reflects not what voters want but what the political system is able to deliver. A further consequence is that, under costly regulation, two societies that share every parameter except their level of income inequality can end up with very different welfare states. More equal societies still benefit from the corrective effect of regulation, while more unequal ones do not, so that inequality determines whether a society can reach the redistributive outcome at all.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Bank Profitability: What Really Matters?
affiliations: , Prometeia, Prometeia SpA and Prometeia

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Bank Profitability: What Really Matters?
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between digitalization and bank performance by constructing a novel text-based index of digital engagement from the annual reports of more than 50 major banks worldwide over 2009-2023. Using natural language processing, we quantify banks' attention to digital themes and trace their evolution over time. We document a steady increase in digital engagement and find a positive association with profitability indexes. To refine the analysis, we employ large language models to classify AI-related paragraphs by use case and implementation stage. The results show that aggregate AI adoption is linked to profitability and cost reduction; the relation is stronger if AI is fully operational-particularly in customer support, client profiling, and internal process optimization-contributing to efficiency gains. By contrast, early-stage initiatives and applications in regulatory reporting or credit scoring still have to generate measurable returns and represent a tangible cost for the banking system. Overall, our findings highlight that the impact of digitalization depends not only on its intensity but also on the maturity and functional orientation of AI adoption.

title: Horseshoe meets Knockout Filter
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Horseshoe meets Knockout Filter
detail.abstract: The knockoff filter of Barber and Candès (2015) and Candès et al. (2018) controls the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples by constructing synthetic features that are exchangeable with the originals under the null. This is a genuine achievement, but it carries three costs that are rarely accounted for: the model-X variant conditions its guarantee on a known covariate law PX; the procedure returns a bare selected set rather than a posterior; and its operating point is an exogenous level q rather than a risk-optimal threshold. We show, in theory and through empirics, that horseshoe shrinkage equipped with the moderate-deviation threshold tcrit = p log(πn/2) dominates the knockoff filter on the axes that matter for scientific discovery. The Carvalho-PolsonScott log-pole and super-efficiency bounds are the finite-sample precursors of an asymptotically-Bayes-optimal-under-sparsity testing rule whose threshold is derived by integrated-risk minimisation and adapts to unknown sparsity through the global scale. We further place horseshoe selection within the mixture-envelope hierarchical duality of Polson and Scott (2016), which supplies a proximal, trend-filtering-ready dual that the knockoff construction lacks. Making the latent-variable representation explicit shows the horseshoe and trend filtering to be one Gaussian scale-mixture family differing only in whether coordinates or their differences are shrunk; we prove the knockoff construction has no structured analogue and collapses on the near-singular trend-filtering basis. Empirically, across independent and autoregressive designs the horseshoe controls FDR at the nominal level while delivering up to 5.5× the power of knockoff+ and detecting signals where knockoff+ has none, with the advantage widening under dependence; it is essentially deterministic (selection-set coefficient of variation 4% versus 137% for re-drawn knockoffs, which return the empty set 62% of the time on identical data); in a trend-filtering change-point task it recovers 97% of the change-points at controlled FDR while the knockoff filter, defeated by the near-singular step basis, detects none; and on a real, strongly collinear design it recovers a quarter of the planted signals at controlled FDR while the equicorrelated knockoff construction makes no discoveries. The one axis on which knockoffs lead is finite-sample validity; everything else, the horseshoe wins.

title: Quasi-Linear Means and Monotone Comparative Statics
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Quasi-Linear Means and Monotone Comparative Statics
detail.abstract: We unify two intellectual traditions in the foundations of choice under uncertainty that have, surprisingly, never been written down together. The first is the 1930s Italian axiomatic theory of the mean as a certainty equivalent (Chisini 1929, Nagumo 1930, Kolmogorov 1930, de Finetti 1931), extended in the 1990s by Muliere, Parmigiani, Scarsini, Petrone, and the Bayesian-robustness school of Cifarelli, Regazzini, Fortini, and Ruggeri. The second is the 1990s American theory of monotone comparative statics (Topkis 1978, 1998; Milgrom and Shannon 1994; Athey 1995, 2002). We prove that Athey’s single-crossing condition paired with the monotone likelihood ratio (MLR) is the parametric comparative-statics dual of de Finetti’s quasi-linear-mean characterization. Where de Finetti axiomatizes the certainty-equivalent operator Mφ(F) = φ −1 ( R φ dF), Athey characterizes when Mφ(F(·; θ)) is monotone in θ. The bridge is the Whitt-Karlin-Rinott uniform conditional stochastic order: MLR is equivalent to monotonicity of every conditional certainty equivalent. Parallel results follow for inverse stochastic dominance with the dual cone of n-monotone utilities, and for the rank-dependent (Yaari-Chew) extension: the maximal class of universallyMLR-preserving distortions is characterized by three pointwise conditions on log α ′ corresponding exactly to the three monotonicity consequences of MLR (FOSD shift, reverse-hazard-rate, hazard-rate); the Beta-CDF cone is a strict sub-cone. Three further extensions complete the picture: a joint HLP-Pratt and Athey comparative statics on the certainty-equivalent surface; a multivariate Athey synthesis via Karlin-Rinott; and a characterization of MLR-preservation for generative transports via a single sign condition on the transport Hamiltonian Hθ = ∂yvθ +vθρθ. The Cifarelli-Regazzini concentration function is the unifying coordinate: the Yaari distortion is the concentration function it produces, and any cdf-functional perturbation π(θ) ∝ h(Π0(θ))π0(θ) of a baseline prior preserves the entire predictive synthesis. Five of the six concrete problems we identify are resolved; one is largely resolved.

title: HSR and the Quality of Merger Policy
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: HSR and the Quality of Merger Policy
detail.abstract:
The Hart-Scott-Rodino Act of 1976  (HSR) required pre-merger notification and review of certain proposed acquisitions.  The statute changed the timing of most, but not all, government challenges from post-acquisition to pre-acquisition. For pre-acquisition challenges the Agencies have no data about post-acquisition performance, so evaluation must be made on the basis of predicted effects. This increased the role of economic modeling in merger analysis. The Clayton Act actually contemplated that development, even though HSR itself was not foreseen by its drafters. By using the language “where the effect … may be substantially to lessen competition,” Section 7 of the Clayton Act invited the use of probable effects to predict merger harm.  The statutory language also made intent irrelevant.

Pre-acquisition evaluation also permits the use of much less intrusive remedies dominated by temporary restraining orders and prohibitory injunctions, rather than the costly divestitures that accounted for most pre-HSR merger remedies. Many mergers are terminated upon a district court’s issuance of a preliminary injunction. This is particularly important because a preliminary injunction can issue long before a full trial on the merits resolves all essential issues.

HSR was not intended to change substantive standards of illegality. Nor was it intended to raise an additional non-substantive bar to merging.  The HSR process, which is costly to participants, was intended to be “enforcement neutral.” It should neither make socially beneficial mergers more risky nor shield harmful mergers from challenge.  Congress itself stated that the process should “neither deter nor impede consummation of the vast majority of mergers and acquisitions.”  To that end, the HSR legislation authorized the Agencies to require only information that was “necessary and appropriate to enable [them] to determine” whether a proposed acquisition was lawful.

Assuming that a significant subset of mergers are harmful, identifying this subset ex ante with some accuracy can be very valuable. Intuitively, one might think that pre-acquisition evaluation is less accurate than post-acquisition evaluation.  Predicted results are never as accurate as actual ones.  In fact, as this paper argues, the differences are not as substantial as one might think.

title: National Policy Integration and Private Governance: SDG Implementation in Romania

detail.title: National Policy Integration and Private Governance: SDG Implementation in Romania

publicationDetails.detailsText: Romanian Journal of European Affairs, Vol. 26, No. 1, June 2026

detail.abstract: In the context of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, this paper investigates how Romania implements the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and conducts an analysis at two levels of governance, namely national policy integration and private governance. It finds that these two levels have a limited interaction, something which could be improved in the future, given the significant role of non-state actors in the achievement of the SDGs. Furthermore, the study identifies that the national policy integration level displays some policy interlinkages, thus avoiding the trap of working in silos, which could hinder the implementation of the goals. While progress has been achieved in terms of data access, organisational structures and policy formulation, more can be done to improve policy coherence, especially concerning SDG 13 on climate action for which a case study was conducted herein. In our view, contradictory policy signals could jeopardise the implementation of this SDG. Along these lines, other risk factors for the 2030 Agenda, in general, are related to the tendency to cherry-pick certain SDGs to focus on, rather than take a holistic approach and integrate all of them across different policy domains.

title: The Law and Economics of the Ai Excuse: Liability, Perception Bias, and the Case for Epistemic Calibration

detail.title: The Law and Economics of the Ai Excuse: Liability, Perception Bias, and the Case for Epistemic Calibration
detail.abstract: Large language models err persuasively, distorting users' beliefs about AI reliability through an architecturally induced perception bias. We model the interaction between a developer, an LLM, and a boundedly rational human decision-maker, and prove three results. First, Liability Separation Failure (Theorems 1 and 1′): no pure liability regime-strict human liability, strict developer liability, or negligence-can implement the first-best across the full range of AI capabilities. Second, Paradox of Human Oversight (Section 5): a reasonableness standard collapses into the biased decision rule, rendering mandated oversight structurally hollow. Third, Restoration Theorems (Theorems 2 and 3): a Calibrated Reliability Score mandate, paired with conditional liability, restores the first-best. Embedded in a Grossman-Hart-Moore framework, perception bias shifts optimal asset ownership toward the AI developer-a new verticalintegration prediction-and a CRS mandate substitutes for ownership reallocation.

title: The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education
affiliations: Stockholm University - Institute for International Economic Studies (IIES), The University of Hong Kong - University of Hong Kong and University of Hong Kong

detail.title: The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education

declarations.ethicsApproval: The data collection and use for this project were approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of Hong Kong (reference number: EA260129). The study involves analysis of administrative school records and a student survey.

detail.abstract: Using 30 months of panel data on 26,811 Chinese students in grades 7-12, we study how generative AI a¤ects homework productivity and learning. The data combine monthly closed-book exams, high-school and college entrance exams, and homework scores and completion time across nine subjects. We exploit staggered AI adoption in a di¤erence-in-di¤erences design. AI adoption raises homework scores by 18% and reduces completion time by 30%, but lowers monthly exam scores by 20% within six months. High-stakes entrance-exam scores fall by 18 and 24%, with the full penalty emerging only after about two years. The losses are largest in social science subjects, followed by STEM and languages, and are especially large for junior students, high-achieving students, and boys. The learning losses are concentrated among roughly 80% of AI users whose behavior is consistent with homework outsourcing, as indicated by exceptionally short homework completion time coupled with high homework scores. AI users who maintain similar homework completion time as non-AI users experience small learning losses.
