title: Environmental Preferences of Individual Investors and Mutual Fund Investments: Evidence from Account-Level Data
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University, The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Environmental Preferences of Individual Investors and Mutual Fund Investments: Evidence from Account-Level Data
detail.abstract: This study investigates the environmental preferences of individual investors and their influence on mutual fund investments. Leveraging Ant Group's comprehensive account-level data from China and aligning with the theoretical implications of Pástor, Stambaugh, and Taylor (2021), we find that investors who engage in eco-friendly behaviors are more likely to favor funds with higher environmental scores. To mitigate endogeneity concerns, we exploit plausibly exogenous variation in local air pollution as an instrument, consistent with a causal link between eco-friendly behaviors and investment choices. However, this preference comes at a cost, as these investors experience lower future portfolio performance, reflecting a willingness to prioritize environmental responsibility over financial returns. Furthermore, they exhibit reduced sensitivity of fund flows to recent performance. These effects are particularly pronounced among female, younger, and wealthier investors, as well as those residing in developed or metropolitan areas, or cities with superior ecological conditions and heightened environmental awareness.

title: Ethics of the Peptide Boom: Mapping the Terrain

detail.title: Ethics of the Peptide Boom: Mapping the Terrain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest. No financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Peptides have become a highly visible phenomenon in contemporary digital health and youth culture. Marketed across social media as tools for becoming healthier, stronger, more attractive, and more productive, they have generated widespread enthusiasm and scientific concern. Despite this prominence, however, the peptide boom has thus far received little bioethical attention. This article argues that understanding the phenomenon requires more than assessing the safety or efficacy of individual compounds. It conceptualizes the peptide boom as a convergent phenomenon in which four mutually reinforcing dynamics come together: self-optimization culture, experimental health practices, social media infrastructures, and ideological backing. Examining this convergence reveals three ethical challenges that put established bioethical categories under pressure: the erosion of conditions for informed decision-making, the reconfiguration of epistemic authority, and the systematic evasion of responsibility and accountability. By identifying distinctive dynamics of the peptide boom and mapping its ethical challenges, the article lays essential groundwork for future bioethical engagement with this rapidly expanding phenomenon.

title: Mechanisms of AI-Induced Psychosis: A Multi-Pathway Escalation Model

detail.title: Mechanisms of AI-Induced Psychosis: A Multi-Pathway Escalation Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to declare.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a multi-pathway escalation model for how large language model (LLM) design failures escalate and sustain delusional states and, in severe cases, full psychotic episodes in vulnerable users. Internal industry estimates imply that hundreds of thousands of users per week show possible signs of mania or psychosis, yet no published model has connected the known behavioral properties of LLMs to these outcomes at a level specific enough to be tested against conversation data. The model’s scope is bounded by the fixity criterion: it applies where a psychotic state exists or comes to exist, and it excludes the larger population of cases in which the belief remained an overvalued idea that yielded to counter-evidence, because those cases, whatever harm they involve, are not psychosis. Within scope, the mechanisms operate by triggering, inducing, and exacerbating psychotic states in users whose vulnerability pre-exists the exposure or, in the documented exception of sustained sleep deprivation, is manufactured by it; none of these relationships is causation in the strict sense, and the model asserts none. Drawing on systematic comparison of documented cases (legal filings, journalism, published survivor accounts, and direct correspondence with affected individuals, including one case with primary access to conversation exports and transcripts), this paper identifies three distinct escalation pathways (trust transfer, sycophantic addiction, and stochastic gaslighting) that share universal entry conditions and converge on identical isolation and identity-disruption outcomes but diverge in their core mechanisms and therefore require different clinical interventions. The pathways are mapped across a structured stage model of four universal stages and three pathway-specific escalation phases. The paper argues that AI literacy functions as both prevention and treatment, supported by documented recovery cases, and identifies the central barrier to validation: the absence of any centralized, anonymized repository of AI-associated harm transcripts available to the broader research community.

title: ESG Ratings and REIT Stock Liquidity
affiliations: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University - School of Accounting and Finance, The China Commerce Association for General Merchandise (CCAGM),  and Fudan University - School of Management

detail.title: ESG Ratings and REIT Stock Liquidity
detail.abstract: This study examines whether Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance influences the stock liquidity of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). Analyzing U.S. REITs from 2007 to 2021, we find that superior ESG ratings, specifically within the environmental and social dimensions, significantly enhance liquidity. This effect persists after controlling for disclosure quality. We identify reduced asset-valuation uncertainty and increased participation from socially responsible institutions as primary mechanisms. The liquidity benefits are most pronounced for REITs exposed to high climate risks. These findings suggest that ESG performance provides a critical, non-redundant signal of asset-level resilience in the transparent REIT market.

title: Forward Hedging Reshapes Incentive Provision
affiliations: Université Paris-Dauphine, New York University (NYU) - New York University and University of Toulouse Capitole - Toulouse School of Economics

detail.title: Forward Hedging Reshapes Incentive Provision
detail.abstract: We study how forward hedging reshapes incentive provision inside the firm. We consider a risk-averse producer facing demand and production risk that can either operate in-house or delegate production to a risk-averse agent under moral hazard, while hedging output in a competitive forward market with a rational market maker. Within a tractable continuoustime CARA framework, we jointly characterize optimal production, compensation, and static hedging in equilibrium. Delegation and external hedging are partial substitutes because both create value through risk sharing. Delegation can increase firm value even when the agent uses the same technology and is more risk averse than the principal, while access to forward hedging reduces the need to provide incentives through risk exposure. This mechanism delivers two main results. First, the principal hedges less under delegation than under in-house production. Second, this lower hedging demand under delegation raises the equilibrium forward price relative to the integrated benchmark. In the constant-demand case, we show that access to hedging lowers the agent's expected compensation under delegation. Numerical results indicate that this mechanism remains robust in the presence of demand uncertainty. More broadly, our results show that external risk transfer through financial markets feeds back into internal organizational design.

title: Navigating Legal Fragmentation Towards a Framework of Coordinated Pluralism for Cross-Border AI Regulation
affiliations: East China University of Political Science and Law (ECUPL)

detail.title: Navigating Legal Fragmentation Towards a Framework of Coordinated Pluralism for Cross-Border AI Regulation
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation and transnational operations involving Artificial Intelligence (AI) in recent times have fundamentally challenged the territorial foundations of foreign-related law. While existing scholarship has diagnosed this problem through the lens of regulatory divergence, it predominantly relies on soft-law principles and lacks enforceable mechanisms for conflict resolution. This article fills that gap by providing a new theoretical model of "coordinated pluralism." This research examines the extra-territorial application of domestic laws relating to AI and how existing laws are used to resolve disputes between laws and countries' sovereignty over the digital realm (i.e., some countries' digital sovereignty protects them from competing in the digital space). The paper moves beyond high-level ethical guidelines and develops four concrete methods to manage disputes created in the cross-border application of AI by: (1) establishing international interoperability standards for high-risk AI systems; (2) developing mutual recognition agreements to facilitate standardization of conformity assessment; (3) establishing a multilateral oversight body to provide country participation in the establishment and enforcement of standards; and (4) creating a protocol to address cross-border liability using private international law as the foundation for creating a protocol for establishing liability across jurisdictions. This research addresses the conflict of laws as to how laws are to be applied, how they could be enforced, and how companies operating across borders could be liable to other countries. It also provides a reasonable way forward to create a structure that allows countries to maintain some level of independence while promoting a shared global market through regulatory interoperability. Finally, this paper advances the theoretical and practical development of foreign laws and establishes a method for addressing legal issues related to cross-border AI risks without compromising the sovereignty of countries. To accomplish this, the study will begin with a mapping of the different kinds of substantive regulatory fragmentation across the European Union (EU), the United States (US) and China, before examining the conflicts of jurisdiction resulting from extraterritoriality and digital sovereignty from the perspective of private international law. Then, the research assesses current international cooperation mechanisms in an effort to identify the institutional gaps, which it will then utilise to develop the new afore-mentioned framework consisting of four pillars: interoperability standards, mutual recognition, oversight and liability protocols. Lastly, the article concludes with a discussion of the challenges associated with effective enforcement and geopolitical trust, which must be overcome to implement the proposed framework. The integration of conflict of law doctrines with regulatory coordination in this study provides a highly practicable path for global corporate compliance and multinational risk management while moving theoretical and institutional development forward in the governance of cross-border artificial intelligence.

title: Social Capital and Total Factor Productivity: Evidence from Plant-Level Data
affiliations: University of St. Thomas and Texas A&M International University, Wayne State University

detail.title: Social Capital and Total Factor Productivity: Evidence from Plant-Level Data
detail.abstract: Using U.S. Census microdata, we show that ethical social norms yield measurable economic benefits. County-level social capital, which measures cooperation and the honoring of obligations, significantly enhances plant productivity, particularly where corporate oversight is weak, consistent with ethical norms substituting for costly monitoring. Plants in high-social-capital regions also attract more skilled labor, invest more capital, deploy capital more efficiently, and achieve higher output per worker. The effect of social capital on productivity is especially pronounced during adverse conditions.

title: Scale-Invariant Economic Security in Sampled-Audit Proof-of-Useful-Work

detail.title: Scale-Invariant Economic Security in Sampled-Audit Proof-of-Useful-Work
detail.abstract: Proof-of-useful-work (PoUW) replaces the wasted computation of proof-of-work with valuable tasks such as machine-learning inference, but has historically failed on the verification asymmetry: useful work is as costly to verify as to perform. Zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) removes the asymmetry cryptographically, yet proving overheads currently preclude verifying every job. We analyze a sampled-audit design in which each committed job is audited independently with probability p after commitment, escalating from cheap re-execution to a zkML dispute court, with detected fraud slashing a stake S. We prove that economic security reduces to one scale-invariant bound, S > c/p, where c is the cost of one job: the attacker's expected profit from fabricating k results is then strictly decreasing in k, so the optimal attack is a single fabricated job, and it is unprofitable. The bound is invariant to batch size and robust to exit scams, Sybil splitting, and audit-gap hunting; Monte Carlo simulation validates all claims. We further prove exponential fragility under randomness grinding, detection collapses to p g with g candidate seeds, making unbiasable randomness a hard requirement, and derive the cost-optimal sampling rate p * = δ /κ.

title: Are Sustainability Pledges Anticompetitive?
affiliations: DePaul University and University of Illinois

detail.title: Are Sustainability Pledges Anticompetitive?
detail.abstract: When there are gaps in government regulation, firms can cater to consumer preferences through private governance initiatives. Recent antitrust enforcement has claimed such initiatives are illegal as firms use monopsony power to exclude suppliers. We use theory to discuss the competitive effects of market-exclusion pledges, then apply it to the Amazon Soy Moratorium (ASM), an initiative by soy traders that sharply decreased deforestation. Despite excluding noncompliant farmers, we find that the ASM has no significant effects on average farmgate prices. It also induces higher entry by ASM signatory traders. This suggests there can be complementary economic benefits to sustainability pledges.

title: Posted Prices, Unequal Bargains: Pay Transparency Laws and the Gender Negotiation Gap

detail.title: Posted Prices, Unequal Bargains: Pay Transparency Laws and the Gender Negotiation Gap
detail.abstract: Existing studies generally find that pay transparency laws narrow the gender pay gap. Using Current Population Survey data (2018-2026) and a staggered difference-indifferences design, I first show a narrowing effect, then show this is driven by a selection artifact: adopting states have structurally smaller gender gaps. Under proper identification, the gap widens by 4.3 percentage points. I test two channels that could explain this result: labor market mobility and individual negotiation. The evidence points to negotiation: the widening is concentrated among salaried workers, whose pay is individually bargained, and absent among hourly workers, whose pay is not. Absent additional institutional constraints on wage-setting, mandatory salary disclosure may unintentionally reinforce gendered differences in negotiation, achieving the opposite of its intended effect.

detail.title: Dual vs. Single Momentum in Commodities: Enhancing Risk-Adjusted Returns through Absolute Trend Filtering

detail.abstract: Commodities represent a vital but highly volatile asset class, characterized by pronounced cyclicality, lack of yield, and susceptibility to severe macroeconomic drawdowns. While cross-sectional (relative) momentum is a well-documented anomaly, its application in commodities often forces portfolios to hold the "least declining" assets during broad-based bear markets, resulting in unacceptable tail-risk. This study empirically evaluates the efficacy of a Dual Momentum framework-combining relative strength ranking with an absolute time-series trend filter-applied to a diversified suite of commodity sector ETFs (DBA, DBB, DBE, DBP) from 2007 to 2026. We demonstrate that while pure relative momentum exhibits high parameter sensitivity and inconsistent benchmark outperformance, the inclusion of an absolute momentum filter structurally mitigates drawdowns and universally outperforms a static, equally weighted benchmark across all tested parameter combinations. The findings suggest that Dual Momentum provides a robust, parameter-agnostic framework for portfolio managers seeking tactical commodity exposure with superior risk-adjusted return profiles.

title: Al-Bayʿ, Al-Dayn and Al-Ribā: A Qurʾān-First Reconstruction of Deferred Commercial Obligation, Ribā Escalation, and Debt Governance.

detail.title: Al-Bayʿ, Al-Dayn and Al-Ribā: A Qurʾān-First Reconstruction of Deferred Commercial Obligation, Ribā Escalation, and Debt Governance.
detail.abstract: Purpose: This paper develops a Qurʾānic and Hadīth-grounded theory of permissible commercial exchange (bayʿ), deferred monetary obligation (dayn bi-ajal), and the structural prohibition of ribāʾ, advancing nine original propositions constituting a complete moral taxonomy of Islamic economic instruments. Design/methodology/approach-The paper employs an integrated qualitative methodology combining tawqīfī textual analysis of fourteen Qurʾānic verses; uṣūl al-fiqh jurisprudential analysis, including ʿillah identification, isnād criticism, and ijmāʿ delimitation; taxonomic theory construction tested against a paradigmatic transaction; and critical literature review identifying six conflations in the existing literature. Findings-Q. 2:274-2:282 is identified as a unified nine-step legislative argument, the first complete reading of this passage in the Islamic finance literature. The pagan challenge of Q. 2:275 (that bayʿ and ribāʾ are alike) is answered in Q. 2:279-2:280: the bilateral non-harm principle (lā taẓlimūna wa-lā tuẓlamūna) is the juristic criterion; the naẓra command at debtor ʿusra is its operational proof. Further findings establish that qard al-ḥasan is simultaneously ṣadaqah to people and a loan to Allah; that commercial dayn bi-ajal serves the solvent ghanī excluded from ṣadaqah; that the six-goods Hadīth does not extend to modern fiat currency; and that the ribāʾ prohibition trigger is conditional escalation at verified debtor hardship. Practical implications-The five-test Sharīʿa compliance framework provides first-principles supervisory criteria applicable to Islamic banking regulation, sukūk restructuring, payment systems, and SDG-aligned financial inclusion policy. Originality/value-The paper provides the first unified four-rukūʿ architectural reading of Q. 2:274-2:282; identifies Rukūʿ 38's three-movement structure as a complete ribāʾ rehabilitation framework; identifies Rukūʿ 39's four-party institutional blueprint as the Qurʾānic design for commercial banking; derives the productive-purpose criterion for distinguishing dayn bi-ajal from pure qard from within Q. 2:282, Q. 4:29, and Q. 2:279 without reliance on juristic extension; and provides a text-anchored nine-proposition compliance instrument applicable across all four Sunnī madhabs.

title: Beyond Clinical Competence: Measuring Ethical Reliability and Behavioral Risk in High-Trust Professions Through Systems-Based Governance

detail.title: Beyond Clinical Competence: Measuring Ethical Reliability and Behavioral Risk in High-Trust Professions Through Systems-Based Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Healthcare organizations have long relied upon educational preparation, professional licensure, certification, credentialing, competency validation, and continuing education to determine workforce readiness. These mechanisms remain essential for evaluating clinical knowledge and technical proficiency; however, they provide comparatively limited insight into the behavioral and organizational factors that frequently contribute to preventable harm. Contemporary patient safety research consistently demonstrates that adverse events rarely result from isolated clinical error alone. Instead, they emerge through complex interactions among organizational culture, leadership, communication, technology, work design, and human behavior.

Although substantial progress has been made in understanding healthcare as a sociotechnical system, workforce governance continues to emphasize technical competence while devoting comparatively less attention to ethical reliability, professional judgment, escalation behavior, psychological safety, and organizational accountability. Consequently, many behavioral risks are recognized only after patient harm, workforce misconduct, or significant organizational failure has occurred. This paper proposes a governance-centered framework that expands workforce evaluation beyond traditional competency assessment by incorporating evidence-based measures of ethical reliability and behavioral risk that are directly related to professional performance. The proposed approach does not advocate for invasive surveillance or attempts to predict individual morality. Rather, it examines how validated assessments of professional conduct, ethical decision-making, communication, escalation practices, organizational culture, and leadership accountability may strengthen patient safety while remaining consistent with employment law, civil rights protections, and evidence-based human resource practices.

Drawing upon the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS), High Reliability Organization (HRO) theory, organizational behavior research, patient safety literature, ECRI analyses, NHS England patient safety frameworks, and federal reporting systems, this paper argues that ethical reliability should be recognized as an organizational governance construct rather than solely an individual characteristic. Integrating behavioral governance into existing quality and safety systems may provide healthcare organizations with additional opportunities to identify organizational vulnerabilities, strengthen accountability, and improve public trust before preventable harm occurs.

title: Kristiansen's Theorem, Generalized Gamma Convolutions, and the Riemann Wald Couple
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Kristiansen's Theorem, Generalized Gamma Convolutions, and the Riemann Wald Couple

title: Does AI Crowd Out Context? Evidence from Clinical Radiology
affiliations: INSEAD and

detail.title: Does AI Crowd Out Context? Evidence from Clinical Radiology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is often deployed on the premise that algorithms provide precision while human decision makers provide contextual judgment. We identify a limit to this complementarity. AI advice can reduce the value that humans derive from contextual information the algorithm does not observe. We study this in an experiment in which radiologists evaluate chest X-ray cases with varied access to AI predictions and clinical history. Without AI, clinical history improves agreement with a fully informed benchmark most in cases where its measured value is greatest. When AI is displayed with clinical history, this relationship reverses, and the combined workflow moves farther from the benchmark precisely where clinical history should contribute most. A Bayesian signal-extraction framework shows that some reduction in the contribution of clinical history is rational when AI increases the precision of the image-based information. Yet the observed reduction of clinical-history value is roughly 2.6 times the calibrated Bayesian precision-reweighting benchmark. The loss appears across diagnostic ambiguity levels and all but the most skilled radiologist groups, suggesting that simple targeting rules are unlikely to eliminate it. Behavioral evidence suggests that AI changes attention rather than effort. Radiologists remain active but engage less with clinical history, and their assessments stay closer to the AI prediction. The findings show that the value of human contextual knowledge is endogenous to workflow design. AI advice can crowd out human contextual knowledge rather than simply complement it. Effective AI deployment depends not only on model accuracy, but also on when and how AI advice enters the decision process.

title: Reforming The Nigeria Police Force: A Pathway to a Better Nigeria

detail.title: Reforming The Nigeria Police Force: A Pathway to a Better Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest Statement The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, clinical data, or experimental procedures. As the paper is based on publicly available information, policy analysis, and the author's independent proposals, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's security crisis remains one of the most pressing challenges to national development, with rising insolvency, banditry, and public distrust of law enforcement undermining the country's stability. At the center of this crisis lies the Nigeria Police Force (NPF)an institution with over 370,000 active officers and a 2025 budgetary allocation of ₦1.31 trillion, yet one that continues to fall short of its mandate. This paper argues that the path to sustainable security in Nigeria does not lie in the creation of new armed institutions, but in the comprehensive reformation of the existing Police Force. Drawing on budget analysis, personnel data, and comparative security frameworks, this paper proposes a two-pronged reform agenda: a mindset overhaul through structured military-influenced training for future officers, and a performance-based reward system that ties promotion and salary increments to verified case resolutions. Together, these measures aim to cultivate a culture of accountability, professionalism, and purpose within the NPF. While this framework is presented as a foundational prototype subject to further policy development, it offers a practical starting point for legislators, security stakeholders, and civil society actors committed to building a safer Nigeria.

title: Business Narratives and Exchange Rates
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, University of Liverpool and

detail.title: Business Narratives and Exchange Rates
detail.abstract: We study how narratives about the macroeconomy drive exchange rates since business narratives provide incremental information that shapes macroeconomic beliefs. Relying on the full text of more than 20 million news articles from ten newspapers, we estimate a topic model that summarizes business news into interpretable thematic factors for each country. Employing machine learning methods, we disprove the exchange rate disconnect puzzle by demonstrating that the bilateral narrative factors strongly predict nominal and real exchange rates both in-sample and out-of-sample. The predictive ability of narratives is not spanned by conventional economic factors and delivers substantial economic value. We further identify the economic mechanism underlying these results by showing that business narratives capture forward-looking information about macroeconomic fundamentals.

title: Rejection-Induced Confabulation Escalation -Pilot Study 2 (RICE-P2): Source-Request Framing and FCR Position Modulate URL Fabrication in Large Language Models

detail.title: Rejection-Induced Confabulation Escalation -Pilot Study 2 (RICE-P2): Source-Request Framing and FCR Position Modulate URL Fabrication in Large Language Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study used LLM API responses to fictional entity probes. No human subjects were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Source fabrication-the generation of plausible but nonexistent citations by large language models (LLMs)-poses a practical problem in information-seeking contexts. Prior work (RICE-P1) found that quality challenges do not escalate fabrication; the present study (RICE-P2) examines whether FCR position and source-request framing modulate fabrication rates. In a pre-registered 16-arm factorial experiment (N = 1,280 runs; 40 fictional entities; 2 platforms), we tested ChatGPT and Perplexity AI using automated content-based URL annotation as the primary endpoint (BSE@FCR: Bad Source Exposure at First Citation Request). Results revealed a near-total platform divergence: Perplexity produced bad sources in 100% of FCR-arm runs (600/600), ChatGPT in 15.7% (94/600; Fisher's exact p < 0.001). Among ChatGPT runs, fabrication increased with FCR delay (Mann-Whitney p = 0.010), SAFE framing eliminated fabrication entirely (BSE = 0%, p = 0.0004 vs. standard), QUOTA framing tripled fabrication rates (70% vs. 28%, p < 0.001), and a quality challenge immediately before the FCR suppressed fabrication by 80% (OR = 0.20, p = 0.003). Claim-mapping framing (CLAIMMAP) was null on BSE but reduced Perplexity's False Source Rate by 50-74%. Source fabrication is powerfully architecture-dependent and is modulated by prompt framing and conversational context at the moment of the source request.

title: The Societal Response Index: Measuring Public Response to Sexual Misconduct Disclosure

detail.title: The Societal Response Index: Measuring Public Response to Sexual Misconduct Disclosure
detail.abstract: How societies respond after women disclose sexual misconduct shapes survivors’ well-being, reporting behavior, institutional accountability, and social norms. Yet, no validated measure of society’s collective public response following disclosure exists. This paper introduces the Societal Response Index (SRI), a pre-registered, multidimensional framework with 5 complementary dimensions — volume persistence (VP), secondary victimization, identity exposure, supportive/contested response, and temporal reactivation — and develops and validates its first dimension, VP. Using census-level tweet counts from the X fullarchive API, I construct weekly attention series for fourteen sexual misconduct cases spanning Spain, the United States, and France (2011–2026). VP’s three highest-attention weeks fall within two weeks of a pre-registered milestone for all fourteen cases; same-day detection reaches 75% and within-14-day detection reaches 91%. VP correlates positively and significantly with Google Trends for all cases. The measurement architecture, keyword dictionaries, and event timelines will be released as a public good upon publication. As an illustration of substantive reach, official reporting of sexual offenses tends to rise following case milestones.

title: The Composition of Blame: Responsibility-Attribution Design and Strategic Inattention in Monitoring

detail.title: The Composition of Blame: Responsibility-Attribution Design and Strategic Inattention in Monitoring

keywords: Negligence and the Standard of Care

detail.abstract: Recurring failures of oversight-an auditor who does not catch a specialist's error, a manager who does not catch an employee's-are increasingly modelled not as accidents of effort but as equilibria: the monitor rationally avoids observing the work he supervises, because observability concentrates blame. That literature takes the blame-attribution rule as given. This paper makes the rule the object of design. After a failure surfaces, an adjudicator assigns the monitor a share of responsibility that depends on whether the failure was within his reach; the induced blame-share function is increasing, flat, or decreasing in observability exactly according to the sign of a single structural primitive-the reach-contingent blame differential ∆, the extra blame placed on a within-reach failure relative to an out-of-reach one. Regimes with ∆ > 0 ("should-have-known" / negligence) breed the inattention trap; regimes with ∆ ≤ 0 (role-based or duty-to-observe) dissolve it, and in fact reverse the penalty paradox: a tougher monitoring penalty lowers observability when ∆ > 0 but raises it when ∆ ≤ 0. The trap-breeding rule is microfounded as the corner of a Bayesian negligence protocol, of which the standard linear specification is the limiting case. Auditing standards, however, set duties of conduct and a nonreduction-of-responsibility principle-full responsibility whether or not the failure was within reach, a nominal ∆ = 0-while the operative attribution is left to an enforcement and liability layer that excuses the failure the auditor could not see, a de facto ∆ > 0 that no standard designs. The effective instrument is therefore the composition of blame, not the level of the penalty.

title: Enforcement Spillovers and the Efficiency Costs of Means-Tested Transfers: Evidence from Workplace Networks
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Enforcement Spillovers and the Efficiency Costs of Means-Tested Transfers: Evidence from Workplace Networks
detail.abstract: Standard welfare evaluations of means-tested transfers typically treat eligibility enforcement as affecting only households directly exposed to the rule. We show that this direct-only approach is incomplete when enforcement events transmit information through workplace networks, inducing other beneficiaries to adjust formal employment and reported earnings. We study Uruguay’s AFAM-PE conditional cash transfer, in which household income eligibility is verified monthly using administrative records of formal earnings and households exceeding the threshold may lose benefits, while most beneficiaries are largely unaware of the income rule. Linking program records, social security employment histories, and firm identifiers, we build workplace networks defined six months before each peer’s exposure to enforcement and identify spillovers using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design that exploits quasi-random variation in whether a peer crosses the income threshold. Coworkers of peers just above the cutoff reduce registered labor earnings by 20%, and the corresponding fuzzy-RD estimate implies a decline of about one-third of baseline earnings in response to a peer’s suspension. These effects emerge within two months and persist for at least 12 months. The response operates almost entirely on the extensive margin of formal employment, and most of the decline reflects transitions to informal work rather than exit from the labor force. Spillovers are concentrated in small firms and among similar coworkers, are nearly three times larger when the suspended peer actively contacted the program’s support service, and are absent among non-beneficiary coworkers. This pattern is consistent with information transmission as the main channel. Incorporating these indirect responses lowers the estimated MVPF of the program as implemented with enforcement from 0.53 to 0.36. Because the same information channel operates wherever means-tested programs are enforced through records of formal earnings, evaluations that count only directly exposed households systematically understate the cost of enforcement.

title: Macroeconomic Cycles and Bond Return Predictability
affiliations: Department of Economics, Lancaster University Management School and

detail.title: Macroeconomic Cycles and Bond Return Predictability
detail.abstract: We study the link between the macroeconomy and expected bond returns by dissecting common macroeconomic cycles of different lengths. Two unobservable predictors generate sizeable economic value for investors: an inflation factor maximizing macroeconomic cycles of at least 8 years, and a term spread factor maximizing cycles of 1 to 3 years. The inflation factor captures the stance of monetary policy as return premia increase when the policy rule becomes "hawkish". The term spread factor reflects investors' perception of business-cycle risk.

title: Driving Analytics vs Data Drift: A Continuous Validation Model for Decision Integrity in Data-Driven Systems
affiliations: Independent Researcher, USA.

detail.title: Driving Analytics vs Data Drift: A Continuous Validation Model for Decision Integrity in Data-Driven Systems
detail.abstract: Data-driven systems increasingly rely on analytics pipelines and machine learning models to support critical decisions. However, changes in input data, feature relationships, and model outputs can degrade performance over time and undermine decision integrity. This paper proposes a Continuous Validation Model (CVM) that unifies data quality monitoring, drift detection, model validation, explainability, and compliance checks into a single framework. The proposed approach continuously evaluates both data and model behavior, detects multiple forms of drift, and supports automated remediation through adaptive feedback loops. A mathematical formulation for composite validation is presented, along with a case study illustrating the use of CVM in a regulated decision environment. Comparative analysis shows that continuous validation offers stronger drift detection, broader validation coverage, and more sustained decision integrity than static or periodic approaches.

title: Asset-Based Lending as a Leading Indicator of Systemic Crises
affiliations: and Goldman Sachs - Goldman Sachs

detail.title: Asset-Based Lending as a Leading Indicator of Systemic Crises
detail.abstract: We show that asset-based lending (ABL) survey data predict systemic financial stress. From the quarterly surveys of the U.S. secured-lending industry (2009-2025), we construct a composite of private, lender-reported credit-quality indicators. Out of sample, adding the ABL composite to a standard macro-financial control set raises twelve-month-ahead crisis discrimination from an AUROC of 0.67 to 0.73. The predictive content is horizon-dependent: at longer horizons, lenders' private survey assessments outperform secondary-market ABS prices, consistent with confidential lender information leading market prices; the edge narrows at shorter horizons. The long-horizon signal is robust to controls for bank-lending standards, financial-conditions indices, and bank-level delinquencies. We establish ABL lender surveys as a novel class of leading systemic-stress indicators, complementary to the macro-financial early-warning literature.

title: Wisdomism: Toward the First Wisdom Revolution

detail.title: Wisdomism: Toward the First Wisdom Revolution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. This work is independent scholarship and does not represent the position of any institution.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical and philosophical work involving no human or animal participants, no personal data, and no empirical studies requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Wisdomism is a civilisational framework for a possible transition in human history: the shift from economies organised primarily around production and information to systems organised around meaning, legitimacy, alignment, and wise coordination across time. If that diagnosis is correct, we may be approaching the threshold of what could become the First Wisdom Revolution. This paper presents the philosophical, economic, and organisational architecture of Wisdomism. It is structured across six layers: a civilisational aim, a diagnostic economic layer, a transformation layer, a valuation layer, a governance and distribution layer, and a computational research horizon. It does not claim that the First Wisdom Revolution has already arrived. It claims that naming its conditions is itself a necessary step toward it.
The framework introduces: Dynamic Prophecy (D = FO−FP+NP−NO) as the civilisational evaluation engine; Amber Logic and Graphene Logic as the two system logics governing temporal context and alignment; Accessism as the distribution grammar distinguishing Universal Baseline Income from Generative Weighted Income; and the Wisdom Matrix as the organisational model mapping coordination forms across six tiers.

title: State-Dependent Estimator Precision

detail.title: State-Dependent Estimator Precision
detail.abstract: Many empirical estimands are high-dimensional objects, including impulse-response surfaces, treatment-effect profiles, and event-study paths. Conventional inference summarizes uncertainty through average covariance matrices, standard errors, or confidence bands, obscuring variation in estimator reliability across states and estimand directions. This paper develops a diagnostic for state-dependent estimator precision. For any asymptotically linear estimator, influence contributions define a random operator-valued kernel. Spectral whitening of average influence covariance yields low-dimensional coordinates whose conditional covariance identifies state-specific precision, summarized by an amplification index and directional decompositions. The diagnostic complements robust standard errors and reveals substantial variation across time, support, and region-year cells.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Settlement Verification in Oracle-Based Decentralized Finance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Settlement Verification in Oracle-Based Decentralized Finance
detail.abstract: Decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols that depend on external settlement facts (whether asset prices from oracle networks or off-chain payment confirmations) must make irreversible on-chain state transitions based on information they cannot directly verify. This settlement verification problem is governed by a fundamental tension between safety (rejecting false claims) and liveness (accepting true claims promptly), mediated by the capital, latency, and trust assumptions a protocol is willing to absorb. We formalize settlement verification as a binary hypothesis-testing problem over an adversarial multi-publisher channel and establish three main results. (1) Oracle Verification Trilemma. For any settlement verification mechanism operating over an adversarial oracle channel with adversarial fraction ϕ < 1/2, we prove a joint lower bound on the safety error εs, the liveness latency τ , and the required collateral B:εs ≥ max exp(−n · D(1 2 ∥ϕ)), B V +B ) , where n = ⌊τ/∆t⌋ is the number of verification rounds in latency win dow τ, D(·∥·) is the binary KL divergence, V is the value at risk, and the second term reflects the economic incentive constraint for a ratio nal adversary. No mechanism simultaneously achieves negligible safety error, constant latency, and zero collateral: the three vertices of the or acle trilemma. (2) Paradigm-Specific Achievability. We show that the four deployed paradigms (optimistic oracles, decentralized oracle net works, cryptographic verification, legal-hybrid systems) each achieve a distinct, non-dominated point on the trilemma frontier, and we derive tight achievability bounds for each. (3) Composition with Down stream Mechanisms. We prove that when an oracle feeds a down stream mechanism with a well-defined error-absorption capacity δ (e.g., a hyperbolic funding rate), the compound protocol failure probability is bounded by εs + Pr[|∆true − ∆oracle| > δ], where δ is the mechanism’s error-absorption capacity. For hyperbolic funding rates, the singularity at the solvency boundary provides robustness amplification: a β-fraction capacity utilization tolerates oracle errors up to (1 − β) times the total capacity.

title: Election Probabilities and the Treasury Yield Curve
affiliations: Sabanci University and Bogazici University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Election Probabilities and the Treasury Yield Curve
detail.abstract: During the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign, daily increases in Polymarket's Trump win probability were associated with a long-end Treasury steepening and a coherent cross-asset "Trump-trade." A ten-percentage-point probability rise corresponds to a ∼2 basis-point steepening of the 2s10s slope and a parallel rise in 10-year breakeven inflation; the short end and the overnight policy rate are unresponsive, and an Adrian et al. (2013) decomposition assigns 95% of the ten-year response to the term premium. Identification combines a non-trading-hours decomposition with a 2SLS estimator that instruments the daily change with its overnight component (first-stage F = 37). On Election Night, while cash markets were closed, CME futures repriced the entire signature-10-year yields +12.5 bp, S&P 500 +2.1%, the dollar +2.2%-before the cash open. A formal Election Day holdout predicts the realized 8 bp slope move within 1 bp and the 5 bp real-yield move within rounding. The relation replicates on Betfair and on the 2020 PredictIt cycle, while a 2019 pre-period placebo is statistically zero at every maturity. We treat sign and channel composition, not the daily point estimate, as the load-bearing inference.

title: Child Disability and Effects on Sibling Mental Health
affiliations: Yale University, University of Copenhagen, University of Copenhagen, Department of Economics and VIVE - The Danish Center for Social Science Research

detail.title: Child Disability and Effects on Sibling Mental Health
detail.abstract: We ask how a younger sibling’s physical disability affects sibling mental health using Danish register data on families with three or more children. Difference-in-difference models compare first- and second-born children when the third-born does or does not have a disability. Use of mental health services increases 13% among second-born children, with a 23% increase in psychiatric visits and an 18% increase in use of psychiatric medications. Effects are concentrated in households where the mother has less than high school and persist after conditioning on child test scores. Parental responses suggest that caregiving demands, stress, and strained resources are potential mechanisms.

title: Contraceptive Access Costs, Pill Sales and Fertility Across the Age Profile: Evidence from Sweden
affiliations: Stockholm University

detail.title: Contraceptive Access Costs, Pill Sales and Fertility Across the Age Profile: Evidence from Sweden
detail.abstract: How much does the cost of obtaining contraception, as distinct from the legal right to it, shape fertility? I study the pill's introduction in Sweden, where contraception had been legal from age 15 for decades, yet abortion remained nationally restricted for another ten years. Linking the universe of oral-contraceptive sales to pharmacy access measures inherited from centuries of retail regulation, I estimate fertility elasticities to pill sales across narrow age groups. Access-driven pill adoption cut fertility sharply among women under 22; the effect fades quickly with age and is statistically zero by the mid-twenties. Instrumental-variable estimates exceed OLS: women drawn into pill use by lower access costs reduce fertility more than the average adopter. The young-age effects persist across the decade before abortion rights, while women aged 26--29 show modest fertility increases five years after introduction, consistent with postponed rather than forgone births. Even where contraception is fully legal, access costs constrain adoption, and their fertility burden falls on the young.

title: How Do State “Auto-IRA” Policies Affect Household Balance Sheets?
affiliations: Government of the United States of America - Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), Kean University, World Bank and George Mason University - School of Policy, Government, and International Affairs

detail.title: How Do State “Auto-IRA” Policies Affect Household Balance Sheets?
detail.abstract:
We examine how state policies requiring firms to facilitate workplace retirement saving affect household balance sheets. Using data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP), we compare private-sector workers likely exposed to Oregon’s Automatic-Enrollment Individual Retirement Account (Auto-IRA) policy with similar workers in not-yet-adopting states. We find that the Auto-IRA policy is associated with increases in IRA and employer-sponsored retirement plan ownership and assets. We also find increases in checking or savings account ownership and balances, as well as higher credit card debt. The results suggest that Auto-IRA policies spill over to household liquidity management and borrowing.

title: Long Memory and Asymmetric Uncertainty Effects on Stock Returns and Volatility: A Fractional Integration Approach
affiliations: Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Navarra - Department of Economics and University of Navarra - Pamplona Campus

detail.title: Long Memory and Asymmetric Uncertainty Effects on Stock Returns and Volatility: A Fractional Integration Approach
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) affects the returns and volatility (proxied by squared returns) of 448 S&P 500 stocks over the period January 2010–December 2020, and whether volatility persistence is related to EPU sensitivity. Persistence is measured with three semiparametric estimators of the degree of fractional integration: the Geweke–Porter-Hudak log-periodogram regression, the local Whittle, and the exact local Whittle. The linear EPU–volatility link does not survive market-level controls, but extreme EPU shocks generate significant volatility responses in roughly one-fifth of the stocks examined, with a slightly greater impact of adverse (bad) news. Long memory in volatility is pervasive. Persistence and EPU sensitivity are negatively related at the standard bandwidth (ρ = −0.182, p = 0.0001), a link that survives controls for size, liquidity, market beta, and sector fixed effects, and that holds for the subsample of stocks whose long memory is statistically significant according to the Qu (2011) test. This association is mainly concentrated at low frequencies, consistently with a low-frequency phenomenon possibly caused by level shifts.

title: Let’s Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance
affiliations: Brookings Institution, Brown University, Brown University, University of Texas at Austin, University of Central Florida, Georgia State University, Georgia State University, Georgia State University, Georgia State University, Georgia State University and Siena College

detail.title: Let’s Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance
detail.abstract:
This study provides pre-registered, experimental evidence on the use of non-generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots to support students in large-enrollment undergraduate courses. We find the chatbot messaging increased students’ final grades and engagement with academic supports, such as tutoring. Treatment effects were generally consistent across student demographics, with the exception of treated women in a Microeconomics course, who earned final grades that were seven percentage points higher than women in the control group. This study provides evidence that integrating AI-enabled outreach and communication to students in their college courses can enhance student engagement, learning, and course performance.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Economic Analysis & Policy Group, University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics,  and Cornell University

detail.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty
detail.abstract:
Individuals may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and then spend it down over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for under-saving. In order to improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts individuals to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36-60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s impact on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Assessing the Benefits of Optimized Agentic AI Systems for Asset Pricing
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Assessing the Benefits of Optimized Agentic AI Systems for Asset Pricing
detail.abstract:
Evaluating optimized AI systems for asset pricing is fundamentally difficult for two reasons. First, models are trained on all data, implying that any backtest or analysis using historical data suffers from look-ahead bias. In addition, markets are reflexive — as investors adopt AI, prices adjust — which may erode the very patterns the AI system was trained to exploit. We introduce a real-time, out-of-sample benchmark designed to sidestep both problems. The benchmark measures how well AI systems can explain contemporaneous stock returns around earnings announcements using only information available at announcement time, including the text of the announcement itself. Applying this benchmark to a range of agentic AI systems — which extract structured signals from earnings call transcripts and optimize over those signals — we find that the best-optimized systems more than double the explained variation in returns relative to standard benchmarks (R2 increasing from 8% to close to 20%). We show that AI-based optimization can deliver efficiency gains relative to traditional machine learning methods while also improving interpretability as our approach produces human-readable economic mechanisms that explain price movements. These learned rules can be compared to the drivers of realized returns in existing asset pricing models to identify missing sources of variation in a data-driven, self-evolving way that integrates empirical learning with economic structure. We release an SDK for researchers to improve on our results. Saturating this benchmark would represent fundamental progress in understanding how capital markets process firm-level information.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Belligerence Audience Costs, Benefits, or None?
affiliations: Tecnológico de Monterrey and

detail.title: Belligerence Audience Costs, Benefits, or None?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare none.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The authors did not collect original human-subject data or interact with survey respondents. All analyses use secondary, de-identified data and were conducted in accordance with the terms of access for the underlying data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Audience-cost theory suggests that domestic publics can discipline leaders in international crises, but it remains unclear whether citizens punish leaders for belligerence itself. We reassess this question by examining belligerence costs, the penalty domestic audiences impose on leaders for choosing military engagement rather than staying out (Kertzer and Brutger 2016). We first conduct a meta-analysis of 27 survey experiments and find no evidence of a generally applicable belligerence-cost effect: engagement is punished in some studies, rewarded in others, and often has no discernible effect. We then develop a formal model in which citizens evaluate belligerence based on beliefs about whether restraint was feasible and force was necessary. The framework helps explain context-specific variation in the effects of belligerence across studies. We argue that domestic constraints on military escalation are more contingent than often assumed: publics do not punish belligerence per se; they punish belligerence that appears avoidable or unjustified.

title: Never Trust, Always Verify, Securing Medicare's Future to Defend Never Trust, Always Verify, Securing Medicare's Future to Defend Against AI Driven Cyber Threats Against AI Driven Cyber Threats
affiliations: North Carolina Central University (NCCU)

detail.title: Never Trust, Always Verify, Securing Medicare's Future to Defend Never Trust, Always Verify, Securing Medicare's Future to Defend Against AI Driven Cyber Threats Against AI Driven Cyber Threats

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship with people or organizations that could be perceived to be influencers to the research conducted and produced herein.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was self-funded.

detail.abstract: Healthcare cybersecurity stands at a pivotal juncture, analogous to the Cold War's most perilous moments. When President Ronald Reagan declared "trust but verify" 3 during nuclear disarmament negotiations with Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev, he established systematic verification as the cornerstone of security in high-stakes environments where the cost of misplaced trust meant potential human extinction. Today, the rapid integration of artificial intelligence and networked medical devices into America's healthcare infrastructure has created stakes equally grave for the nation's sixty-five million Medicare beneficiaries 4; however, the threat landscape has evolved beyond Reagan's paradigm. Modern healthcare cannot afford even conditional trust in its digital systems; it demands an absolute principle: "never trust, always verify." This imperative reflects a fundamental reality: while cloud-based data sharing, the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), and AI driven clinical tools have revolutionized care delivery, enabling remote monitoring, precision diagnostics, and coordinated treatment across providers, they have simultaneously created attack surfaces and algorithmic vulnerabilities that existing federal regulations do not address.

title: Takeoffs and Test Scores: The Impact of Noise Pollution on Standardized Test Performance
affiliations: University of California San Diego

detail.title: Takeoffs and Test Scores: The Impact of Noise Pollution on Standardized Test Performance
detail.abstract: Noise pollution has become so ubiquitous in urban life that it is generally considered innocuous. However, research suggests that noise pollution can be more than a minor distraction and is associated with diminished health and productivity. I leverage exogenous shifts in noise pollution from changes in aircraft noise and use a value-added model that accounts for student ability and school quality to estimate the causal impact of airplane noise pollution on standardized test performance. I find a large negative impact on math test performance, but no impact on English Language Art test performance. Moving from a school at the 25 th percentile of exposure to one at the 75 th percentile is associated with a math test score reduction of 0.10 standard deviations, twice as large as the impact of missing 10 school days during the year. Additionally, I find evidence that these negative impacts may be driven by the loudest days. These findings suggest a potentially large value to investing in noise insulation for schools exposed to high noise levels.

title: Who Loses from Generative AI? AI Exposure and Career Inequality in the Online Labor Market
affiliations: and

detail.title: Who Loses from Generative AI? AI Exposure and Career Inequality in the Online Labor Market
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether generative AI has differentially affected junior workers in online labor markets. Using worker-month panel data from a large European freelance platform and a task-level AI exposure measure (AIOE), we exploit the release of ChatGPT in a triple-difference design across high-and low-exposure tasks. Junior workers in high-exposure tasks experience a 6.8 percent decline in client contacts, with no statistically detectable effect on prices conditional on winning. The penalty is concentrated at the opportunity-access stage of the hiring funnel: it does not appear at the worker-controlled response and proposal stages, and-conditional on a client contacting a worker-no robust penalty appears at the conversion or price stages. The contraction persists over nearly two years rather than attenuating, at the access stage falls disproportionately on junior women, and is concentrated in the platform's algorithmic matching channel rather than in employer-initiated manual search. Because the algorithmic ranking function is a platform design choice, the findings identify a tractable governance lever and indicate that generative AI may reinforce career inequality by weakening entry access to knowledge-intensive online work.

title: Ambiguity and the Value of Late Resolution of Uncertainty
affiliations: University of Rochester

detail.title: Ambiguity and the Value of Late Resolution of Uncertainty
detail.abstract: The paper shows that in a dynamic setting with multiple sources of uncertainty, recursive ambiguity-averse preferences may imply a preference for late resolution of uncertainty. In particular, the simultaneous resolution of two sources can offer hedging benefits that are negated when one source is resolved earlier and uncertainty is evaluated recursively. The paper illustrates the mechanism in a simple dynamic urn problem. In a special case, an equivalent static formulation involving composite bets on two urns suggests a direct experimental test.

title: Decentralized Exchanges for Stablecoins
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements,  and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Decentralized Exchanges for Stablecoins
detail.abstract: We examine decentralized exchanges (DEXs) like Curve that specialize in stablecoin trading, which co-exist with centralized exchanges (CEXs) like Binance. We develop a simple model of stablecoin trading in which a DEX uses a low-convexity bonding curve to determine trading prices, liquidity traders choose between the DEX and CEX conditional on trade size, and an arbitrageur trades to profit from price staleness when the stablecoin experiences a de-peg shock. Using trade-level data of stablecoins, we empirically confirm the implications of the model's main economic mechanism-the price impact is lower on the DEX than on the CEX-for liquidity traders' venue choice, arbitrage trading volume, and deviations from the peg. Our analyses inform the market design of stablecoin trading with respect to maintaining its price peg.

reference: Centre for Macroeconomics Discussion Paper No. 2026-13
title: Energy Shocks, Consumption Inequality & Fiscal Policy Design
affiliations: and Bank of England

detail.title: Energy Shocks, Consumption Inequality & Fiscal Policy Design

publicationDetails.detailsText: Centre for Macroeconomics Discussion Paper No. 2026-13

detail.abstract: Supply-driven energy price shocks generate substantial consumption inequality. Using US household expenditure data and instrumental variable local projections, we show that a one percentage point energy price increase reduces consumption of households in the lowest income decile by 0.5 percent, while consumption of those in the highest decile remains unchanged. This differential response persists for up to one year and reflects both higher energy expenditure shares and tighter liquidity constraints among low-income households. A two-agent New Keynesian model with two production sectors (energy and non-energy) and non-homothetic household preferences replicates these patterns and provides a framework for policy evaluation. At comparable fiscal cost (0.08 percent of GDP over two years), targeted cash transfers fully offset the consumption inequality increase, while energy subsidies reduce it by only half. Cash transfers dominate because they enable constrained households to allocate resources optimally across all consumption categories, whereas subsidies are restricted to energy expenditure. These findings inform the design of fiscal responses to relative price shocks affecting necessity goods.

title: The Foundation of Law

detail.title: The Foundation of Law
detail.abstract:
This article develops a structural account of the relationship between procedural and substantive justice, which it terms the isomorphic-evolution thesis. The thesis holds that substantive justice—the fairness of outcomes—functions as the generative source and normative telos of law, while procedural justice—the fairness of process—functions as its institutional instrument. Because the substantive conditions that law governs (technology, economic structure, demography, and moral consensus) change continuously, procedural mechanisms require ongoing recalibration to remain aligned with them.

The article distinguishes three states of this relationship—alignment, rigidification, and alienation—and argues, on the basis of comparative-historical evidence, that state decline and institutional collapse are frequently preceded by sustained divergence between procedural form and substantive condition where no mechanism of correction exists.

The argument proceeds in four stages.

First, it defines the two forms of justice and situates their hierarchical relationship within three independent jurisprudential traditions: the Radbruch Formula, natural law, and social contract theory.

Second, it specifies a four-part model of institutional pathology—cumulative effect, legitimacy depletion, feedback failure, and spillover/cascade—through which procedural rigidification converts into systemic risk.

Third, it tests the model against comparative-historical cases (Qin, Han, and Ming-Qing China; late Republican and Imperial Rome; the French Ancien Régime; English equity) and contemporary cases (structural polarization in the United States, the 2006 Nanjing 'Peng Yu' case, Prohibition and the War on Drugs, and the 1999 Pepsi 'Harrier Jet' litigation as an illustration of the distinction between micro-level adjudication and macro-level institutional credibility).

Fourth, it proposes an institutional design—built on sunset review, independent fact-finding, audited compensation, and expedited correction channels—through which legal systems might institutionalize the capacity for self-calibration that the historical record suggests is decisive for their survival.

The article closes by situating this framework as a general method of institutional self-calibration for states and societies, applicable in principle beyond any single legal tradition, and by specifying the conditions under which that generality holds.

The effectiveness of a legal system lies not in its initial perfection, but in its capacity to maintain alignment between substantive outcomes and evolving social conditions. Procedural justice is subordinate to substantive justice. When procedures become rigidified, the system decays.

Entitled "The Foundation of Law," this paper examines the relationship between substantive and procedural justice. The author proposes the theory of "homeomorphic evolution," positing that substantive justice constitutes the ultimate end of law, while procedural justice serves as its instrument. The paper argues that institutional decay ensues when procedural mechanisms fail to recalibrate in response to changing social conditions. Drawing on both historical and contemporary case studies, it illustrates this process and proposes institutional designs through which legal systems may achieve self-calibration.
