detail.title: Son Preference and Fertility Decisions: A Dynamic Model of Sex Selection in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The field survey component of this study received ethics approval from the Institutional Review Board at Rice University in April 2026. All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by Rice University. The funder had no role in the study design, analysis, or writing of the paper.

detail.abstract: India accounts for nearly half of the world's missing women, with 13.5 million girls absent due to sex-selective practices. States run numerous cash-transfer schemes for girls, yet existing evaluations recover net effects and cannot, by themselves, disentangle fertility stopping from prenatal sex selection or indicate which design margins matter. Using Rajasthan's Rajalakshmi Scheme, I show that daughter-targeted transfers reduce fertility but leave the sex ratio at birth unchanged. I then estimate a dynamic model of fertility and sex selection on nationally representative birth histories, validate it out of sample against two quasi-experimental policy settings, and compare alternative transfer designs. Counterfactuals varying payment schedules, eligibility, and conditionalities show that transfer size alone is not enough: design governs whether incentives reduce sex imbalance or shift stopping behavior. The most effective redesign narrows 13% of the sex-ratio gap at birth, equivalent to reducing son-preference intensity by 8%. These birth histories predate much of India's recent fertility decline, so I field a 2026 survey that elicits the same preferences through a discrete choice experiment in which respondents play out a full fertility career. Son preference has not weakened, but its distortion now runs through stopping rather than selection, a margin a well-designed transfer still reaches.

title: Monetary Poverty and Female Labor Informality in Colombia: An Endogeneity Problem?

detail.title: Monetary Poverty and Female Labor Informality in Colombia: An Endogeneity Problem?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this study. The author has no competing interests to report.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses secondary, de-identified microdata from Colombia's Gran Encuesta Integrada de Hogares (GEIH), a publicly available household survey administered by DANE (Colombia's National Statistics Department). The data contain no personally identifiable information and were not collected by the author. As the study involves analysis of publicly available, anonymized statistical data rather than direct research with human participants, formal ethics board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agency. It was conducted as part of the author's Master's thesis at Universidad Nacional de Colombia and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: What are the determinants of a woman in Colombia being poor and holding informal employment? This paper estimates the probability of informality and the probability of poverty, treating gender as a key variable, using microdata from Colombia's Gran Encuesta Integrada de Hogares (GEIH) for 2020 and 2021 (the pandemic period). Two bivariate logit models are specified on more than 37,000 observations of the employed population, controlling for gender, age, schooling, household headship and income. Being a woman raises the probability of both informality and poverty, even after controlling for these factors; gender, schooling and income are the shared, most significant predictors in both models. A causal-path analysis and the Hausman test document a bidirectional relationship between poverty and informality and an endogeneity problem when poverty is the dependent variable (p = 9.29×10⁻⁸), which the paper proposes to address through instrumental variables. Three policy avenues follow: insurance for homemakers, expansion of the care system, and safeguards for equal labor-market opportunity.

title: Health Insurance in Jharkhand: PMJAY from Promise to Practice

detail.title: Health Insurance in Jharkhand: PMJAY from Promise to Practice
detail.abstract: Eight years into its operation, the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY) exposes sharp contradictions between its promise and practice. Conceived to provide cashless health coverage to poor and vulnerable households, the scheme in Jharkhand illustrates how hospitalization insurance functions within a low-capacity, private-dominated health system. Drawing on hospital-level data from Ranchi, interviews with officials, and the HCES 2022-23 survey, this article examines its implementation on the ground. Public hospitals remain under-resourced, while private hospitals participate selectively and face delays in claim settlement. Although enrolment has expanded, coverage remains uneven, with particularly low enrolment among the poorest households. Self-reported coverage in HCES is nearly ten times lower than official administrative figures, revealing a substantial gap between formal coverage and actual participation. Many eligible households remain excluded, and those enrolled continue to incur out-of-pocket expenditures. These findings suggest that PMJAY is structurally constrained in delivering equitable access and financial protection. Without greater public investment, improved identification of eligible households, and stronger state capacity, the scheme risks reinforcing existing inequalities in healthcare.

title: Was It The Pandemic, or Did It Start Way Before COVID-19? The Factors Behind The Downtrend in the Turkey-Germany Bilateral Trade Relationship
affiliations: and Universidade de Santiago de Compostela - Faculty of Economic Science and Business Studies

detail.title: Was It The Pandemic, or Did It Start Way Before COVID-19? The Factors Behind The Downtrend in the Turkey-Germany Bilateral Trade Relationship
detail.abstract: This research paper sheds light on whether COVID-19 was responsible for the downtrend in the bilateral trade relationship between Turkey and Germany. COVID-19 had significant economic effects around the world. During COVID-19, the trade volume between Turkey and Germany decreased, and the weight of Germany-originated or destined products decreased in total Turkish imports and exports. However, the findings of this research paper show that this downtrend started way before the COVID-19 pandemic, visible from 2013 to 2024. Even after the pandemic lost its significance, the trade level between Turkey and Germany, and the weight of Germany-originated or destined products on Turkish trade, did not get back to their pre-COVID-19 levels. This indicates that there are other factors that are the reason for this downtrend. Through statistical and qualitative approaches, data gathered from national and international institutions, and index values, it was concluded that COVID-19 was not the main reason for the downtrend in the Turkey-Germany bilateral trade relationship. The following factors were considered for the reasons behind this downtrend: weak and volatile exchange rates, use of non-traditional monetary policy that violated the Taylor principle, corruption, rule of law, economic uncertainty, governance, regulatory quality, and political stability. This work is significant to researchers as this is almost a one-of-a-kind research, shedding light on a topic that has not been much explored before, using statistical approaches and credible data that is hardly gathered together.

title: Laws, Policies, and Guidelines Addressing School-Related Gender-Based Violence in Kenya A Systematic Review
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Laws, Policies, and Guidelines Addressing School-Related Gender-Based Violence in Kenya A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: School-Related Gender-Based Violence (SRGBV) affects millions of children globally, with nearly half of Kenyan adolescents experiencing physical violence and many facing sexual or emotional abuse. Despite an increasingly robust legal and policy framework, SRGBV remains prevalent in Kenyan schools, highlighting persistent implementation challenges. This systematic review analyzed 43 policy and legal documents using the Subject, Objectives, Coverage, and Type of sources framework and Sabatier and Mazmanian’s policy implementation model. Findings show that Kenya has developed a comprehensive SRGBV policy architecture encompassing constitutional protections, sector laws, operational guidelines, and multi-sectoral frameworks. Implementation is supported by whole-school approaches, teacher training, and partnerships but constrained by inadequate resources, weak reporting systems, fragmented coordination, and socio-cultural norms. Strengthening SRGBV prevention requires consolidating existing policies, improving implementation, ensuring equitable resourcing, and enhancing evidence-to-policy feedback mechanisms.

title: Tax Regulation of the Tobacco Products Market
affiliations: , State Tax University, State Tax University and Independent Researcher

detail.title: Tax Regulation of the Tobacco Products Market
detail.abstract: This work covers the challenges of excise duty collection from tobacco products and nicotine-containing products, driven by the tobacco market development. It also studies the in-depth theoretical basis of excise taxation of heated tobacco products and e-cigarettes in the context of achieving fiscal and regulatory goals. It describes the types and general approaches to the classification of novel tobacco products and nicotine-containing products. This research determines the tendencies and features of excise duty collection from heated tobacco products and e-cigarettes in EU countries in terms of the broader distribution of these products on national markets. It describes specific aspects of the tobacco products excise policy in Moldova and Georgia. It also analyses the specifics of the transformation of the domestic tobacco products market due to the high excise duty burden carried by these products. The work also proposes ways of improving excise taxation of heated tobacco products and e-cigarettes in Ukraine to boost the budget and regulate the tobacco market development. The survey findings can be useful to the state agencies and a broad range of other stakeholders when developing proposals regarding the formation and implementation of the excise policy for tobacco products and alternatives.

title: Do T-Bills Outperform Stocks? A Tale of Three Percentages
affiliations: San Diego State University - Finance Department

detail.title: Do T-Bills Outperform Stocks? A Tale of Three Percentages
detail.abstract: Bessembinder (2018) shows that 57.4% of the stocks in the 1926-2016 CRSP database underperformed T-Bills over their lifetimes. We consider the application of this result to three stock populations: (a) stocks in the database, (b) newly-listed stocks, and (c) stocks in the market at a given time. Its application to (a) and (b) follow from the methodology. Its application to (c) has not been established, and the percentage of stocks which underperform T-Bills is likely to be considerably lower. We also examine Bessembinder's fixed horizon and bootstrap simulation results, and his breakdown by listing status.

title: Closing the Insurance Affordability Gap: How Insurers and Housing Nonprofits Can Make Coverage Affordable Again

detail.title: Closing the Insurance Affordability Gap: How Insurers and Housing Nonprofits Can Make Coverage Affordable Again
detail.abstract: Insurance affordability has become one of the most visible cost-of-living pressures in the United States, and nowhere is the strain sharper than in homeowners insurance. Average premiums have risen by double digits for several consecutive years, far outpacing wage growth and general inflation, while insurers have raised deductibles and withdrawn from the highest-risk markets. This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed research and authoritative industry, government, and nonprofit sources to address three questions: why homeowners insurance has become unaffordable for a growing share of Americans; what insurers and other companies can do to ease the barrier; and how housing-focused nonprofits help close the gap. The affordability problem is driven less by insurer profiteering than by a structural rise in expected losses, escalating climaterelated catastrophes, higher reconstruction costs, growing exposure, and costlier reinsurance, transmitted through annually repriced contracts. The consequence is a sharp rise in uninsurance and underinsurance that erodes household financial security and slows community recovery. The paper argues that affordability is best addressed by attacking the underlying risk rather than merely the price, and it develops this argument with detailed case studies of three nonprofits-Habitat for Humanity, SBP (formerly the St. Bernard Project), and Smart Home America and of the partnerships through which insurers such as State Farm, Travelers, and Zurich fund resilient building, mitigation research, and disaster recovery. Resilience-linked pricing (for example, discounts for IBHS FORTIFIED construction), parametric and community-based insurance designs, and nonprofit-led building and retrofitting form the core of an integrated, publicprivate-nonprofit strategy that lowers physical risk-the most durable path to affordable coverage. AI Disclosure In preparing this paper, the author used AI assistant to help identify and organize source material and to support drafting and language editing. All data points were verified against the cited primary and authoritative sources, and the author reviewed, edited, and takes full responsibility for the entire content, analysis, and conclusions of this work.

title: Bitcoin Runs on a Clock: Why Every Price Indicator Dies and the Halving Clock Doesn't

detail.title: Bitcoin Runs on a Clock: Why Every Price Indicator Dies and the Halving Clock Doesn't

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author operates a media channel advocating this framework, a conflict we disclose

detail.abstract: Every widely followed Bitcoin cycle indicator (the Pi Cycle Top, MVRV, the Mayer Multiple, the Puell Multiple, the 200-week moving average) called the market's tops and bottoms with striking precision for a decade, then degraded in a common sequence: precise, then early, then silent. We show that this is not a series of independent failures but a single structural phenomenon. Using daily data spanning the four halving epochs (2011-2026; the fourth is still in progress), we document three things. First, the per-cycle maxima of the five major top-calling oscillators decline monotonically across all four epochs while their per-cycle minima end the era higher than they began, so any threshold calibrated on past cycles must eventually stop firing. Second, the predictive power of short-horizon price indicators decays toward zero across epochs and in several cases inverts sign. Third, Bitcoin's time structure remains fixed: the three mature-cycle tops occurred 525, 546, and 534 days after their respective halvings, and the three completed bear-market bottoms 406, 364, and 366 days after their tops. These turns are identified retrospectively by a fixed mechanical rule (an all-time high followed by a ≥45% drawdown), not from a real-time forecasting record. Under uniform timing-free nulls, the joint probability of both clusters ranges from 5×10⁻⁶ to 1×10⁻³ across every window choice and inclusion variant we examine, including the variant least favorable to the claim. A harder empirical null, in which block-bootstrapped Bitcoin return paths are processed by the identical turn rule, never reproduces the top-timing regularity under its deterministic construction (zero of 10,000 paths across five block lengths; a conservative variant that grants the null free selection among candidate tops yields 0.10-0.25%). The same null reveals that the bottom-timing regularity is largely intrinsic to the drawdown process itself, reproduced by 31-43% of null paths: the clock evidence is concentrated in the tops' halving-phase alignment, and we weight our predictions accordingly. A causally fit power law in time-since-genesis (exponent converging to 5.6) is the only signal in the formal inference battery whose direction is stable across every mature epoch, whose long-horizon relationship replicates on an independent price source and on Ethereum with a different exponent, and whose risk-adjusted timing edge over buy-and-hold improves monotonically across all four cycles, turning positive in the current one (a single-window holdout, suggestive rather than decisive). We deliberately rest none of this on per-epoch significance testing: a dependence-preserving rotation null shows that autocorrelation-robust (HAC) inference overrejects severely for persistent signals at these sample sizes (empirical size up to 0.33 at nominal 0.05), rendering the apparent two-epoch significance of the power-law cell statistically indistinguishable from chance (empirical p = 0.21). We report this diagnostic in full, because it disqualifies not only our own per-epoch p-values but the entire genre of such claims for persistent indicators in this literature. Candidate macro drivers (M2 growth, the yield curve) exhibit the same era-dependent sign instability as the price indicators and are eliminated in a joint horse race; in the 2024-26 episode, liquidity kept expanding while Bitcoin topped on schedule and entered a bear market. The halving clock further outperforms every look-alike four-year cycle we test (the US election cycle, a fixed calendar, and 2,000 random four-year clocks), and the whole boom-bust-recovery path, not just the turns, repeats when cycles are aligned by days since halving. We summarize the asset's state in two time-anchored coordinates, days since halving and power-law deviation, under which Bitcoin's history traces a damped spiral: the amplitude is dying, the clock is not. The framework yields pre-registered, falsifiable predictions: a cycle bottom window of October 5 to November 16, 2026, and a next cycle top window 525 to 546 days after the following halving (provisionally late September to mid-October 2029, pending the halving's exact date).

title: Optimal pricing over vertically differentiated qualities under loss aversion
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Nanjing University of Finance and Economics and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

detail.title: Optimal pricing over vertically differentiated qualities under loss aversion
detail.abstract: We investigate optimal pricing in a vertically differentiated market with loss-averse customers and analyze how two types of consumer preferences influence pricing strategies.We find that under bundled preferences, the seller’s revenue-optimal pricing is independent of loss aversion, whereas the social planner must account for loss aversion in pricing and may even set negative price for the low-quality good to provide psychological compensation. Under unbundled preferences, the impact of loss aversion on seller pricing is asymmetric: the price of the high-quality good decreases with the degree of loss aversion, while the direction of price changes for the low-quality good depends on the prior distribution of quality. The social planner, in contrast, lowers the price of the high-quality good and raises that of low-quality ones to mitigate the welfare loss caused by loss aversion. Our findings offer managerial insights for firms in implementing refined pricing strategies and for policymakers in enhancing market efficiency.

title: Why Capability Is Becoming the World's Most Valuable Productive Asset

detail.title: Why Capability Is Becoming the World's Most Valuable Productive Asset

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The research was conducted in the author's capacity as Founder of The Global Structure Network Limited and The Global Structure Diamond International and Advocacy, serving as part of an independent conceptual research programme.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This manuscript is a theoretical and conceptual working paper establishing economic frameworks and architectural doctrines. It did not involve empirical studies with human participants, patients, or tissue samples, and therefore did not require institutional ethics committee approval or written patient consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The Capability Infrastructure Field research programme is entirely self-funded and independently sustained by the author and their affiliated organizations, The Global Structure Network Limited and The Global Structure Diamond International and Advocacy.

detail.abstract:
For much of modern economic history, competitive advantage has been explained through the accumulation of physical capital, technological innovation, institutional quality, and human capital. While these frameworks continue to explain important dimensions of economic growth, they increasingly fail to account for an emerging structural constraint common to advanced and developing economies alike: the capacity of individuals and households to sustain the cognitive, metabolic, emotional, financial, and social capabilities required to participate effectively within increasingly complex economic systems.

This paper argues that capability should no longer be understood as an individual characteristic, a behavioral outcome, or a public health concern. Rather, capability is proposed as a form of productive infrastructure that conditions the returns generated by labor, technology, institutions, and financial capital. As economies become more technologically mediated, cognitively intensive, and organizationally complex, capability increasingly determines whether productive assets can be converted into durable economic value.

Building upon the Capability Infrastructure framework, this paper develops a theory of capability as productive capital. It argues that behavior represents the observable expression of deeper structural capability conditions rather than an independent driver of economic performance. To ensure empirical validity, the framework establishes concrete, falsifiable parameters across household economics, behavioral durability, total factor productivity, and technology integration.

The paper further proposes that modern institutions already recognize capability indirectly through the pricing, absorption, and redistribution of its consequences. Health systems, labor markets, insurers, financial institutions, and governments continuously respond to variations in capability despite lacking a common economic framework through which these dynamics can be understood. This observation provides the basis for introducing the concept of the Capability Premium: the increasing economic value attached to environments, households, and institutions capable of sustaining high levels of adaptive capability within environments characterized by technological acceleration and structural complexity.

From this perspective, the household is reinterpreted not primarily as a unit of consumption but as the foundational production system through which societies generate capability. National competitiveness therefore depends increasingly upon the capacity of households to produce resilient participants capable of navigating complex institutional environments. Investment in capability infrastructure should therefore be understood not as social expenditure but as productive investment that strengthens competitiveness, reduces future liabilities, and expands the long-run productive capacity of nations.

title: The Composition of Fiscal Consolidation: Tax Versus Spending Adjustments and Their Effects on Debt Reduction and Economic Growth
affiliations: George Mason University - Mercatus Center

detail.title: The Composition of Fiscal Consolidation: Tax Versus Spending Adjustments and Their Effects on Debt Reduction and Economic Growth
detail.abstract: This paper examines the differential effects of tax-based versus spending-based fiscal consolidations on debt sustainability and economic growth using narrative consolidation data for 17 advanced economies from 1978 to 2016. The Adler et al. (2024) dataset, published as International Monetary Fund (IMF) Working Paper 24/210, provides a comprehensive revision of the Alesina et al. (2015, 2019) narrative data, extending coverage to 17 countries including the Netherlands and updating shock magnitudes throughout the sample period. Macroeconomic outcome variables are drawn from World Bank, Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and IMF primary sources. The narrative shock sample is bounded in 2016 to ensure the three-year debt outcome window remains pre-pandemic; local projections use shocks through 2014 to guarantee all five horizons avoid COVID contamination. Employing country and year fixed-effects panel regressions with clustered standard errors, local projections methods, and linear probability models, this paper reveals that spending-based consolidations are associated with higher probabilities of debt reduction and more favorable growth outcomes than tax-based consolidations. A one-percentagepoint tax-based consolidation reduces GDP growth contemporaneously by 0.59 percentage points, versus 0.29 percentage points for spending-based consolidations. Local projections reveal that tax-based consolidations impose increasingly negative effects over time (reaching-2.94 percentage points cumulatively five years after the event), while spending-based consolidations generate a trajectory that turns positive after two years and reaches +1.81 percentage points after five years. Tax-based consolidations reduce the probability of substantial debt reduction by 9.5 percentage points and of debt stabilization (debt-to-GDP ratio does not increase over three years) by 12.4 percentage points. Spending-based consolidations significantly raise the probability of substantial debt reduction by 11.1 percentage points. These results are robust to heterogeneity by initial debt level.

title: Physician Associate Practice Modernization in North Dakota
affiliations: Appalachian State University and Archbridge Institute

detail.title: Physician Associate Practice Modernization in North Dakota

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge receiving a grant from the American Academy of Physician Associates to support this research.

detail.abstract: We study North Dakota as the first adopter of reforms aligned with the American Academy of Physician Associates' (PA) Practice Modernization after enactment of House Bill 1175 in 2019. We build a county-year panel for 2016 to 2022 by merging National Plan and Provider Enumeration System physician associate listings, County Health Rankings outcomes, and American Community Survey county population estimates. The sample includes all counties in North Dakota and all counties in Minnesota, South Dakota, and Montana as border-state comparators. We estimate associations between a North Dakota post-2019 indicator and physician associate density per 10,000 residents, and between that indicator and county health measures, with county and year fixed effects and county-specific linear trends. For density we report negative binomial models, population-weighted estimates, stateclustered standard errors, and rural subsamples based on Rural-Urban Continuum Codes. The results inform workforce and access policy discussions by showing how a modernized scope-of-practice environment aligns with modeled county workforce and health outcomes in this panel.

title: A Bayesian Bivariate Analytics Framework for Joint Modeling of Psoriasis Disability and Quality of Life
affiliations: Rangsit University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Rangsit University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Bayesian Bivariate Analytics Framework for Joint Modeling of Psoriasis Disability and Quality of Life
detail.abstract: Psoriasis imposes substantial functional and psychosocial burden, yet the Psoriasis Disability Index (PDI) and Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) are conventionally analyzed as independent univariate outcomes, ignoring their shared variance. This study jointly modeled PDI and DLQI in 150 Thai psoriasis patients using a Bayesian bivariate regression framework fitted via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, with model-averaged variable selection applied to candidate predictors screened by ordinary least squares. Five predictors: age, Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), comorbidity, smoking status, and marital status were retained for posterior inference. Age was the strongest and most consistent predictor, showing a decisive inverse association with both outcomes (BFincl = 1515.5 for PDI; 713.5 for DLQI), while higher PASI scores predicted greater burden on both indices (BFincl = 44.4 and 62.2, respectively). Smoking and comorbidity displayed outcome-specific divergence: current smoking exerted a stronger effect on PDI, whereas comorbidity exerted a stronger effect on DLQI. After adjusting for all predictors, the residual correlation between PDI and DLQI remained strong (𝜌 = 0.72, 95% CrI: 0.55–0.84), indicating substantial shared, unmeasured determinants of burden. Posterior predictive checks and information criteria (WAIC, LOO-CV) favored the bivariate specification over independent univariate models, supporting joint outcome evaluation as a more efficient and clinically informative approach to assessing psoriasis burden.

title: AI and the Productivity-Income Gap: A Theory of Demand Decoupling

detail.title: AI and the Productivity-Income Gap: A Theory of Demand Decoupling
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical model to explore what happens when AI drives up economic productivity but leaves average wages behind. The core contribution is analytical: this paper specifies the Productivity-Income Gap condition under which AIdriven output expansion fails to generate proportional purchasing power. Now, here is the mechanism is distributional. When AI reduces labor's share of income, denoted λ, and when the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) out of labor income exceeds that out of capital income, aggregate consumption grows more slowly than productive capacity. This paper do not claim this condition has already materialized. U.S. data from Q1 2026 are presented as illustrative evidence only: labor productivity rose 2.8% year-over-year while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%, and labor's share fell to 53.7%. These facts show what a Productivity-Income Gap would look like; they do not establish AI as the cause. Confounding factors include monetary tightening, energy-price normalization, COVID-era sectoral shifts, and measurement lags. Historically, demand shortfalls induced institutional innovation that recoupled production and purchasing power. The AI era may require analogous institutional innovation. The framework's contribution is to identify when such innovation becomes necessary, while recognizing that market adaptation-including the emergence of new job categories-will be among the primary mechanisms through which economies adjust (Fig 1).

title: Psychological Costs of Productivity: A Comparative Analysis of Japan's Collectivist Employment Model and the United States' Individualist Work Culture

detail.title: Psychological Costs of Productivity: A Comparative Analysis of Japan's Collectivist Employment Model and the United States' Individualist Work Culture
detail.abstract:
This study examines the extent to which Japan's collectivist employment model and the United States' individualist work culture sustain labour productivity while generating distinct psychological costs for workers. Using a comparative interdisciplinary approach that draws upon economic, anthropological, sociological, and public health literature, the research analyses historical developments, labour market institutions, productivity indicators, and mental health outcomes. Data from organisations including the OECD, World Health Organization, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare are evaluated alongside academic research on work culture, organisational behaviour, and employment systems.

The findings suggest that although both countries maintain high levels of productivity, they do so through fundamentally different cultural and institutional mechanisms. In Japan, productivity is closely associated with collective responsibility, organisational loyalty, and social conformity, contributing to recognised phenomena such as karōshi (death from overwork) and karōjisatsu (suicide related to overwork). In contrast, the United States emphasises individual achievement, flexibility, and labour market competition, producing psychological strain through job insecurity, performance pressure, and the internalisation of occupational stress. While both employment models generate measurable economic output, they also impose significant mental health costs that are not fully captured by conventional productivity indicators.

The study concludes that productivity cannot be evaluated solely through economic performance. Instead, long-term assessments of labour systems should incorporate worker wellbeing, psychological sustainability, and cultural context to provide a more comprehensive understanding of national productivity.

title: Universal FAFSA Mandates and the Activation of Student Aid
affiliations: and University of California, Santa Cruz

detail.title: Universal FAFSA Mandates and the Activation of Student Aid

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Hard universal FAFSA mandates require high school seniors to complete the FAFSA, submit an alternative state aid form, or obtain a waiver before graduation. We study early graduation-linked mandates in Louisiana, Illinois, Alabama, and Texas, building on prior state-specific causal evidence. We estimate completion effects with school-level Sun-Abraham event studies and downstream responses with state-year fixed-effects models. Our estimates indicate that hard mandates increase FAFSA completion by 12.3 percentage points. Federal student aid applicants rise by 0.087 applicants per senior. In later post years, state grant and scholarship aid rises by 3.5 percentage points of average public in-state tuition and required fees. Enrollment estimates are positive but statistically indistinguishable from zero. The results suggest that hard mandates generate a strong filing first stage, but the associated rise in grant and scholarship aid may be too modest to incentivize additional enrollment effects.

title: The Perceived Importance of Olfaction in Eating Behaviour: Independent Effects of Culture, Age, and BMI in Adults aged over 55 Years
affiliations: University of Sri Jayewardenepura, Rambhai Barni Rajabhat University, Thailand, Southwest University, University of Nottingham, Massey University, Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University), Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University), Macquarie University, Dresden University of Technology, Deakin University and

detail.title: The Perceived Importance of Olfaction in Eating Behaviour: Independent Effects of Culture, Age, and BMI in Adults aged over 55 Years

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest. None of the commercial products used in this study causes conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research was primarily approved by the College Human Ethics Advisory Network at RMIT University, Australia (Low Risk Ref: 23866) and conducted in accordance with the National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2007). For international data collection, the RMIT ethics approval was reciprocated or supplemented based on the requirements of each co-author’s institutional ethics board. In cases where local ethics approval was required, separate applications were submitted and approved. In countries where reciprocal approval was permissible, data collection proceeded under the oversight of RMIT’s ethics protocol, in consultation with local collaborators.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Using an online survey, we investigated how the importance of olfaction influences eating behaviour among adults aged 55 and over across six countries/regions (n=627): Australasia (Australia and New Zealand), China, Germany, Sri Lanka, Thailand, and the United Kingdom (UK). Participants (self-reported as healthy) were assessed on four olfactory importance subdomains: application, consequence, association, and aggravation. Additional self-reported measures included body mass index (BMI). Both univariate and multivariate analyses revealed significant country/region-level differences with participants from Western countries reporting lower overall olfactory importance than those from Asian countries (F(5,618) = 20.79, p<0.001). Country/region-level analyses further confirmed this pattern, with the higher scores on overall olfactory importance observed in China, Sri Lanka, and Thailand, and lower scores in Australasia, Germany, and the UK. Notably, these cultural and country/region differences remained consistent irrespective of age, gender, or BMI. However, age and BMI showed independent effects: individuals over 70 years reported greater olfactory importance than younger groups (F(5,618)=4.77, p=0.020), while higher BMI was associated with lower importance ratings (F(5,618)=3.92, p=0.037). Principal component and cluster analyses identified two distinct clusters: one with higher olfactory importance, primarily consisting of participants from Asian countries/regions, and another with lower importance, predominantly from Western countries/regions. These clusters were unrelated to age, gender, or BMI. The findings indicate that cultural context plays a stronger role than individual demographic factors in shaping the perceived importance of olfaction during eating. This suggests the need for culturally sensitive approaches when designing olfactory interventions and highlights the significance of assessing perceived relevance alongside psychophysical measures when evaluating the importance of olfaction in eating behaviour in older people.

title: Algorithmic Joint Business Planning (JBP): A Twelve-Dimension Framework for Reshaping Supplier-Retailer Commercial Relationships in Agent-Mediated Trade

detail.title: Algorithmic Joint Business Planning (JBP): A Twelve-Dimension Framework for Reshaping Supplier-Retailer Commercial Relationships in Agent-Mediated Trade

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: The Joint Business Plan is the dominant commercial governance instrument between consumer goods suppliers and retail trade partners across grocery, consumer electronics, beauty, and adjacent categories. The instrument was engineered for a human-to-human commercial era. It assumes two human parties negotiating annual terms through relationship, escalation, and judgement. Algorithmic mediation collapses that assumption. When the retailer's buyer is an AI procurement agent, the supplier's pricing logic is a structured data feed, or both, the traditional Joint Business Plan breaks across specific, identifiable dimensions. This paper introduces the Algorithmic Joint Business Planning framework. The framework specifies twelve dimensions of the traditional Joint Business Plan that change structurally under algorithmic mediation, prescribes the supplier-side and retailer-side capability adaptations required for each dimension, and maps four retailer archetypes onto the framework to handle heterogeneity in agentic exposure. The argument is anchored in capability theory (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997; Teece, 2007; Day, 1994, 2011) and dyadic relational governance (Hingley, Lindgreen, & Grant, 2015; Shahzad et al., 2018). It is positioned against the existing Joint Business Planning and category management literature. Two illustrative empirical anchors are offered: a 1,000-respondent Brazilian grocery shopper panel fielded by Appinio in April 2026, and a documented in-market diagnostic of AI agent behaviour in the São Paulo consumer electronics category in May 2026. Both anchors are illustrative, not validatory. Full empirical testing is reserved for subsequent work. The paper contributes a structured conceptual scaffold that suppliers, retailers, and researchers can use to diagnose and redesign the supplier-retailer commercial interface for conditions of agent-mediated trade.

title: The Fifth Quadrant: A New Category of Economic Existence in the Age of Infinite Replication

detail.title: The Fifth Quadrant: A New Category of Economic Existence in the Age of Infinite Replication
detail.abstract: Robert Kiyosaki's Cashflow Quadrant framework (Employee, Self-Employed, Business Owner, Investor) provided a dominant late-twentieth-century taxonomy of economic positioning. However, the emergence of the digital economy, characterized by zero marginal cost replication and autonomous system orchestration, has created a new category of economic existence that escapes this four-fold classification. This paper proposes a "Fifth Quadrant": the Engine Builder. The Engine Builder is an individual who constructs autonomous, self-propagating digital systems (engines) that generate value and operate independently of continuous human labor, physical presence, geographic location, or institutional credentials. This paper distinguishes the Fifth Quadrant from traditional software-as-a-service (SaaS) and traditional entrepreneurship, maps the economic and transaction cost parameters of this new category using Coasean firm theory, and introduces a formal diagnostic metric: the Engine Builder Index (EBI). It examines the implications of this framework for the future of work, wealth creation, and career transition in a post-geographic world.

reference: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 09/2026
title: CIP Violations as Functional Components of the Dynamic Cross-currency Basis Curve
affiliations: Swiss National Bank and Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund (Suva)

detail.title: CIP Violations as Functional Components of the Dynamic Cross-currency Basis Curve

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 09/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss National Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The general search for US dollars in forward currency markets, combined with the balance-sheet constraints of intermediary dealers, induces persistent failure of covered interest parity (CIP). We investigate these CIP deviations across the entire maturity spectrum by analyzing the daily dynamics of the USD/CHF cross-currency basis curve. Applying functional principal component analysis, we identify three components that explain virtually all curve dynamics: a persistent, slow-moving level component, a temporary steepener, and a short-end component inducing sharp basis widenings and contractions around quarter-end dates. We provide empirical evidence that CIP-implied carry opportunities and US monetary policy announcements widen the entire basis curve, whereas Fed swap line announcements tend to narrow it. During periods of global turmoil, the slope inverts in response to rising credit and capital stress among dealer banks, while funding stress steepens the curve as swap line usage mitigates short-end distortions. Reporting date effects, funding stress, and deteriorating market liquidity widen the basis primarily at the short- end. We further show that regulatory reporting dates generate systematic window-dressing distortions not only at the short end but also in the slope of the basis curve. This effect has weakened since 2022, which is consistent with recent changes in the regulatory landscape.

title: OM Grand Challenges: SDG 7 - Managing Decentralized Assets and Actors for the Clean Energy Transition
affiliations: Harvard University - Technology & Operations Management Unit, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Stanford University

detail.title: OM Grand Challenges: SDG 7 - Managing Decentralized Assets and Actors for the Clean Energy Transition
detail.abstract: Achieving SDG 7 requires closing persistent energy access gaps while simultaneously scaling renewable generation and reliably integrating intermittent supply into electricity systems. In 2024, 655 million people remain without access to electricity, and about 2 billion still rely on polluting cooking fuels. Simultaneously, clean energy technologies are increasingly cost-competitive and deployment is accelerating. Still, adoption and scaling remain constrained by affordability, supply-chain and infrastructure bottlenecks, coordination failures among decentralized actors, financing, and institutional frictions. We highlight the grand challenges behind these operational frictions and discuss how the operations management research community can contribute to the progress towards SDG 7 targets.

title: Intelligent Monitoring and Fault Detection Systems for Gas Pipeline Networks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Intelligent Monitoring and Fault Detection Systems for Gas Pipeline Networks

keywords: Petroleum and Gas Engineering Intelligent Monitoring Systems

detail.abstract:
Gas pipeline networks are critical components of modern energy infrastructure, responsible for the safe and efficient transportation of natural gas from production facilities to end users. Ensuring the reliability, safety, and operational efficiency of these networks is a major challenge due to factors such as pipeline aging, corrosion, leaks, equipment failures, and external environmental impacts. Traditional monitoring and inspection methods often rely on periodic maintenance and manual assessments, which may be insufficient for detecting faults in real time and preventing operational disruptions. In recent years, intelligent monitoring and fault detection systems have emerged as advanced solutions for enhancing pipeline integrity and operational performance through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Internet of Things (IoT), sensor technologies, and real-time data analytics. 

This study examines the role of intelligent monitoring and fault detection systems in gas pipeline networks, focusing on their applications in leak detection, anomaly identification, predictive maintenance, and infrastructure health monitoring. Advanced AI-driven models, including deep learning algorithms and pattern recognition techniques, are capable of analyzing large volumes of sensor and operational data to identify abnormal conditions and predict potential failures before they occur. The findings indicate that intelligent monitoring systems significantly improve fault detection accuracy, reduce response times, minimize operational downtime, and enhance overall pipeline safety. Furthermore, these technologies contribute to cost savings, environmental protection, and regulatory compliance by enabling proactive maintenance and risk management strategies. Despite these advantages, challenges such as data quality issues, cybersecurity risks, high implementation costs, and integration with legacy infrastructure remain significant barriers to adoption. The study concludes that intelligent monitoring and fault detection systems are essential for the development of resilient, efficient, and sustainable gas pipeline networks and highlights future research opportunities in digital twins, edge computing, and explainable artificial intelligence.

reference: Journal of Information Technology, Online first, 2025. DOI:10.1177/02683962251380597
title: Promoting Societal Development through Digital Activism: A Case Study of a Guatemalan Tragedy
affiliations: California State University, Los Angeles, University of Auckland Business School and The University of Kansas

detail.title: Promoting Societal Development through Digital Activism: A Case Study of a Guatemalan Tragedy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Information Technology, Online first, 2025. DOI:10.1177/02683962251380597

detail.abstract: Digital activism is on the rise as activist organizations worldwide rely on information and communication technology (ICT) to mobilize public support for their causes. In this article, we focus on ICT’s capabilities to cultivate values relevant to societal development in environments characterized by political repression. We examine how activist organizations can use ICT to bypass barriers in traditional communication channels, enabling them to promote values pertinent to broader societal development. Our findings demonstrate how ICT enables activists to challenge dominant narratives by presenting alternative perspectives, which are then integrated into a unified message that amplifies values of solidarity and accountability. We propose that these capabilities stem from the interplay of two distinct and innovative framing mechanisms: divergent framing and convergent framing. This study advances the IS research literature by enriching our understanding of ICT’s role in opening spaces that contribute to the reinforcement of values essential for advancing societal development. The full paper is available at  https://doi.org/10.1177/02683962251380597
