title: Long-term Vertical Contracts, Geography, and the Persistence of Brand Shares
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, Queen's University and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Long-term Vertical Contracts, Geography, and the Persistence of Brand Shares

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: Previous research documents persistent regional differences in national brand market shares, often attributed to geographic differences in consumer preferences and early entry advantages (Bronnenberg et al. 2007, 2009). This paper asks how much of this persistence is a feature of demand and how much operates through retailers. Using NielsenIQ data from the same product categories as Bronnenberg et al. (2007), we decompose the variance in national-brand shares into Brand × Retailer and Brand × Market components using the leave-out estimator of Abowd et al. (1999) and Kline et al. (2020). Retailer effects explain more than half of the variance, compared with under a fifth for market effects, and roughly half of the well-known "city of origin" gradient disappears once retailer heterogeneity is absorbed. We interpret these patterns as evidence of steering rather than consumer sorting, with asymmetric vertical arrangements such as category captaincy and slotting agreements as the leading candidate mechanism.

title:
The Doctrine of the Affected Party 
Realigning Standing, Notice, and the Burden of Proof in Interdependent Urban Structures
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
The Doctrine of the Affected Party 
Realigning Standing, Notice, and the Burden of Proof in Interdependent Urban Structures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is self-represented in ongoing civil and administrative proceedings in Portugal concerning matters structurally similar to those discussed in this paper. The theoretical framework presented here was developed in part through that practical engagement and is offered in general form independent of any specific proceeding; no specific party, case, or jurisdiction is addressed in this paper. The author is also the founder of a commercial venture (KYC.co) whose broader product and policy work intersects with some of the institutional design concepts discussed here.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and doctrinal legal analysis; it does not involve human subjects, personal data collection, or empirical research requiring ethics review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: Portuguese administrative and civil law treat physically interdependent properties inconsistently, and the inconsistency runs in a predictable direction. Article 68(1) of the Código do Procedimento Administrativo grants legitimacy to constitute oneself as an interested party broadly enough, on its text, to capture the owner of a structurally connected property1 — yet municipalities routinely deny that status through a doctrine holding that any effect on a neighbouring property is a mere reflexo de facto, outside the scope of a licensing decision. Article 1347 of the Civil Code, governing excavation damage, then assigns liability to whoever performed the works regardless of precautions taken, without asking whether the damaged structure’s condition was already compromised and documented before anyone broke ground. The same two properties, in other words, are legal strangers when one of them seeks to be heard, and a single interdependent system the instant liability needs somewhere to land. The convenience of switching between those two characterisations is the whole of the problem, and it does not stop at liability. It reappears, in exact mirror, on the side of benefit. Where two units stand on one shared structure under a single alvará, a municipality will treat them as one interdependent whole when it grants and charges the first owner for a structural enhancement — a deeper foundation, an added storey — yet as two separate properties when the second owner later needs the very same enhancement. That need is not a matter of preference: the two units share a single foundation system, and a structure built to one depth standing against a neighbour later built to another is among the most common causes of differential settlement and cracking at the join — the same physical interdependence Criterion A is built to recognise produces, on the benefit side, a structural necessity to match what the first owner was already granted. The second owner therefore pays again for an entitlement the shared structure requires regardless of preference, or goes to court to establish a parity the municipality itself created and then declined to recognise. Liability flows to whoever is treated as connected; benefit is withheld from whoever is treated as separate; and which characterisation applies is determined, in both directions, by whichever answer costs the institution least. This paper argues that the inconsistency is not incidental but mechanical: it is the means by which Portuguese law converts ordinarily compliant property owners into bad-faith ones, by rewarding concealment and silence at every stage where disclosure would be cheap and contesting it later is not. Drawing on a documented administrative history before the Câmara Municipal de Cascais and a structurally comparable incident in Lisbon, this paper proposes the Parte Afetada — the Affected Party — a status triggered only by objective, thirdparty-verified conditions, operating through a notice protocol that protects builders as much as neighbours, and requiring no new courts, no new institutions, and no admission of fault from any party it touches. The reform is structured so that every institution it implicates — the município, the courts, and the insurer underwriting the property — has reason to adopt it independently of whether the others do.

title: Mindful or Mindless? How and why Virtual Communities Fail to Contain Information Pollution Across Different Disasters
affiliations: University of Southampton, Durham University Business School, Missouri University of Science and Technology and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Mindful or Mindless? How and why Virtual Communities Fail to Contain Information Pollution Across Different Disasters
detail.abstract: People visit virtual communities to find trusted information (i.e. verifiable, accurate and reliable information) during disasters. Virtual communities are open spaces where people interact and share information. However, virtual communities often suffer from information pollution (including too much information and false or contradictory information) which decreases peoples’ ability to find trusted information. Oddly, some virtual communities will develop useful practices for combatting information pollution during one disaster, but subsequently fail to effectively employ the same practices or adapt them in subsequent disasters. We conducted a longitudinal, exploratory cross-case study to better understand how and why this occurs. Using the lenses of organisational mindfulness/mindlessness, we find three factors: (i) organisational forgetting, (ii) blaming, and (iii) social fracturing that may cause virtual communities to act mindlessly and prevent them from containing information pollution during a disaster. Practically, virtual communities may avoid mindlessness by (i) codifying past successful practices and adapting them, (ii) monitoring the rhetoric of blame and building trust in authorities, and (iii) avoiding inconsequential debates and promoting shared values. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1177/02683962251376678

title: Disclosure in the Shadow of Bankruptcy: From Reckoning to Reemergence
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business, University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and University of Southern California Gould School of Law

detail.title: Disclosure in the Shadow of Bankruptcy: From Reckoning to Reemergence
detail.abstract: For firms in financial distress, the choice of what and how much to disclose about their straits presents a challenge, since their counterparties' responses can have sharper consequences for their real operations and control. Forthright disclosure could facilitate survival through, e.g., recapitalization by reducing information asymmetry, or accelerate decline in a "self-fulfilling prophecy." But research to date provides little understanding of how such disclosure affects outcomes for non-bank firms. We measure how much distressed firms disclose about their financial straits using a large language model (LLM) in a process that is hallucination-free by construction, highly reproducible, and substantially more predictive than prior textual feature measures, within a sample of firms that are matched on ex ante bankruptcy risk and fundamentals. To address remaining endogeneity, we instrument firms' distress-year disclosures with their preestablished disclosure practices. We find that disclosure drives faster negative market reactions, customer pullback, tighter supplier credit, and deterioration in the capital-market conditions that could facilitate recapitalization, and hastens and increases the probability of bankruptcy filing. But after filing, once the bankruptcy court's powers are in place, the same prior disclosures facilitate smoother resolution. High-disclosure firms are valued more accurately upon entering bankruptcy, emerge faster, and are more likely to resolve through a Section 363 sale, consistent with disclosure reducing the valuation uncertainty that drives holdouts. We contribute by identifying how distress disclosure affects bankruptcy for non-bank firms, and tracing its impact through the resolution process, with an improved measurement approach.

title: Contextual factors influencing the performance of clinical preceptors: A scoping review protocol
affiliations: Universidad San Sebastian, Universidad San Sebastian, Universidad San Sebastian, Universidad San Sebastian and Universidad San Sebastian

detail.title: Contextual factors influencing the performance of clinical preceptors: A scoping review protocol
detail.abstract: The clinical preceptor plays a fundamental role in health professionals training. Their performance influences the acquisition of clinical competencies, the development of professional identity and the integration of ethical standards by students. Although interventions exist to strengthen preceptors' teaching competencies, there is a gap concerning the contextual factors that affect the transfer of these competencies into real clinical training settings. The aim of the present study is to describe contextual factors that influence the performance of clinical preceptors in health professions, explicitly documenting differences across health disciplines and by countries’ income levels. The review will follow JBI and PRISMA-ScR guidelines.

title: Managerial Work in Tech Startups: Subjectivity and Politics of Cooperation

detail.title: Managerial Work in Tech Startups: Subjectivity and Politics of Cooperation

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by a SSHRC Joseph-Armand Bombardier CGS Doctoral Scholarship (#767-2020-1100)

detail.abstract: This article explores managerial labour as a form of political labour in relation to the concepts of bio-power and virtuosity. Based on my interviews with managerial workers in tech startups, I argue that immaterial and affective labour embodies crucial role in reproduction of workers' subjectivities as communicative, emotionally transparent, and cooperative. Virtuosity as performance of being in the presence of others and bio-power as a form of control over life are instrumental concepts in the theories of Paolo Virno and Maurizio Lazzarato. Virno's theorization of the general intellect which includes the codes and rules of capitalist social relations, and Lazzarato's description of contemporary workplaces as specially designed "worlds" for workers, reveal how contemporary workplaces are political terrains that enclose social relations and the potentialities of labour-power. I conclude that understanding affective and immaterial labour of managerial workers as political labour can expand the meaning and implications of these concepts.

title: Load-Sensitive Fluid Policies for Network Revenue Management
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen,  and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: Load-Sensitive Fluid Policies for Network Revenue Management
detail.abstract:
We study finite-capacity network revenue management policies that implement an ex-ante fluid LP through online randomized control. A natural question is whether one fluid-LP policy can produce a smooth performance certificate connecting capacity-independent worst-case constants with capacity-sensitive finite-instance guarantees that converge to one as capacities grow. We answer this question by introducing a load-sensitive one-resource envelope Γ(c, θ), defined as the worst-case approval probability of a c-unit resource under total offered load at most θc for θ ∈ [0, 1]. The envelope interpolates between light-load and full-load regimes. At θ = 1, it recovers the usual full-load one-resource OCRS/magician guarantee, while for smaller θ it captures the stronger marginal guarantees available after thinning. We characterize Γ(c, θ) through a Poisson-limit ODE and establish structural lower bounds that can be plugged into network-level guarantees.

We use this envelope to construct a load-sensitive fluid-LP perturbation policy. After applying a common thinning factor θ, each resource-wise controller is certified at its induced normalized load, which is at most θ, and a product is accepted only if all required resources approve. The resulting guarantee recovers the full-load resource-wise certificate 1-L/√(3+c_min) as the no-thinning endpoint, where L is the maximum number of resources consumed by any product and c min is the minimum resource capacity. Optimizing over the thinning factor yields a finite-capacity certificate at least 1/(4L-2), strictly improving the classical uniform 1/(4L) perturbation bound. Moreover, when c_min ≥ 3, the optimized guarantee strictly exceeds 1/(1+L) , an important benchmark for finite-instance NRM policies.

title: Systematic Insights into Digital Transformation in Healthcare: A Comprehensive Review of Reviews
affiliations: Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa and Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna

detail.title: Systematic Insights into Digital Transformation in Healthcare: A Comprehensive Review of Reviews

declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded by Sant ’Anna School of Advanced Studies, in the framework of the Progetto di Interesse Nazionale (PRIN) - DIGITRANS-PAR: Drivers and impact of digital transformation of the Italian PA at the regional level (Prot. 2022RCSPF3). The views and opinions expressed are solely those of the authors.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is reshaping how society addresses new challenges and opportunities (Kraus et al., 2021; Schiavone et al., 2021). The pandemic has accelerated DT in the public sector, ensuring the continued provision of services through non-physical means. DT is defined as “a process that aims to improve an entity by triggering significant changes to its properties through combinations of information, computing, communication, and connectivity technologies” (Vial, 2019). Recently, there has been a growing body of research on DT. While some has focused on the conceptual and terminological aspects of DT (Dal Mas et al., 2023), practical implications, particularly in the healthcare sector, remain underexplored. Given this shift and the emphasis on new paradigms, there is a pressing need to systematize and organize the existing literature on DT in healthcare. This is essential to understand the uses and applications of digital health initiatives that are transforming and redesigning healthcare processes. In order to fill this gap, this study employs a review of reviews and examines the practical implications and adaptation of digital transformation in healthcare by analyzing the current state of reviews on DT inhealthcare, in the context of the European Union. This study aims at answering the following key questions: (i) What is the current stage of research in the field of DT in healthcare reviews? (ii) What are the types of innovations, units of analysis, and practical applications DT in the healthcare sector? To address these questions, we conducted an extensive review of reviews by performing a literature search to gather all relevant literature on our topic. We then organized our findings into relevant categories, providing a snapshot of the major trends, gaps, and barriers in the practical applications of DT that are transforming the healthcare sector. A review of reviews was conducted and presented following PRISMA methodology. The databases Scopus and Web of Science were searched for original publications in English between the 1st of January 2010 and 30th of May 2024. Studies were included for title and abstract screening if they were review article published in English discussing digital transformation in healthcare. A categorization of selected article was determined on several attributes, namely: innovation type; unit of analysis; sub-unit of analysis; contextual framework; gaps; barriers; dimension under study. The search yielded a total of 1319 articles. After duplicate removal and title/abstract screening, at the actual stage 16 review studies were included, meanwhile, another 49 articles are still being reviewed by the authors to determine whether to include them in the study. Of the included papers, four reported on the use of digital health technology among practitioners and two reported on the use of digital health technology among patients. Three studies analyzed the role of digital health literacy in the digital health transformation. Other studies analyzed the implementation of electronic patient records in hospitals or the implementation of specific devices in healthcare. Our preliminary findings revealed both promising implications and noticeable gaps. Many studies have analyzed the role of practitioners and their involvement in new models of health service deployment. Patients are also well-represented in research, highlighting their fundamental role in DT initiatives. However, not all stakeholders within the healthcare system, such as nurses, are adequately represented. This creates opportunities for further research and the need for deeper analysis. An emphasis on digital methods for learning and training healthcare staff has emerged, highlighting the importance of developing innovative approaches to address the new challenges arising from the diffusion of DT. At the current stage of research, this study aims to contribute to scholars, practitioners, and managers alike. For scholars, it offers a valuable systematization of existing research, outlining the current state of the field and paving the way for future studies. Practitioners can gain clear insights into practical examples of digital innovations in healthcare, enhancing their understanding of digital technology trends and their application in real-world contexts. Finally, the study provides managers with summarized directions and suggestions for future practical tools, aiding in the design of organizational change to ensure the successful implementation of digital transformation initiatives.

title: The Impact of Interest Rates on U.S. Housing Prices: Evidence from the Pre- and Post-COVID-19 Periods

detail.title: The Impact of Interest Rates on U.S. Housing Prices: Evidence from the Pre- and Post-COVID-19 Periods

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, professional, or financial relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this study. The author has no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human subjects, personal health information, or animal research. The research is based on publicly available data, published literature, and secondary sources. Therefore, institutional ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between U.S. interest rates and housing prices from January 2015 to December 2024, focusing on whether the COVID-19 pandemic altered this relationship structurally. Using 120 monthly observations from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) and the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) multiple regression model is estimated with the seasonally adjusted Housing Price Index (HPI) as the dependent variable, the Federal Funds Rate as the primary explanatory variable, and a binary COVID-19 dummy variable that captures the structural shift beginning in March 2020. The results show a statistically significant positive coefficient on the Federal Funds Rate (β1 = +16.974, p < 0.001). After controlling for the COVID-19 structural break, a 1-percentage-point increase in the Federal Funds Rate is associated with a 16.97-point increase in the HPI. This positive relationship reflects the co-trending of rising rates and prices during the economic expansion of 2015 to 2019, underscoring the importance of controlling for structural breaks in time-series housing data. The COVID-19 dummy variable is also strongly positive and significant (β2 = +103.867, p < 0.001), confirming a major structural upward shift in housing prices following the onset of the pandemic. Together, these two variables explain 93.4% of the variation in U.S. housing prices over the sample period (R 2 = 0.9341, F = 828.67, p < 0.001). These findings add to the growing empirical literature on monetary policy, structural shocks, and housing markets, and they offer evidence relevant to current debates on housing affordability in the United States.

title: Faith Leaders as First Responders: Countering COVID-19 Sectarian Misinformation Through Interfaith Risk Communication in Pakistan - A Practitioner's Design Case Study, Situated in International Crisis Communication Practice

detail.title: Faith Leaders as First Responders: Countering COVID-19 Sectarian Misinformation Through Interfaith Risk Communication in Pakistan - A Practitioner's Design Case Study, Situated in International Crisis Communication Practice
detail.abstract: A Note on Scope This paper analyses the design of a rapid-response USAID/DAI grant activity, "Bringing Communities and Groups Together on COVID-19," which I personally conceived and managed as DAI's point of contact under the Azm-e-Pakistan (AeP) programme in April-May 2020. The analysis draws on the original grant agreement, which specifies the intervention's design, partnership structure, and theory of change in detail. As with my related work on this programme, this paper analyses intervention design against international crisis communication practice; it does not claim independently evaluated outcome data beyond what the design documents specify as intended.

title: When Systems Break: Statistical and Evolutionary Approaches to Systemic Transformation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: When Systems Break: Statistical and Evolutionary Approaches to Systemic Transformation
detail.abstract: Contemporary complexity frameworks-including self-organized criticality, early-warning signals, complex adaptive systems, NK-landscapes, and informational synergetics-treat crisis triggers as atomized, structureless, and memoryless perturbations defined solely by magnitude. This article demonstrates that this foundational assumption creates a systemic explanatory gap, leaving the specificity, asymmetric scaling, and directional determination of individual transformations systematically unanswered. To resolve this limitation, this study introduces an alternative paradigm based on the theory of Concentrative Causality. This approach reconceives the trigger as a historically structured entity co-evolved with systemic vulnerabilities within a shared macro-historical process. The article provides a conceptual formalization of this relational framework, replacing the orthodox assumption of stochastic independence with a conditional probability model of topological fit. Ultimately, this reorientation shifts the analytical focus from the aggregate epidemiology of crisis populations to the precise causal anatomy of singular systemic events.

title: Kenya's Fiscal Pressure and the Productivity of Infrastructure
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Kenya's Fiscal Pressure and the Productivity of Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: This paper reads the World Bank's July 2026 Kenya Economic Update: Sustaining Macroeconomic Gains, Advancing Fiscal Reforms against Amonya's Infrastructure Productivity: The Metabolism of Capital Formation. The World Bank presents an economy that has preserved important elements of macroeconomic stability while facing weakening growth, persistent revenue shortfalls, rising expenditure pressures, high debt-service costs, growing dependence on domestic borrowing and limited creation of productive formal employment. The conflict in the Middle East has intensified fuel, food and external-account pressures, but the deeper vulnerabilities are domestic and structural. Amonya's framework extends the diagnosis by asking how Kenya converts gross fixed capital formation into economic capability. Using the concepts of scaling appetite, metabolic response and metabolic pathology, the paper distinguishes construction activity from long-term transformation. Kenya has historically shown a strong appetite for capital formation and a meaningful association between investment and growth. Yet the current fiscal position suggests that debt obligations, maintenance demands and recurrent spending may now be advancing faster than the productive and revenue gains generated by recent investment. The comparison reveals a problem of infrastructure coupling: roads, energy, finance, firms, skills, maintenance, markets and public revenue do not always move as one system. The paper concludes that Kenya's next phase of infrastructure policy must be judged by conversion. Capital formation must enlarge productive capacity, formal employment, resilience and fiscal strength. The central task is therefore to improve the metabolism through which infrastructure becomes economic life.

title: The Class Pay Gap in Public Accounting: Does Socioeconomic Background Matter?
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business, Stockholm School of Economics, Stockholm School of Economics and Stockholm School of Economics

detail.title: The Class Pay Gap in Public Accounting: Does Socioeconomic Background Matter?

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study has been evaluated and approved by the Regional Ethical Review Board in Stockholm, Sweden (Dnr 2023-07508-02).

detail.abstract: We examine whether there is a class pay gap in the auditing profession. We explore this question using 20 years of unique administrative data in Sweden, an egalitarian society and top-ranked meritocracy. We document a significant income disparity across all professional levels within Big 6 firms between auditors from higher-and lower-socioeconomic backgrounds (SEB), with the gap peaking at the partner level. We explore two potential underlying mechanisms: differential performance and workplace segregation. While we find no evidence that high-SEB auditors deliver higher quality audits, we find robust evidence of substantial workplace segregation. Higher-SEB CPAs manage larger portfolios and more prestigious clients (indicating horizontal segregation), and are more likely to qualify as CPAs, reach partnership, and join Big 6 boards (indicating vertical segregation). Beyond these disparities in economic and professional achievements, class-based inequality also appears to take a toll on mental health: we find that auditors from lower-SEB backgrounds are significantly more likely to be diagnosed with depression, suggesting that the psychological burdens of the profession fall disproportionately on those from less privileged origins. Collectively, these findings challenge the meritocratic narrative of public accounting and serve as a call to action for audit firms to ensure equal opportunity and address systemic class-based inequalities.

title: LIA: A Scope-Contract Control Plane for Surgical, Auditable Contract Editing

detail.title: LIA: A Scope-Contract Control Plane for Surgical, Auditable Contract Editing
detail.abstract: AI contract-editing systems often replace whole clauses where expert redlines use smaller, distributed tracked changes. We call this descriptive difference the surgicality gap. It may arise from model judgment, the editing harness, or both. This paper presents LIA, a proposed control-plane architecture, and a prospective protocol for estimating the harness contribution while preserving rubric-defined sufficiency. LIA adapts computer-assisted-translation concepts—segmentation, precedent memory, match-rate leverage, and banded routing—and applies the narrower security principle that a model may propose an action while code outside the model determines whether the action is permitted. The architecture uses a hierarchical document map with versioned structural anchors and cross-revision reconciliation; a leverage pass that separates reuse similarity from policy-based action eligibility; hard-veto features for predefined high-risk differences; scope contracts enforced at the only document-write boundary; run-scoped provisional memory; and a fresh-session whole-document audit that cannot retrieve the current run’s unapproved outputs. Its intended guarantee is limited and mechanical: edits that violate an expressible scope rule are rejected before document mutation. It does not guarantee legal correctness, complete detection of meaning reversal, or immunity from prompt injection. We contribute the architecture, a scope-contract schema and enforcement model, provenance-aware diagnostics, and a paired two-harness evaluation design with falsifiable morphology and rubric-defined sufficiency hypotheses. LIA is under active implementation, and this paper reports no experimental results.

title: Racing Against Automation: Dynamic Incentives When AI Can Preempt the Human
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics,  and

detail.title: Racing Against Automation: Dynamic Incentives When AI Can Preempt the Human
detail.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), and AI agents in particular, are reshaping innovation by enabling autonomous search, evaluation, and iteration toward new discoveries. Yet human researchers remain essential in novel and poorly structured settings. A human agent may be more productive but privately chooses effort, creating a moral hazard problem; the AI agent requires no incentives but is costly to operate and can preempt the human agent’s success. This raises a natural question: When, if ever, should the firm race the AI agent against the human agent rather than rely on either one alone? We develop a continuous-time principal–agent model in which a principal draws on both a human agent and an independent AI agent in the search for innovation. We establish that when the AI agent is not cost-effective, the principal never deploys it and relies on human-alone search. In contrast, when the AI agent is cost-effective, a natural conjecture is that the principal should always keep it active as a rival, since it can accelerate breakthroughs and, by threatening to preempt the human agent, strengthen the human agent’s incentives. We show that this intuition can fail: persistent AI rivalry may lower both the human agent’s and the principal’s payoffs relative to human-alone search, so aggressive competition can hurt both parties. Instead, the optimal contract may begin with human-alone search, transition to a human–AI race, and finally switch to autonomous AI search if no breakthrough occurs. Relative to a human–human benchmark, deploying the AI agent alongside the human can also align the preferences of the principal and the focal human agent over whether competition should come from an AI agent or another human. In an extension with imperfect AI-generated outcomes, the optimal contract features time-varying verification. In sum, AI rivalry is a double-edged sword: it can accelerate discovery and discipline human effort, but deploying it too early crowds out valuable human-alone search, so firms may optimally delay it even when the AI is productive.

detail.abstract:
Background: In Osaka Prefecture's annual motor vehicle tax (category-based) exemption renewal filing process, applicants whose details have not changed since the previous filing may file online, yet preliminary administrative data indicate that most continue to file by post. 

Objective: To evaluate whether a nudge package modifying the outer envelope, renewal form, and procedural instruction sheets increases the rate of timely completed online filings. 

Methods: In the Kitakawachi area, 400-1,000 prior-year exemption applicants will be randomized 1:1 to the intervention or control group. The primary outcome is the rate of timely completed online filings among all randomized participants; secondary outcomes include any timely filing, late filing, nonfiling, duplicate filing, deficiencies, inquiries, equity, and cost. The primary analysis will follow the intention-to-treat principle and report the risk difference with a 95% confidence interval. 

Conclusion: This data-free study protocol presents a transparent and inclusive framework for evaluating both the benefits and potential harms of administrative digitalization.

title: Charity Efficiency Metrics and the Employment Ceiling: An Institutional Analysis of Donor-Funded Food Distribution in India

detail.title: Charity Efficiency Metrics and the Employment Ceiling: An Institutional Analysis of Donor-Funded Food Distribution in India
detail.abstract: Approximately 82 to 90 percent of the Indian workforce is employed in the informal sphere, and distribution of community food has become an effective response to food insecurity across the country. While there is adequate research into the role of community food distribution as a nutrition intervention, but rarely do studies look into the way it creates jobs for people. There seems to be very little research on whether these jobs created in the food distribution sector are real, sustainable, and progressive or whether we are simply talking about "employment" as a nice term referring to labor that doesn't cost anything. The aim of this paper is to discuss whether donor-funded food distribution can allow genuine paid work, especially for women; however, this kind of employment hits the problem with employment structure, primarily because of the pricing mechanism employed for the funding obtained. This paper analyzes five cases in which genuine work existed in the food distribution systems, namely, the Robin Hood Army, Amma Unavagam, and the schemes of the ICDS Anganwadi project, as well as the Akshaya Patra Foundation and DAY-NRLM self-help groups.

title: Managing the Human Fallback: Skill Investment Under Improving AI and Worker Mobility
affiliations: ,  and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Managing the Human Fallback: Skill Investment Under Improving AI and Worker Mobility
detail.abstract: When firms deploy autonomous AI, they must decide how much work to leave to the system and how much to keep workers engaged. This decision affects current output and future human capital. We develop a parsimonious two-period model in which AI may outperform the worker when it functions, but may fail with positive probability. A firm chooses worker engagement; engagement lowers current output for below-benchmark workers, but changes future skill through learning and erosion. We distinguish two dimensions of AI progress: capability, the system's output when it works, and reliability, the probability that it works. In a single-firm benchmark, engagement is valuable only as fallback investment. The firm engages the least-skilled workers most, because they have the largest skill gaps and are least costly to bring toward a useful fallback level. With worker mobility, engagement also affects labor-market sorting: workers prefer jobs that build more valuable skill trajectories. This sorting motive targets higher-skill workers near the AI frontier, where skill gains are more valuable and engagement is less costly. Mobility can therefore reverse the engagement pattern, shifting investment from the least-skilled toward the most-skilled workers below the AI benchmark. Mobility also reshapes how AI progress affects engagement: greater capability raises engagement by increasing the value of the skill trajectory a firm offers, whereas greater reliability can raise or lower it because it reduces fallback need while also changing learning opportunities. Under worker mobility, human–AI work design becomes a problem of human-capital investment, in which allocating work today shapes future skill.

title: Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings
affiliations: HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings
detail.abstract: New venture start-ups need to "survive" through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Methodology/results: Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple (≥ 3) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Managerial implications: Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

title: From Static Assessment to Adaptive Well-Being Action: An AI-Enabled, CFIR-Guided Model for Entrepreneurial and Employee Well-Being in Work 4.0 A Conceptual Framework Paper
affiliations: Quantic School of Business and Technology

detail.title: From Static Assessment to Adaptive Well-Being Action: An AI-Enabled, CFIR-Guided Model for Entrepreneurial and Employee Well-Being in Work 4.0 A Conceptual Framework Paper
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship and the broader shift toward Work 4.0 have produced a persistent, well-documented pattern of chronic stress, burnout risk, and diminished psychological well-being among founders, employee-entrepreneurs, and hybrid knowledge workers. The field has accumulated substantial descriptive evidence of this pattern but has not produced an integrated, implementable model connecting how well-being is measured, how support is delivered, and how that support is adopted and sustained in real organizational settings. This paper proposes the Global Well-Being Intelligence System (GWIS), a three-layer conceptual framework comprising adaptive, AI-enabled measurement; poly-digital micro-interventions grounded in the logic of aggregated marginal gains; and CFIR-guided implementation and sustainment. The paper’s novelty is architectural rather than componential: each layer draws on an established literature, but assessment, intervention, and implementation science have not previously been integrated into a single, recursive model purpose-built for entrepreneurial and employee well-being in Work 4.0. Rather than claiming empirical effects, the paper offers a design-science rationale, a small set of distinct and testable propositions, and a staged research agenda for future validation. It builds on the author’s prior work on AI-driven reconstruction of legacy psychometric instruments and on the published poly-digital and aggregation-of-marginal-gains literature in digital mental health. The paper closes with stakeholder implications and a roadmap for the empirical studies required to test the model, with detailed supporting tables provided as supplementary appendices.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and automation technologies has intensified the volume, velocity, and variety of data generated within IT-intensive organizations, simultaneously heightening regulatory scrutiny across global jurisdictions. This paper proposes a comprehensive, enterprise-wide Information Governance (IG) framework for organizations operating in the IT Automation and Compliance sector. Employing a systematic literature review methodology, the study synthesizes peer-reviewed scholarship, regulatory analysis, and industry research to examine the risks posed by unmanaged "dark data," the legal obligations arising from electronic discovery mandates, and the emerging governance challenges introduced by agentic AI systems. The paper argues that organizations must evolve beyond reactive Records Management (RM) toward a strategic IG super-discipline that integrates legal compliance, cybersecurity, data quality assurance, and AI ethics. A phased implementation roadmap is proposed, encompassing dark data remediation, Master Data Management (MDM), Zero Trust security architecture, and alignment with the EU AI Act, GDPR, and CCPA. Key performance indicators are identified to measure program efficacy and demonstrate return on investment to executive stakeholders. Findings indicate that robust IG is not merely a compliance function but a foundational prerequisite for responsible AI innovation, organizational resilience, and long-term competitive advantage in the digital economy.

detail.title: Not All that can be Automated should be Automated -strategic Minimalism as a Disciplined and Ethically Grounded Approach to AI Adoption

publicationDetails.detailsText: Business Ethics and Leadership, volume 9, issue 4, 2025[10.61093/bel.9(4).57-66.2025]

detail.abstract: As organizations accelerate the adoption and use of artificial intelligence, a common misconception arises that equates automation with progress and strategic necessity. This paper argues that not all that can be automated should be automated. It introduces Strategic Minimalism, a disciplined and ethically grounded approach to AI adoption that values purpose, proportionality, and prudence over speed and scale. Drawing on bounded rationality, virtue ethics, and frugal innovation, the study reframes technological restraint as a form of higher intelligence and responsible governance. Methodologically, the framework emerges from a structured conceptual synthesis and abductive reasoning process: the three traditions are integrated into two core dimensions (automation intensity and retained human judgment), whose intersection yields four strategic quadrants (Virtuous Minimalism, Balanced Synergy, Automation Excess, and Performative Minimalism). The framework is then conceptually stress-tested against rival explanations and boundary conditions to ensure internal coherence and analytic validity. By classifying automation into necessary, excessive, and performative types, the paper advances Responsible AI scholarship by identifying restraint as a strategic virtue that strengthens accountability, human oversight, and organizational resilience. Ultimately, it contends that in the age of intelligent machines, leadership wisdom lies not in automating more, but in knowing precisely when and why to stop.

detail.abstract:
Public confidence in higher education has declined even as the workforce value of postsecondary credentials has remained comparatively durable, a divergence that calls for treating institutional trust as a governance variable in its own right rather than as a byproduct of performance or a synonym for reputation. Building on the Convergent University Framework introduced in the first paper of this series — which positioned institutional trust as a partial mediator between governance and institutional performance — this paper develops the conceptual architecture of institutional trust itself.

The paper distinguishes trust from confidence, reputation, and satisfaction, and specifies the Institutional Trust Index (ITI) as a single construct expressed across five constituency-specific dimensions: Faculty Shared Governance Trust, Student ROI Confidence, Trustee Fiduciary Confidence, Philanthropic and Donor Stewardship Confidence, and Community Social License to Operate. It articulates the conceptual boundaries that distinguish these dimensions while noting that they are theorized as distinguishable but not necessarily independent. The paper then interprets the standing level of institutional trust as an accumulated stock — Trust Capital when high, Trust Debt when depleted — distinguishing the stock from the governance flows that raise or lower it, and treating the accounting vocabulary as interpretive metaphor rather than literal measurement. It specifies trust production as the governance processes through which institutional trust is accumulated, preserved, or depleted, and links the resulting trust stock to institutional resilience.

As a conceptual and measurement-development paper, this study presents no survey instrument, scoring scheme, or validated scale, and makes no reliability, validity, or causal claims. It establishes definitions, dimensional architecture, and the stock interpretation of trust, and identifies a measurement-development agenda — including the unresolved empirical relationship between trust and constituent-facing confidence — for future work. Empirical estimation, instrument validation, and causal assessment are reserved for later papers in the series, with application to public land-grant institutions and empirical testing addressed in the third and fourth installments respectively.

detail.title: The Mandatory-Directory Dilemma: Dialectics of an Odyssey through the Conundrum of Pre-arbitral Procedures to Decipher its Nature
detail.abstract: With the increasing number of cases and growing burden over the courts throughout the world, 'Alternative dispute redressal methods' have come as a life saver for both the judicial system and the parties in dispute. Resolution of disputes even before invocation of arbitration is both time saving and financially viable option for the parties. Promoting pre-arbitral procedures with minimum judicial intervention has been prioritized by the governments. While there is no dispute regarding the need and effectiveness of these alternative dispute redressal methods, there is ample scope for debate regarding the 'mandatoriness' of the pre-arbitral procedures. Indian Courts have differed in their views regarding this matter through various judgements with no common consensus till date. In multiple cases 'Tribunal v. Claim Test' has been used to determine whether the pre-arbitral procedures are mandatory or directory. This paper is the brainchild of a doctrinal attempt to understand the prelude of pre-arbitral MTDR ('Multi-tiered Dispute Resolution') in the melodrama of arbitration with all its nuances through the light and shades of various case laws and a try to decipher the riddle of ambiguity regarding the 'mandatoriness' of these pre-arbitral procedures.

detail.abstract: Multinational enterprises (MNEs) navigating fragmented transnational regulatory regimes face a structural trilemma: doctrinal legal mapping remains jurisdictionally siloed, socio legal empiricism lacks operational specificity, and RegTech platforms cannot synthesise conflicting geopolitical signals into defensible compliance architectures. This paper introduces the Strategic Compliance Synthesis Model (SCSM), a sequential mixed methods framework engineered for the rigours of International Business Law (IBL) and grounded in Global South epistemology. The SCSM bridges this integration gap by fusing epistemic pluralism with hard-law conflict resolution mechanisms. It introduces five novel operational metrics: (1) a Regulatory Fragmentation Index (RFI) quantifying doctrinal divergence; (2) an Extraterritorial Conflict Coefficient (ECC) addressing “impossible compliance” scenarios triggered by overlapping jurisdictional assertions and Blocking Statutes; (3) an Institutional Capacity Modifier (ICM) calibrated for Global South enforcement realities; (4) a Treaty Conflict and ISDS Vulnerability Coefficient; and (5) a Multi Directional Compliance Posture typology adjusted for Power Asymmetry, enabling differential architectural responses for North-South, South-South, and South-North regulatory relationships. Crucially, the model confronts the theoretical and practical tensions inherent in transnational compliance. It treats Investor State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) not as a normative governance ideal, but as a de facto structural risk; this transparency empowers MNEs to make accountable, board level choices between treaty based litigation exposure and legitimate host state regulatory autonomy, safeguarded by mandatory human rights due diligence aligned with the UN Guiding Principles (UNGPs) and, where applicable, regional mHRDD regimes (EU CSDDD, LkSG). To resolve the “impossible compliance” dilemmas flagged by the ECC, the SCSM mandates a strict Hierarchy of Conflict Resolution prioritising applicable treaty overrides (consistent with VCLT Article 30), then UNGP based human rights baselines, and finally a documented ‘geopolitical compliance exception’ approved at board level, with full audit trail. This hierarchy does not eliminate legal conflict but renders the MNE’s choice transparent and accountable. Furthermore, the paper explicitly addresses the resource intensity paradox of Global South methodologies, proposing modular deployment and academic practitioner consortium pathways to democratise access beyond highly resourced enterprises. By embedding WTO national security exceptions (including the self-judging nature of GATT Article XXI), extraterritorial anti-corruption regimes, and transnational supply chain liability into a unified blueprint, the SCSM provides general counsel, compliance strategists, and policymakers with a geopolitically resilient, ethically accountable methodology for transnational regulatory integration. All metrics are accompanied by a validation protocol (inter coder reliability κ≥0.80, criterion validity Pearson’s r≥0.70) and a planned open-source Transparency Registry.

title: The Epistemic Alibi: Opacity, Delegation, and the Structural Erosion of Dignity in AI-Mediated Decisions.

detail.title: The Epistemic Alibi: Opacity, Delegation, and the Structural Erosion of Dignity in AI-Mediated Decisions.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
When AI-generated judgment operates at a complexity that systematically exceeds the human subject's capacity to verify it, something beyond accountability is at stake. The Axiomatic Theory of Tragic Subjecthood (ATTS) has established that delegation does not sever the ontological connection between a normative subject and the space of losses opened by its decision (T1), and that concealing this connection undermines legitimacy (S6, S7). These results concern the visibility of responsibility. This article addresses a different problem: not whether the bearer is visible, but whether the decision can remain the bearer's own when its inferential grounds are structurally inaccessible.
The central claim is this: structural opacity in AI systems produces a condition — the epistemic alibi — that is distinct from the algorithmic alibi, the moral crumple zone (Elish 2019), and the responsibility gap (Matthias 2004). The algorithmic alibi conceals the bearer. The epistemic alibi does not: it erodes the ontological condition of dignity under A10, which holds that dignity is the capacity to bear the irreversible consequences of one's own choices. Own in A10 is an agentive predicate, not a causal one. The agentive condition requires evaluative access to inferential grounds — grounded independently through hierarchical theories of autonomy (Frankfurt 1971; Christman 1991, 2009).
The article operationalises structural opacity through a Verification Capacity Ladder (L1–L4), establishes L3 (interpretable reconstruction) as the minimum threshold for dignity under A10, and explains why post-hoc approximation methods cannot satisfy it. Three governance criteria follow: the verification floor, the interpretability threshold, and the dignity-preserving deployment test. These are applied to COMPAS and mapped onto GDPR Article 22 and EU AI Act requirements. The article also addresses the tragic trade-off between epistemic alibi and the risk of unaided human judgment error, locating it as a structural tragic tension — irreducible by optimisation — through the Axiom of Tragedy (A6). The falsification condition is stated explicitly: the argument would be defeated by a demonstration that structural inaccessibility of inferential grounds is compatible with full dignity under A10.

title: The Boutique of the Self: Niche-Hood, Sugar-Capital, and the Influencer as Tamagotchi in Late Platform Capitalism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Boutique of the Self: Niche-Hood, Sugar-Capital, and the Influencer as Tamagotchi in Late Platform Capitalism
detail.abstract: There is a particular tone of voice — bright, vaguely conspiratorial, pedagogically intimate — in which contemporary platforms inform a young woman that she is, in fact, unique. It is the tone of the lecture advertised in the first document under review here, a popular online seminar promising to explain "Нишевость: как капитализм научился продавать индивидуальность" — Nichehood: how capitalism learned to sell individuality — and to show "how 'niche-ness' makes everyone the same," positioned explicitly against Thorstein Veblen's Theory of the Leisure Class and the sociology of culture more broadly (Правое полушарие Интроверта, n.d.). The very existence of such a lecture, marketed through the affectively saturated rhetoric of demystification — free, no registration, the secret is finally being told — is itself the primary exhibit in the case this essay wishes to build. We are dealing with a closed loop: capitalism manufactures the desire for distinction, monetizes the discourse that explains how capitalism manufactures the desire for distinction, and then monetizes the audience's relief at having been let in on the joke. Nobody escapes the loop by understanding it; understanding the loop is simply the loop's newest product line.

title: CFD-Based Optimization of Key Design Parameters for Peak Temperature Control and Storage Capacity Enhancement in CAES Roadway Caverns​
affiliations: Hunan University of Technology, Hunan University of Technology, Hunan University of Technology and Hunan University of Technology

detail.title: CFD-Based Optimization of Key Design Parameters for Peak Temperature Control and Storage Capacity Enhancement in CAES Roadway Caverns​
detail.abstract: Compressed air energy storage (CAES) in abandoned mine roadway caverns faces charging challenges: localized high-temperature accumulation, non-uniform temperature distribution, and limited storage capacity. This study uses CFD simulations incorporating transient flow, conjugate heat transfer, and real-gas properties. Five key design parameters (inlet air temperature, charging mass flow rate, initial operating pressure, inlet pipe diameter, and cavern aspect ratio) are systematically investigated. Constant-mass-flow and variable-mass-flow charging strategies are compared. Results show that lowering inlet temperature, extending charging duration, and reducing inlet diameter enhance storage capacity but poorly suppress localized high temperatures, failing to eliminate extreme hazards. Increasing initial operating pressure (4–6 MPa recommended) significantly suppresses high temperatures and thermal stratification, although excessive pressure reduces storage capacity. Short-and-wide caverns (aspect ratio 4.5) completely avoid extreme local temperatures, achieve uniform temperature distribution, and slightly improve storage capacity – the optimal geometry. High mass flow rate (750 kg/s) induces cavern-wide circulating flow and intense turbulent mixing, outperforming low-flow charging. The optimized variable-mass-flow strategy (Case 4: low-flow initiation, stepped high-flow charging, intermittent idle periods) achieves the best performance, with a maximum temperature of 378.1 K and cumulative injected air mass of 3.10 kt, realizing synergistic optimization of temperature-rise suppression and storage capacity enhancement. This study provides theoretical guidance for the safe and efficient design and operation of CAES roadway caverns.

title: The Black Iceberg: A Diagnostic Framework for Epistemic Collapse and Moral Desynchronization

detail.title: The Black Iceberg: A Diagnostic Framework for Epistemic Collapse and Moral Desynchronization
detail.abstract: Why do societies that the standard instruments of crisis analysis judge to be alike go on to follow radically different paths? Weimar Germany and the United States met the same Depression with comparable measures of structural stress and opposite fates; the late Soviet Union and present-day Russia share a moral configuration yet travel in opposite epistemic directions. This work offers a diagnostic framework built to discriminate where the standard instruments cannot. Its central concept is the Black Iceberg: the moment at which a society's organizing seeming truth, long held while quietly disbelieved, collapses into mutual recognition through a cascade of latent knowledge into common knowledge. We distinguish two types of this eventone triggered from without by an external shock, one from within by the slow exhaustion of a society's carriers of functional holding, the depleted pooland we read each society through two independent instruments applied in parallel: a Moral Plane with four quadrants of conscience, and a four-position Reality Matrix understood in the Platonic and Aristotelian senses of the real and the true. The framework is demonstrated across four cases-Weimar, the late Soviet Union, post-Soviet Russia, and communist Chinaand yields eleven further, falsifiable implications. For each central claim we state the conditions under which it would be refuted, turning the framework from a universal explanation into a falsifiable one. Its support here is retrospective; the decisive test lies in the prospective application the work invites.

detail.abstract: This research paper provides a comprehensive, policy-oriented analysis of the operational mechanisms driving the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). As the largest free trade area by number of participating countries since the formation of the World Trade Organization, the AfCFTA holds the potential to reshape continental supply chains, foster robust industrialization, and lift over 30 million Africans out of extreme poverty. However, full implementation hinges on the complex resolution of three structural vectors: the strategic sequencing of tariff phaseouts, the optimization and standardization of Rules of Origin (RoO), and the deployment of systematic frameworks for the elimination of Non-Tariff Barriers (NTBs). This paper develops an operational matrix for tracking compliance, outlines the mathematical trade realities underlying competitive deflection, and advances institutional frameworks to safeguard trade facilitation. By providing empirical pathways and granular policy recommendations, this work serves as an actionable framework for public and private sector leadership seeking to realize the Pan-African economic renaissance.

detail.abstract: The study examined the potential for small and medium-sized enterprises in Delta state and by extension Nigeria, to attract more foreign direct investment. The study was motivated by the need to solve the problems associated with foreign direct investment in Delta State. The study was guided by three key objectives, and it was from these that appropriate research questions and hypotheses were derived. Survey design was used for this investigation. The 200 staff members of the chosen SMEs in Delta State were chosen using a simple random selection approach. Using the Cochran (1977) statistical technique, a sample size of 120 respondents was picked from a population of 200 recruited from the management, middle, and lower cadre of the chosen manufacturing enterprises. The study confirmed that SMEs in Delta State have the potential to draw foreign direct investment. Additionally, it was revealed that factors like the lowering of labour movement from rural to urban regions by fair income distribution promote foreign direct investment in Delta State. The study also discovered that SMEs in Delta State face considerable challenges in attracting foreign direct investment. The study, therefore recommended the promotion of policies that will support SMEs in Delta State.

title: Technological Lock-in Due to Environmental Taxation
affiliations: and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Technological Lock-in Due to Environmental Taxation
detail.abstract: We study how a committed emission tax shapes the adoption of successively cleaner technologies that arrive over time under uncertainty. Environmental policy increasingly relies on carbon prices that are set in advance and held fixed while such technologies emerge, and we show that this very commitment can lock firms into an inferior technology. In a two-period model, technologies differ only in their fixed adoption cost and emission rate; a regulator commits to a uniform tax and firms choose whether and when to adopt. Under monopoly with perfect foresight, the regulator can induce adoption of the cleanest technology but is sometimes better off not doing so, when its environmental gain falls short of the adoption cost. Under imperfect information the commitment cuts both ways: under-estimating the likelihood of the cleanest technology sets the tax too low, so the firm waits and stalls on its initial technology, whereas over-estimating it sets the tax so high that adoption is blocked altogether. The misperception distorts only the first-period adoption margin, over a benefit–cost band whose width scales with the size of the error. Competition sharpens the trade-off. With symmetric firms a strictly higher tax is needed to trigger adoption, so competition unambiguously raises the cost of inducing a green transition - even though the welfare ranking of monopoly and duopoly remains ambiguous. When one firm enjoys an adoption-cost advantage, it eases adoption for its rival and relaxes the regulator’s problem, pointing to a role for targeted first-adopter support alongside the tax.

title: AI Adoption, Carbon Intensity, and Rebound Effect: Evidence from China
affiliations: and

detail.title: AI Adoption, Carbon Intensity, and Rebound Effect: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between AI adoption and carbon emission intensity. Using micro-level data from Chinese firms, we find that carbon intensity decreases following the adoption of AI. The effect is particularly pronounced among large firms, those headquartered in AI hubs, and those in high-carbon intensity sectors. We investigate several mechanisms and find that AI adoption is also associated with increases in energy management processes, green innovation, inventory efficiency, overall productivity, and the share of specialized labor. We find that AI-induced carbon reductions are subject to a large rebound effect of approximately 70%.

title: Multi-Plant Firms, Variable Capacity Utilization, and the Aggregate Hours Elasticity
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - Economics Department, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Universidad Carlos III de Madrid

detail.title: Multi-Plant Firms, Variable Capacity Utilization, and the Aggregate Hours Elasticity

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: International Finance Discussion Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: We develop a business cycle model with perfectly competitive product and labor markets in which production requires a minimum labor input, generating endogenous capacity utilization. The aggregate production function is kinked, featuring constant returns to scale below capacity—typically in recessions—and decreasing returns at capacity in expansions. Motivated by new empirical evidence that narratively identified labor tax shocks have significantly larger effects on hours and output when capacity utilization is below trend, we calibrate the model to U.S. data and show that the aggregate hours elasticity is higher in recessions, differing markedly from the micro elasticity implied by preferences.
